paragraphs: The paper analyzes a linear perceptron learning to imitate a teacher perceptron. The learner has N inputs and receives a number of binary training examples proportional to N. Generalization is measured by agreement with the teacher across all possible binary inputs, providing a precisely defined setting for studying how learning develops over time.

The authors solve the dynamics analytically and identify a transition when the ratio of examples to inputs reaches one. At this threshold, the system moves from imperfect to perfect generalization. Away from the threshold, performance approaches its eventual value exponentially, but the approach becomes increasingly slow near the transition.

Exactly at the critical ratio, the approach to perfect generalization follows a power law instead. Noise also degrades generalization, with a particularly strong effect just above the threshold. These findings connect the amount of training data with both the final quality of learning and the time needed to reach it, showing that behavior near the transition is especially delicate.
summary.tldr: A solvable teacher–learner model reveals a generalization threshold accompanied by slow learning and heightened sensitivity to noise.

title: Dynamics of Generalization in Linear Perceptrons

paragraphs: The paper proposes a network for organizing fragmented image contours into groups. Its input is a collection of contour fragments, and its output assigns those fragments to separate groups while giving each group a saliency measure. This addresses an early visual problem: deciding which pieces of an image belong together before identifying particular objects.

Grouping depends on overall length and curvature. The network gives priority to forming salient groups, potentially leaving decisions about less salient structures unresolved. This makes geometric prominence part of the computation itself, reflecting the idea that some combinations of contours should emerge more readily than others during visual organization.

The authors decompose the overall optimization into independent optimal pairing problems at individual nodes. That decomposition lets the computation map onto a uniform network of simple elements connected locally. The approach matters because it connects a whole-image grouping objective with local operations, offering a computational route from fragmented contours to structures that may support segmentation and subsequent object recognition.
summary.tldr: A locally connected network groups contour fragments by solving pairing problems guided by length, curvature, and saliency.

title: Grouping Contours by Iterated Pairing Network

abstract: We present an algorithm for the training of feedforward and recur(cid:173) rent neural networks. It detects internal representation conflicts and uses these conflicts in a constructive manner to add new neu(cid:173) rons to the network . The advantages are twofold: (1) starting with a small network neurons are only allocated when required; (2) by detecting and resolving internal conflicts at an early stage learning time is reduced. Empirical results on two real-world problems sub(cid:173) stantiate the faster learning speed; when applied to the training of a recurrent network on a well researched sequence recognition task (the Reber grammar), training times are significantly less than previously reported .

paragraphs: The paper presents a training algorithm that grows a neural network when its internal representations develop conflicts. It applies to both feedforward and recurrent networks. Training begins with a small network, and the algorithm uses detected conflicts as a reason to introduce additional neurons. Network construction is therefore tied directly to difficulties encountered during learning.

The authors identify two benefits of this approach. First, neurons are allocated only when they are required, allowing training to begin without a large network. Second, resolving conflicts early reduces learning time. The important connection is between representation and architecture: evidence that the current internal organization is inadequate guides the addition of capacity.

Empirical results on two real-world problems support the claim of faster learning. The authors also report substantially shorter training times than previously reported for a recurrent network learning the Reber grammar, a sequence recognition task. Together, these findings support conflict detection as both a guide to network growth and a way to accelerate training on the examined problems.
summary.tldr: Detecting internal representation conflicts guides the addition of neurons and accelerates training in the reported tasks.

title: Constructive Learning Using Internal Representation Conflicts

abstract: Inference is a key component in learning probabilistic models from par(cid:173) tially observable data. When learning temporal models, each of the many inference phases requires a traversal over an entire long data se(cid:173) quence; furthermore, the data structures manipulated are exponentially large, making this process computationally expensive. In [2], we describe an approximate inference algorithm for monitoring stochastic processes, and prove bounds on its approximation error. In this paper, we apply this algorithm as an approximate forward propagation step in an EM algorithm for learning temporal Bayesian networks. We provide a related approxi(cid:173) mation for the backward step, and prove error bounds for the combined algorithm. We show empirically that, for a real-life domain, EM using our inference algorithm is much faster than EM using exact inference, with almost no degradation in quality of the learned model. We extend our analysis to the online learning task, showing a bound on the error resulting from restricting attention to a small window of observations. We present an online EM learning algorithm for dynamic systems, and show that it learns much faster than standard offline EM.

paragraphs: Learning a temporal probabilistic model from partially observed data repeatedly requires inference about hidden quantities. This can be expensive because inference traverses long observation sequences and manipulates data structures that grow exponentially. The paper addresses this computational burden within expectation-maximization, or EM, for temporal Bayesian networks.

The authors use a previously developed approximate monitoring algorithm for EM's forward propagation step and introduce a related approximation for the backward step. They prove error bounds for the combined inference procedure. In a real-world application, EM with this approximate inference runs much faster than EM with exact inference, with almost no loss in learned-model quality. That quality finding is empirical and specific to the reported application.

The paper also considers online learning, where updates can use a limited observation window. It bounds the error introduced by restricting attention to that window and presents an online EM algorithm for dynamic systems. The reported online method learns much faster than standard offline EM. Together, the results connect computational savings to explicit analysis of the approximations involved.
summary.tldr: Approximate forward and backward inference makes temporal-model EM faster, with error bounds and little empirical loss in model quality.

title: Approximate Learning of Dynamic Models

abstract: A Bayes network based classifier for distinguishing terrestrial rocks from meteorites is implemented onboard the Nomad robot. Equipped with a camera, spectrometer and eddy current sensor, this robot searched the ice sheets of Antarctica and autonomously made the first robotic identification of a meteorite, in January 2000 at the Elephant Moraine. This paper discusses rock classification from a robotic platform, and describes the system onboard Nomad.
originalAbstract: A Bayes network based classifier for distinguishing terrestrial rocks from meteorites is implemented onboard the Nomad robot. Equipped with a camera, spectrometer and eddy current sensor, this robot searched the ice sheets of Antarctica and autonomously made the first robotic identification of a meteorite, in January 2000 at the Elephant Moraine. This paper discusses rock classification from a robotic platform, and describes the system onboard Nomad.

paragraphs: The paper describes an onboard classification system that helps a robot distinguish meteorites from terrestrial rocks. Its classifier uses a Bayesian network and runs on Nomad, a robot deployed to search Antarctic ice sheets. The learning-related task is concrete: deciding whether a rock encountered during the search belongs to the meteorite category.

Nomad carries a camera, a spectrometer, and an eddy current sensor. These instruments form the sensing equipment of the robotic platform described in the paper. The important system-level connection is that rock classification operates onboard the searching robot, placing the decision process in the same platform that encounters and examines candidate objects.

During its Antarctic search, Nomad autonomously identified a meteorite at Elephant Moraine. The abstract describes this as the first robotic identification of a meteorite. That finding establishes a successful autonomous identification in the field, while the paper explains the onboard system and the problem of classifying rocks from a robotic platform. Its contribution is a working application of Bayesian-network classification to physical exploration.
summary.tldr: Nomad used an onboard Bayesian-network classifier during an Antarctic search that achieved an autonomous meteorite identification.

title: Bayes Networks on Ice: Robotic Search for Antarctic Meteorites

abstract: The PageRank algorithm, used in the Google search engine, greatly improves the results of Web search by taking into account the link structure of the Web. PageRank assigns to a page a score propor- tional to the number of times a random surfer would visit that page, if it surfed indefinitely from page to page, following all outlinks from a page with equal probability. We propose to improve Page- Rank by using a more intelligent surfer, one that is guided by a probabilistic model of the relevance of a page to a query. Efficient execution of our algorithm at query time is made possible by pre- computing at crawl time (and thus once for all queries) the neces- sary terms. Experiments on two large subsets of the Web indicate that our algorithm significantly outperforms PageRank in the (hu- man-rated) quality of the pages returned, while remaining efficient enough to be used in today’s large search engines.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a query-aware extension of PageRank that combines web links with page content. In the described PageRank model, a hypothetical surfer follows outgoing links with equal probability, and pages receive scores based on long-run visitation. This uses link structure without making those link choices depend on relevance to a particular query.

The proposed intelligent surfer instead follows a probabilistic model of page relevance. Query relevance therefore influences the surfing process used to assign importance. To keep execution efficient when a query arrives, the algorithm precomputes the necessary terms during crawling, with that computation shared across queries.

Experiments on two large web subsets show significantly better human-rated quality of returned pages than PageRank. The authors also report efficiency sufficient for large search engines in the setting they discuss. The contribution couples a ranking change with a computational strategy: content guides the link-based relevance model, while precomputation makes the query-dependent calculation practical. The quality improvement is an empirical result from those two evaluated subsets.
summary.tldr: A relevance-guided PageRank variant improves human-rated search quality on two web subsets while using precomputation to remain efficient.

title: The Intelligent surfer: Probabilistic Combination of Link and Content Information in PageRank

abstract: This paper applies fast sparse multidimensional scaling (MDS) to a large graph of music similarity, with 267K vertices that represent artists, al- bums, and tracks; and 3.22M edges that represent similarity between those entities. Once vertices are assigned locations in a Euclidean space, the locations can be used to browse music and to generate playlists. MDS on very large sparse graphs can be effectively performed by a family of algorithms called Rectangular Dijsktra (RD) MDS algorithms. These RD algorithms operate on a dense rectangular slice of the distance matrix, created by calling Dijsktra a constant number of times. Two RD algorithms are compared: Landmark MDS, which uses the Nystr(cid:246)m ap- proximation to perform MDS; and a new algorithm called Fast Sparse Embedding, which uses FastMap. These algorithms compare favorably to Laplacian Eigenmaps, both in terms of speed and embedding quality.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to turn a large music-similarity graph into locations in Euclidean space. Its graph contains 267,000 vertices for artists, albums, and tracks, connected by 3.22 million similarity edges. Once these entities have spatial coordinates, those locations can support music browsing and playlist generation.

The authors use a family of sparse multidimensional scaling methods called Rectangular Dijkstra algorithms. These methods operate on a dense rectangular portion of the distance matrix, constructed by running Dijkstra’s algorithm a constant number of times. The computation thus centers on a selected distance representation rather than requiring the entire square distance matrix as its working input.

The paper compares Landmark MDS, which uses the Nyström approximation, with a new Fast Sparse Embedding algorithm based on FastMap. Both compare favorably with Laplacian Eigenmaps in speed and embedding quality. The stated findings support this family of methods for embedding very large sparse graphs, with the music graph providing a concrete application where the resulting geometry has practical uses.
summary.tldr: Sparse MDS methods embed a large music-similarity graph and compare favorably with Laplacian Eigenmaps in speed and embedding quality.

title: Fast Embedding of Sparse Similarity Graphs

abstract: Recent developments in grid-based and point-based approximation algo- rithms for POMDPs have greatly improved the tractability of POMDP planning. These approaches operate on sets of belief points by individ- ually learning a value function for each point. In reality, belief points exist in a highly-structured metric simplex, but current POMDP algo- rithms do not exploit this property. This paper presents a new metric-tree algorithm which can be used in the context of POMDP planning to sort belief points spatially, and then perform fast value function updates over groups of points. We present results showing that this approach can re- duce computation in point-based POMDP algorithms for a wide range of problems.
originalAbstract: Recent developments in grid-based and point-based approximation algo- rithms for POMDPs have greatly improved the tractability of POMDP planning. These approaches operate on sets of belief points by individ- ually learning a value function for each point. In reality, belief points exist in a highly-structured metric simplex, but current POMDP algo- rithms do not exploit this property. This paper presents a new metric-tree algorithm which can be used in the context of POMDP planning to sort belief points spatially, and then perform fast value function updates over groups of points. We present results showing that this approach can re- duce computation in point-based POMDP algorithms for a wide range of problems.

paragraphs: Planning in a partially observable Markov decision process must account for uncertainty about the system’s state. Point-based and grid-based approximations make this planning more tractable by working with selected belief points. The approaches discussed in the paper learn value information for those points individually, leaving an opportunity to share computation across the collection.

The paper’s central observation is that belief points occupy a structured geometric space with meaningful distances. It introduces a metric-tree algorithm that organizes the points spatially. Once grouped through that structure, points can receive fast value-function updates together, rather than requiring all update work to be carried out separately for each point.

The reported results show that this organization can reduce computation across a wide range of point-based planning problems. The significance lies in exploiting structure already present in the representation of uncertainty. The method improves the computational handling of belief points within approximate POMDP planning, with the reported benefit expressed as reduced work rather than a universal speed guarantee.
summary.tldr: A metric tree groups belief points spatially so point-based POMDP planners can update values with less computation.

title: Applying Metric-Trees to Belief-Point POMDPs

abstract: Most machine learning researchers perform quantitative experiments to estimate generalization error and compare algorithm performances. In order to draw statistically convincing conclusions, it is important to esti- mate the uncertainty of such estimates. This paper studies the estimation of uncertainty around the K-fold cross-validation estimator. The main theorem shows that there exists no universal unbiased estimator of the variance of K-fold cross-validation. An analysis based on the eigende- composition of the covariance matrix of errors helps to better understand the nature of the problem and shows that naive estimators may grossly underestimate variance, as con£rmed by numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Cross-validation is commonly used to estimate prediction error and compare learning algorithms. Those comparisons also require an account of uncertainty: an estimated error alone does not say how much it might vary. This paper investigates the variance of the K-fold cross-validation estimator and the possibility of estimating that variance without bias.

The main theorem rules out a universal unbiased estimator of this variance. The word universal is central to the result: it concerns an estimator that would be unbiased across the full general setting. The theorem places a fundamental restriction on how broadly a variance estimation method can provide that guarantee.

To explain the difficulty, the authors analyze the covariance matrix of errors through its eigendecomposition. This exposes how the errors vary together and shows that naive variance estimators can substantially understate uncertainty. Numerical experiments confirm that possibility. The practical implication is that apparently precise cross-validation comparisons can rest on uncertainty estimates that are too small.
summary.tldr: No universal unbiased variance estimator exists for K-fold cross-validation, and naive estimates can severely understate uncertainty.

title: No Unbiased Estimator of the Variance of K-Fold Cross-Validation

abstract: We present a method for learning a low-dimensional representation which is shared across a set of multiple related tasks. The method builds upon the well- known 1-norm regularization problem using a new regularizer which controls the number of learned features common for all the tasks. We show that this problem is equivalent to a convex optimization problem and develop an iterative algorithm for solving it. The algorithm has a simple interpretation: it alternately performs a supervised and an unsupervised step, where in the latter step we learn common- across-tasks representations and in the former step we learn task-speciﬁc functions using these representations. We report experiments on a simulated and a real data set which demonstrate that the proposed method dramatically improves the per- formance relative to learning each task independently. Our algorithm can also be used, as a special case, to simply select – not learn – a few common features across the tasks.

paragraphs: Related prediction tasks may benefit from a common compact representation of their inputs. This paper develops a method for learning that representation jointly across tasks. It builds on 1-norm regularization with a new regularizer that controls how many learned features are shared, encouraging the tasks to rely on a limited common feature set.

The authors show that the formulation is equivalent to a convex optimization problem and give an iterative solution method. The algorithm alternates between learning a shared representation in an unsupervised step and learning task-specific prediction functions in a supervised step. This separates what the tasks have in common from how each task uses that common representation.

Experiments on simulated and real data show dramatic improvements relative to learning each task independently. These findings support joint feature learning for the related tasks tested. The same algorithm also includes a simpler special case that selects a few existing features shared across tasks, making the framework applicable to both representation learning and common feature selection.
summary.tldr: A convex formulation learns a small shared feature representation that substantially improves the tested tasks over independent learning.

title: Multi-Task Feature Learning

abstract: In this paper we focus on the issue of normalization of the affinity matrix in spectral clustering. We show that the difference between N-cuts and Ratio-cuts is in the error measure being used (relative-entropy versus L1 norm) in finding the closest doubly-stochastic matrix to the input affinity matrix. We then develop a scheme for finding the optimal, under Frobenius norm, doubly-stochastic approximation using Von-Neumann's successive projections lemma. The new normalization scheme is simple and efficient and provides superior clustering performance over many of the standardized tests.
originalAbstract: In this paper we focus on the issue of normalization of the affinity matrix in spectral clustering. We show that the difference between N-cuts and Ratio-cuts is in the error measure being used (relative-entropy versus L1 norm) in finding the closest doubly-stochastic matrix to the input affinity matrix. We then develop a scheme for finding the optimal, under Frobenius norm, doubly-stochastic approximation using Von-Neumann's successive projections lemma. The new normalization scheme is simple and efficient and provides superior clustering performance over many of the standardized tests.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering uses an affinity matrix to represent similarities between data points, making the treatment of that matrix an important part of the method. This paper focuses on normalization. It interprets established clustering approaches through the problem of finding a nearby doubly stochastic matrix, whose rows and columns each sum to one.

Within this interpretation, the authors show that N-cuts and Ratio-cuts differ in how they measure approximation error: relative entropy for one and the L1 norm for the other. This provides a common framework for understanding their normalization choices. It also makes the choice of error measure an explicit design decision.

The paper then develops a normalization procedure that finds the optimal doubly stochastic approximation under the Frobenius norm. The construction uses Von Neumann's successive projections lemma. The authors describe the procedure as simple and efficient, and report superior clustering performance on many standardized tests. Its contribution combines an explanation of existing methods with a concrete alternative whose empirical benefits are demonstrated across those tests.
summary.tldr: A common view of spectral-clustering normalization leads to a Frobenius-optimal doubly stochastic approximation with improved results on many tests.

title: Doubly Stochastic Normalization for Spectral Clustering

abstract: We study learning formulations with non-convex regularizaton that are natural for sparse linear models. There are two approaches to this problem: (1) Heuristic methods such as gradient descent that only find a local minimum. A drawback of this approach is the lack of theoretical guarantee showing that the local minimum gives a good solution. (2) Convex relaxation such as $L_1$-regularization that solves the problem under some conditions. However it often leads to sub-optimal sparsity in reality. This paper tries to remedy the above gap between theory and practice. In particular, we investigate a multi-stage convex relaxation scheme for solving problems with non-convex regularization. Theoretically, we analyze the behavior of a resulting two-stage relaxation scheme for the capped-$L_1$ regularization. Our performance bound shows that the procedure is superior to the standard $L_1$ convex relaxation for learning sparse targets. Experiments confirm the effectiveness of this method on some simulation and real data.

(2) Convex relaxation such as $L_1$-regularization that solves the problem under some conditions. However it often leads to sub-optimal sparsity in reality. This paper tries to remedy the above gap between theory and practice. In particular, we investigate a multi-stage convex relaxation scheme for solving problems with non-convex regularization. paragraphs: Sparse linear learning seeks models that use a limited set of coefficients. Non-convex regularizers naturally express this preference, but optimizing them creates a tension. Heuristic methods can stop at local minima without guarantees of solution quality, while a convex substitute such as L1 regularization can deliver less satisfactory sparsity in practice.

The paper investigates a sequence of convex relaxations for learning with non-convex regularization. This approach uses multiple optimization stages to address the gap between tractable convex methods and the desired sparse solution. The theoretical analysis focuses specifically on a two-stage scheme for capped-L1 regularization, rather than establishing the same conclusion for every possible non-convex penalty.

For that scheme, the authors derive a performance bound showing an advantage over standard L1 convex relaxation when learning sparse targets. Experiments on simulated and real data also support the method's effectiveness. The contribution combines a theoretical comparison for a particular staged procedure with empirical evidence, giving a more grounded alternative to relying solely on an unguided local search or a single relaxation.
summary.tldr: A staged convex-relaxation approach improves the theoretical bound over standard L1 relaxation for a studied sparse-learning scheme.

title: Multi-stage Convex Relaxation for Learning with Sparse Regularization

abstract: This paper presents an approach to the visual recognition of human actions using only single images as input. The task is easy for humans but difficult for current approaches to object recognition, because action instances may be similar in terms of body pose, and often require detailed examination of relations between participating objects and body parts in order to be recognized. The proposed approach applies a two-stage interpretation procedure to each training and test image. The first stage produces accurate detection of the relevant body parts of the actor, forming a prior for the local evidence needed to be considered for identifying the action. The second stage extracts features that are ‘anchored’ to the detected body parts, and uses these features and their feature-to-part relations in order to recognize the action. The body anchored priors we propose apply to a large range of human actions. These priors allow focusing on the relevant regions and relations, thereby significantly simplifying the learning process and increasing recognition performance.

The second stage extracts features that are ‘anchored’ to the detected body parts, and uses these features and their feature-to-part relations in order to recognize the action. These priors allow focusing on the relevant regions and relations, thereby significantly simplifying the learning process and increasing recognition performance.

paragraphs: Recognizing an action in a single image can require more than identifying a person's pose. Different actions may involve similar poses, with the decisive evidence lying in relationships between objects and body parts. This paper proposes using the actor's detected body parts to guide which local visual evidence the recognition system examines.

The method applies two stages to both training and test images. First, it detects the body parts relevant to the action, establishing a prior over useful local evidence. Second, it extracts features anchored to those parts and uses both the features and their relationships to the parts for classification. The body therefore provides a spatial reference for interpreting the image.

The authors state that these priors apply across a broad range of human actions. By directing attention toward relevant regions and relationships, the approach substantially simplifies learning and improves recognition performance. The contribution is a structured way to use body localization as guidance for action recognition from a still image.
summary.tldr: Detecting body parts first helps a single-image action recognizer focus on relevant features and their relationships to the actor.

title: Using body-anchored priors for identifying actions in single images

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of finding the nearest neighbor (or one of the $R$-nearest neighbors) of a query object $q$ in a database of $n$ objects, when we can only use a comparison oracle. The comparison oracle, given two reference objects and a query object, returns the reference object most similar to the query object. The main problem we study is how to search the database for the nearest neighbor (NN) of a query, while minimizing the questions. The difficulty of this problem depends on properties of the underlying database. We show the importance of a characterization: \emph{combinatorial disorder} $D$ which defines approximate triangle inequalities on ranks. We present a lower bound of $\Omega(D\log \frac{n}{D}+D^2)$ average number of questions in the search phase for any randomized algorithm, which demonstrates the fundamental role of $D$ for worst case behavior. We develop a randomized scheme for NN retrieval in $O(D^3\log^2 n+ D\log^2 n \log\log n^{D^3})$ questions. The learning requires asking $O(n D^3\log^2 n+ D \log^2 n \log\log n^{D^3})$ questions and $O(n\log^2n/\log(2D))$ bits to store.

The contribution shows that comparison-based search can be analyzed through the database's rank structure, with both unavoidable costs and an achievable algorithm expressed in terms of that structure.
summary.tldr: Combinatorial disorder characterizes comparison-based search difficulty and guides a randomized nearest-neighbor retrieval scheme.

title: Randomized Algorithms for Comparison-based Search

abstract: We consider regularized risk minimization in a large dictionary of Reproducing kernel Hilbert Spaces (RKHSs) over which the target function has a sparse representation. This setting, commonly referred to as Sparse Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL), may be viewed as the non-parametric extension of group sparsity in linear models. While the two dominant algorithmic strands of sparse learning, namely convex relaxations using l1 norm (e.g., Lasso) and greedy methods (e.g., OMP), have both been rigorously extended for group sparsity, the sparse MKL literature has so farmainly adopted the former withmild empirical success. In this paper, we close this gap by proposing a Group-OMP based framework for sparse multiple kernel learning. Unlike l1-MKL, our approach decouples the sparsity regularizer (via a direct l0 constraint) from the smoothness regularizer (via RKHS norms) which leads to better empirical performance as well as a simpler optimization procedure that only requires a black-box single-kernel solver. The algorithmic development and empirical studies are complemented by theoretical analyses in terms of Rademacher generalization bounds and sparse recovery conditions analogous to those for OMP [27] and Group-OMP [16].

paragraphs: Sparse multiple-kernel learning seeks a predictor that uses only a small portion of a large dictionary of kernel function spaces. This paper considers the setting where the target function has such a sparse representation. It extends the greedy group orthogonal matching pursuit approach to this non-parametric learning problem.

A central design choice separates two controls that serve different purposes. A direct l0 constraint controls sparsity, while norms within the reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces control smoothness. The authors report that this separation gives better empirical performance than l1-based multiple-kernel learning and simplifies optimization. The procedure requires only a black-box solver for a single kernel.

The paper complements its algorithm and empirical studies with Rademacher generalization bounds and sparse-recovery conditions analogous to those for ordinary and group orthogonal matching pursuit. These analyses address both predictive behavior and recovery of sparse structure. The contribution expands the algorithmic options for sparse multiple-kernel learning while making the distinction between selecting function spaces and regulating their smoothness explicit.
summary.tldr: A group orthogonal matching pursuit framework separates sparsity from smoothness in multiple-kernel learning, with empirical and theoretical support.

title: Non-parametric Group Orthogonal Matching Pursuit for Sparse Learning with Multiple Kernels

abstract: The integration of excitatory inputs in dendrites is non-linear: multiple excitatory inputs can produce a local depolarization departing from the arithmetic sum of each input's response taken separately. If this depolarization is bigger than the arithmetic sum, the dendrite is spiking; if the depolarization is smaller, the dendrite is saturating. Decomposing a dendritic tree into independent dendritic spiking units greatly extends its computational capacity, as the neuron then maps onto a two layer neural network, enabling it to compute linearly non-separable Boolean functions (lnBFs). How can these lnBFs be implemented by dendritic architectures in practise? And can saturating dendrites equally expand computational capacity? To adress these questions we use a binary neuron model and Boolean algebra. First, we confirm that spiking dendrites enable a neuron to compute lnBFs using an architecture based on the disjunctive normal form (DNF). Second, we prove that saturating dendrites as well as spiking dendrites also enable a neuron to compute lnBFs using an architecture based on the conjunctive normal form (CNF). Contrary to the DNF-based architecture, a CNF-based architecture leads to a dendritic unit tuning that does not imply the neuron tuning, as has been observed experimentally. Third, we show that one cannot use a DNF-based architecture with saturating dendrites. Consequently, we show that an important family of lnBFs implemented with a CNF-architecture can require an exponential number of saturating dendritic units, whereas the same family implemented with either a DNF-architecture or a CNF-architecture always require a linear number of spiking dendritic unit. This minimization could explain why a neuron spends energetic resources to make its dendrites spike.

paragraphs: Dendrites can combine excitatory inputs nonlinearly. Spiking dendrites produce a response larger than the sum of separate inputs, while saturating dendrites produce a smaller response. Using a binary neuron model and Boolean algebra, this paper asks how these two behaviors expand the logical functions a single neuron can compute.

The authors confirm that spiking dendrites support linearly nonseparable Boolean functions through a disjunctive normal form architecture. They prove that both spiking and saturating dendrites can support such functions through conjunctive normal form. In the latter architecture, a dendritic unit's tuning need not imply the whole neuron's tuning, consistent with an experimental observation discussed in the abstract.

The architectures differ in efficiency. Saturating dendrites cannot implement the disjunctive construction, and an important function family can require exponentially many saturating units in the conjunctive construction. Spiking units need only a linear number for that family under either construction. This computational saving offers a possible explanation for spending energy on dendritic spikes, rather than establishing that biological explanation as certain.
summary.tldr: Both dendritic behaviors expand a binary neuron's computational capacity, but spiking can require exponentially fewer units for an important family of functions.

title: Spiking and saturating dendrites differentially expand single neuron computation capacity

abstract: We address the problem of estimating the ratio $\frac{q}{p}$ where $p$ is a density function and $q$ is another density, or, more generally an arbitrary function. Knowing or approximating this ratio is needed in various problems of inference and integration, in particular, when one needs to average a function with respect to one probability distribution, given a sample from another. It is often referred as {\it importance sampling} in statistical inference and is also closely related to the problem of {\it covariate shift} in transfer learning as well as to various MCMC methods. Our approach is based on reformulating the problem of estimating the ratio as an inverse problem in terms of an integral operator corresponding to a kernel, and thus reducing it to an integral equation, known as the Fredholm problem of the first kind. This formulation, combined with the techniques of regularization and kernel methods, leads to a principled kernel-based framework for constructing algorithms and for analyzing them theoretically. The resulting family of algorithms (FIRE, for Fredholm Inverse Regularized Estimator) is flexible, simple and easy to implement. We provide detailed theoretical analysis including concentration bounds and convergence rates for the Gaussian kernel for densities defined on $\R^d$ and smooth $d$-dimensional sub-manifolds of the Euclidean space. Model selection for unsupervised or semi-supervised inference is generally a difficult problem. Interestingly, it turns out that in the density ratio estimation setting, when samples from both distributions are available, there are simple completely unsupervised methods for choosing parameters. We call this model selection mechanism CD-CV for Cross-Density Cross-Validation. Finally, we show encouraging experimental results including applications to classification within the covariate shift framework.

title: Inverse Density as an Inverse Problem: the Fredholm Equation Approach

abstract: Variable screening is a fast dimension reduction technique for assisting high dimensional feature selection. As a preselection method, it selects a moderate size subset of candidate variables for further refining via feature selection to produce the final model. The performance of variable screening depends on both computational efficiency and the ability to dramatically reduce the number of variables without discarding the important ones. When the data dimension $p$ is substantially larger than the sample size $n$, variable screening becomes crucial as 1) Faster feature selection algorithms are needed; 2) Conditions guaranteeing selection consistency might fail to hold.This article studies a class of linear screening methods and establishes consistency theory for this special class. In particular, we prove the restricted diagonally dominant (RDD) condition is a necessary and sufficient condition for strong screening consistency. As concrete examples, we show two screening methods $SIS$ and $HOLP$ are both strong screening consistent (subject to additional constraints) with large probability if $n > O((\rho s + \sigma/\tau)^2\log p)$ under random designs. In addition, we relate the RDD condition to the irrepresentable condition, and highlight limitations of $SIS$.

paragraphs: Variable screening quickly reduces a large collection of variables to a manageable candidate set before more detailed feature selection. Its usefulness depends on discarding many variables without losing important ones. The paper studies this problem when the number of variables greatly exceeds the number of observations, a setting where computation and selection guarantees can both become difficult.

For a particular class of linear screening methods, the authors establish a consistency theory. Their central result states that restricted diagonal dominance, abbreviated RDD, is necessary and sufficient for strong screening consistency. This is an exact characterization within the studied class, giving the condition a stronger role than a merely sufficient recipe for success.

The paper then analyzes SIS and HOLP as concrete examples. Under random designs, additional constraints, and the stated sample-size condition, both achieve strong screening consistency with high probability. The authors also connect RDD to the irrepresentable condition and identify limitations of SIS. These results clarify when rapid screening can be theoretically justified while preserving the conditions attached to each method's guarantee.
summary.tldr: Restricted diagonal dominance exactly characterizes strong consistency for the studied linear screening class, with conditional guarantees for SIS and HOLP.

title: On the consistency theory of high dimensional variable screening

abstract: Max-product Belief Propagation (BP) is a popular message-passing algorithm for computing a Maximum-A-Posteriori (MAP) assignment over a distribution represented by a Graphical Model (GM). It has been shown that BP can solve a number of combinatorial optimization problems including minimum weight matching, shortest path, network flow and vertex cover under the following common assumption: the respective Linear Programming (LP) relaxation is tight, i.e., no integrality gap is present. However, when LP shows an integrality gap, no model has been known which can be solved systematically via sequential applications of BP. In this paper, we develop the first such algorithm, coined Blossom-BP, for solving the minimum weight matching problem over arbitrary graphs. Each step of the sequential algorithm requires applying BP over a modified graph constructed by contractions and expansions of blossoms, i.e., odd sets of vertices. Our scheme guarantees termination in O(n^2) of BP runs, where n is the number of vertices in the original graph. In essence, the Blossom-BP offers a distributed version of the celebrated Edmonds' Blossom algorithm by jumping at once over many sub-steps with a single BP. Moreover, our result provides an interpretation of the Edmonds' algorithm as a sequence of LPs.

paragraphs: Belief propagation is a message-passing method that can solve certain combinatorial optimization problems when their linear programming relaxations are tight. An integrality gap breaks that favorable connection: the relaxed problem can admit solutions unavailable to the original discrete problem. This paper develops a sequential belief-propagation algorithm for matching that can work beyond that obstacle.

Called Blossom-BP, the method repeatedly applies belief propagation to modified graphs. These modifications contract and expand blossoms, which are odd sets of vertices. The changing graph is essential: the algorithm does not rely on a single belief-propagation run over the original formulation to handle the integrality gap.

This bound counts runs rather than individual message updates. The authors interpret the approach as a distributed version of Edmonds' blossom algorithm that combines many substeps within one run, and also give an interpretation of Edmonds' algorithm as a sequence of linear programs.
summary.tldr: Blossom-BP solves matching on arbitrary graphs through graph transformations and at most O(n²) sequential belief-propagation runs.

title: Minimum Weight Perfect Matching via Blossom Belief Propagation

abstract: The multivariate normal density is a monotonic function of the distance to the mean, and its ellipsoidal shape is due to the underlying Euclidean metric. We suggest to replace this metric with a locally adaptive, smoothly changing (Riemannian) metric that favors regions of high local density. The resulting locally adaptive normal distribution (LAND) is a generalization of the normal distribution to the "manifold" setting, where data is assumed to lie near a potentially low-dimensional manifold embedded in R^D. The LAND is parametric, depending only on a mean and a covariance, and is the maximum entropy distribution under the given metric. The underlying metric is, however, non-parametric. We develop a maximum likelihood algorithm to infer the distribution parameters that relies on a combination of gradient descent and Monte Carlo integration. We further extend the LAND to mixture models, and provide the corresponding EM algorithm. We demonstrate the efficiency of the LAND to fit non-trivial probability distributions over both synthetic data, and EEG measurements of human sleep.

paragraphs: A conventional multivariate normal distribution has an ellipsoidal shape because it measures distance using Euclidean geometry. This paper changes that underlying geometry. It introduces a smoothly varying Riemannian metric that favors regions with high local data density, allowing the distribution to follow data assumed to lie near a potentially low-dimensional manifold.

The resulting locally adaptive normal distribution, or LAND, still has a mean and covariance as its parameters, although its metric is nonparametric. The authors also characterize it as a maximum entropy distribution under the given metric. This combination preserves a compact parameterization for the distribution while allowing the surrounding geometry to adapt to the data.

To fit LAND, the paper develops maximum likelihood estimation using gradient descent and Monte Carlo integration. It also extends the construction to mixtures and supplies an expectation-maximization algorithm. Demonstrations on synthetic data and human sleep EEG measurements show its ability to fit nontrivial distributions, supporting adaptive geometry as a way to extend normal-distribution modeling.
summary.tldr: LAND generalizes the normal distribution by adapting its distance geometry to local data density and manifold structure.

title: A Locally Adaptive Normal Distribution

abstract: The recursive teaching dimension (RTD) of a concept class $C \subseteq \{0, 1\}^n$, introduced by Zilles et al. [ZLHZ11], is a complexity parameter measured by the worst-case number of labeled examples needed to learn any target concept of $C$ in the recursive teaching model. In this paper, we study the quantitative relation between RTD and the well-known learning complexity measure VC dimension (VCD), and improve the best known upper and (worst-case) lower bounds on the recursive teaching dimension with respect to the VC dimension. Given a concept class $C \subseteq \{0, 1\}^n$ with $VCD(C) = d$, we first show that $RTD(C)$ is at most $d 2^{d+1}$. This is the first upper bound for $RTD(C)$ that depends only on $VCD(C)$, independent of the size of the concept class $|C|$ and its~domain size $n$. Before our work, the best known upper bound for $RTD(C)$ is $O(d 2^d \log \log |C|)$, obtained by Moran et al. [MSWY15]. We remove the $\log \log |C|$ factor. We also improve the lower bound on the worst-case ratio of $RTD(C)$ to $VCD(C)$. We present a family of classes $\{ C_k \}_{k \ge 1}$ with $VCD(C_k) = 3k$ and $RTD(C_k)=5k$, which implies that the ratio of $RTD(C)$ to $VCD(C)$ in the worst case can be as large as $5/3$. Before our work, the largest ratio known was $3/2$ as obtained by Kuhlmann [Kuh99]. Since then, no finite concept class $C$ has been known to satisfy $RTD(C) > (3/2) VCD(C)$.

Earlier bounds also involved the number of concepts; the new result removes that dependence and is independent of the domain size as well.

summary.tldr: The paper bounds recursive teaching dimension solely by VC dimension and constructs classes where their ratio reaches 5/3.

title: On the Recursive Teaching Dimension of VC Classes

abstract: We present a deep learning framework for accurate visual correspondences and demonstrate its effectiveness for both geometric and semantic matching, spanning across rigid motions to intra-class shape or appearance variations. In contrast to previous CNN-based approaches that optimize a surrogate patch similarity objective, we use deep metric learning to directly learn a feature space that preserves either geometric or semantic similarity. Our fully convolutional architecture, along with a novel correspondence contrastive loss allows faster training by effective reuse of computations, accurate gradient computation through the use of thousands of examples per image pair and faster testing with $O(n)$ feedforward passes for n keypoints, instead of $O(n^2)$ for typical patch similarity methods. We propose a convolutional spatial transformer to mimic patch normalization in traditional features like SIFT, which is shown to dramatically boost accuracy for semantic correspondences across intra-class shape variations. Extensive experiments on KITTI, PASCAL and CUB-2011 datasets demonstrate the significant advantages of our features over prior works that use either hand-constructed or learned features.

The method directly learns a feature space preserving the desired similarity, rather than training only a surrogate objective for comparing image patches.

Its fully convolutional architecture and correspondence contrastive loss reuse computations across matches. Training can draw on thousands of examples per image pair for gradient computation. At test time, the abstract reports O(n) feedforward passes for n keypoints, compared with O(n²) for typical patch-similarity approaches. This links the representation-learning objective with a more efficient computation pattern.

The authors also introduce a convolutional spatial transformer that imitates patch normalization in traditional features such as SIFT. It substantially improves semantic matching across within-class shape differences in their experiments. Evaluations on KITTI, PASCAL, and CUB-2011 show significant advantages over the tested handcrafted and learned features, supporting the approach across both types of correspondence.
summary.tldr: A fully convolutional metric-learning network improves geometric and semantic image matching while reusing computation across correspondences.

title: Universal Correspondence Network

abstract: In topic modeling, many algorithms that guarantee identifiability of the topics have been developed under the premise that there exist anchor words -- i.e., words that only appear (with positive probability) in one topic. Follow-up work has resorted to three or higher-order statistics of the data corpus to relax the anchor word assumption. Reliable estimates of higher-order statistics are hard to obtain, however, and the identification of topics under those models hinges on uncorrelatedness of the topics, which can be unrealistic. This paper revisits topic modeling based on second-order moments, and proposes an anchor-free topic mining framework. The proposed approach guarantees the identification of the topics under a much milder condition compared to the anchor-word assumption, thereby exhibiting much better robustness in practice. The associated algorithm only involves one eigen-decomposition and a few small linear programs. This makes it easy to implement and scale up to very large problem instances. Experiments using the TDT2 and Reuters-21578 corpus demonstrate that the proposed anchor-free approach exhibits very favorable performance (measured using coherence, similarity count, and clustering accuracy metrics) compared to the prior art.

Identification matters because it concerns whether the underlying topics can be distinguished from the information the model uses.

summary.tldr: An anchor-free topic model uses second-order statistics to identify topics under a milder condition and performs favorably on two corpora.

title: Anchor-Free Correlated Topic Modeling: Identifiability and Algorithm

abstract: We consider online learning algorithms that guarantee worst-case regret rates in adversarial environments (so they can be deployed safely and will perform robustly), yet adapt optimally to favorable stochastic environments (so they will perform well in a variety of settings of practical importance). We quantify the friendliness of stochastic environments by means of the well-known Bernstein (a.k.a. generalized Tsybakov margin) condition. For two recent algorithms (Squint for the Hedge setting and MetaGrad for online convex optimization) we show that the particular form of their data-dependent individual-sequence regret guarantees implies that they adapt automatically to the Bernstein parameters of the stochastic environment. We prove that these algorithms attain fast rates in their respective settings both in expectation and with high probability.

paragraphs: Online learning algorithms make decisions as observations arrive, and their performance can be measured through regret: the cost of their decisions relative to a comparison strategy. This paper asks whether algorithms with guarantees against adversarial observations can also learn especially quickly when observations follow a favorable stochastic pattern. The goal is to retain robustness while benefiting from easier environments.

The authors study two existing algorithms: Squint in the Hedge setting and MetaGrad in online convex optimization. They describe favorable stochastic environments using the Bernstein condition, also known as a generalized Tsybakov margin condition. Their analysis connects this condition to the particular data-dependent regret guarantees already available for the two algorithms.

That connection shows that both algorithms automatically adapt to the environment's Bernstein parameters. The paper proves fast rates in expectation and with high probability in their respective settings. The result explains how the form of an adversarial guarantee can also support stronger performance under stochastic assumptions, without requiring the learner to be given those parameters.
summary.tldr: Squint and MetaGrad retain adversarial regret guarantees while automatically achieving fast rates under favorable Bernstein conditions.

title: Combining Adversarial Guarantees and Stochastic Fast Rates in Online Learning

abstract: Understanding the 3D world is a fundamental problem in computer vision. However, learning a good representation of 3D objects is still an open problem due to the high dimensionality of the data and many factors of variation involved. In this work, we investigate the task of single-view 3D object reconstruction from a learning agent's perspective. We formulate the learning process as an interaction between 3D and 2D representations and propose an encoder-decoder network with a novel projection loss defined by the projective transformation. More importantly, the projection loss enables the unsupervised learning using 2D observation without explicit 3D supervision. We demonstrate the ability of the model in generating 3D volume from a single 2D image with three sets of experiments: (1) learning from single-class objects; (2) learning from multi-class objects and (3) testing on novel object classes. Results show superior performance and better generalization ability for 3D object reconstruction when the projection loss is involved.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a model can reconstruct a three-dimensional object from a single two-dimensional image. Learning such representations is difficult because 3D data is high-dimensional and objects vary in many ways. The authors frame learning around the relationship between a 3D representation and its 2D projections.

They propose an encoder-decoder network with a projection loss defined through projective transformation. This loss connects the model's 3D output to observations in two dimensions, enabling learning without explicit 3D supervision. The training signal can therefore come from 2D observations even though the representation being learned is a 3D volume.

The evaluation covers learning within one object class, learning across multiple classes, and testing on previously unseen classes. Results show better reconstruction performance and generalization when the projection loss is included. These experiments support the value of making the relationship between two and three dimensions part of the learning objective. The stated achievement is single-image reconstruction without explicit 3D training targets, with the gains demonstrated in the reported experimental settings.
summary.tldr: A projection loss lets an encoder-decoder learn 3D reconstruction from 2D observations without explicit 3D supervision, improving reported reconstruction and generalization.

title: Perspective Transformer Nets: Learning Single-View 3D Object Reconstruction without 3D Supervision

abstract: In this paper, we describe the "PixelGAN autoencoder", a generative autoencoder in which the generative path is a convolutional autoregressive neural network on pixels (PixelCNN) that is conditioned on a latent code, and the recognition path uses a generative adversarial network (GAN) to impose a prior distribution on the latent code. We show that different priors result in different decompositions of information between the latent code and the autoregressive decoder. For example, by imposing a Gaussian distribution as the prior, we can achieve a global vs. local decomposition, or by imposing a categorical distribution as the prior, we can disentangle the style and content information of images in an unsupervised fashion. We further show how the PixelGAN autoencoder with a categorical prior can be directly used in semi-supervised settings and achieve competitive semi-supervised classification results on the MNIST, SVHN and NORB datasets.

paragraphs: The PixelGAN autoencoder combines a latent representation with a PixelCNN image generator. PixelCNN supplies an autoregressive model of pixels conditioned on a latent code. On the recognition side, adversarial training imposes a chosen prior distribution on that code. The architecture therefore combines pixel-level generation with explicit control over the distribution of its latent representation.

The paper shows that the prior influences how information is divided between the code and the decoder. A Gaussian prior can produce a division between global and local information. A categorical prior can separate image style and content without supervision. The prior consequently affects what the representation captures, beyond simply specifying which latent values the model should use.

The categorical version also applies directly to semi-supervised learning, where classification uses both labeled and unlabeled information. The authors report competitive classification results on MNIST, SVHN, and NORB. These findings link the model’s generative structure to a prediction task, showing that the choice governing information decomposition can also support a useful classification representation.
summary.tldr: PixelGAN autoencoders use latent priors to shape information decomposition and achieve competitive semi-supervised classification with a categorical prior.

title: PixelGAN Autoencoders

abstract: We study the generalization error of randomized learning algorithms -- focusing on stochastic gradient descent (SGD) -- using a novel combination of PAC-Bayes and algorithmic stability. Importantly, our generalization bounds hold for all posterior distributions on an algorithm's random hyperparameters, including distributions that depend on the training data. This inspires an adaptive sampling algorithm for SGD that optimizes the posterior at runtime. We analyze this algorithm in the context of our generalization bounds and evaluate it on a benchmark dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that adaptive sampling can reduce empirical risk faster than uniform sampling while also improving out-of-sample accuracy.

paragraphs: Randomized learning algorithms can produce different models depending on choices made during training. This paper studies how such randomness affects generalization: the gap between performance on training examples and performance beyond them. Its main focus is stochastic gradient descent, using a combination of PAC-Bayesian analysis and algorithmic stability to derive generalization bounds.

The distinctive feature is that the bounds cover every posterior distribution over the algorithm’s random hyperparameters, including distributions chosen using the training data. This matters because adapting random choices to observed data changes the learning procedure being analyzed. The framework explicitly accommodates that dependence rather than requiring those choices to remain fixed independently of the data.

The analysis motivates an SGD algorithm that adjusts its sampling distribution while training. The authors examine this adaptive procedure through their bounds and evaluate it on a benchmark dataset. Their experiments show that adaptive sampling can lower training risk faster than uniform sampling while also improving accuracy on unseen examples, connecting the theoretical framework to an observed practical benefit.
summary.tldr: A combined PAC-Bayesian and stability analysis supports data-dependent SGD sampling that improves training speed and unseen-data accuracy in the reported experiment.

title: A PAC-Bayesian Analysis of Randomized Learning with Application to Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have become a crucial tool on learning representations of graph vertices. The main challenge of adapting GCNs on large-scale graphs is the scalability issue that it incurs heavy cost both in computation and memory due to the uncontrollable neighborhood expansion across layers. In this paper, we accelerate the training of GCNs through developing an adaptive layer-wise sampling method. By constructing the network layer by layer in a top-down passway, we sample the lower layer conditioned on the top one, where the sampled neighborhoods are shared by different parent nodes and the over expansion is avoided owing to the fixed-size sampling. More importantly, the proposed sampler is adaptive and applicable for explicit variance reduction, which in turn enhances the training of our method. Furthermore, we propose a novel and economical approach to promote the message passing over distant nodes by applying skip connections. Intensive experiments on several benchmarks verify the effectiveness of our method regarding the classification accuracy while enjoying faster convergence speed.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks learn node representations by gathering information from neighborhoods. Across multiple layers, those neighborhoods can expand dramatically, making training expensive in both memory and computation. This paper targets that expansion through an adaptive sampling procedure that selects the information needed at each layer.

The network is constructed from the top layer downward, with sampling in a lower layer conditioned on the layer above. Different parent nodes share sampled neighborhoods, and fixed-size samples prevent uncontrolled growth. The sampler is also adaptive, allowing explicit variance reduction to improve training. These choices address both how much neighborhood information is processed and how effectively the sampled information supports learning.

The authors additionally use skip connections to promote communication between distant nodes economically. Together, the sampling and connection strategies aim to make graph representation learning faster while preserving useful information. Experiments on several benchmarks report effective classification accuracy and faster convergence. The findings support the proposed combination as a practical response to the computational burden of training graph convolutional networks.
summary.tldr: Adaptive layer-wise neighborhood sampling and skip connections accelerate graph convolutional network training while supporting effective classification.

title: Adaptive Sampling Towards Fast Graph Representation Learning

abstract: PAC-Bayes bounds have been proposed to get risk estimates based on a training sample. In this paper the PAC-Bayes approach is combined with stability of the hypothesis learned by a Hilbert space valued algorithm. The PAC-Bayes setting is used with a Gaussian prior centered at the expected output. Thus a novelty of our paper is using priors defined in terms of the data-generating distribution. Our main result estimates the risk of the randomized algorithm in terms of the hypothesis stability coefficients. We also provide a new bound for the SVM classifier, which is compared to other known bounds experimentally. Ours appears to be the first uniform hypothesis stability-based bound that evaluates to non-trivial values.

paragraphs: PAC-Bayes analysis seeks to estimate prediction risk using a training sample. This paper combines that approach with stability, which describes how sensitive a learned hypothesis is to changes in training data. The setting covers algorithms whose outputs lie in a Hilbert space, allowing the risk analysis to incorporate properties of the learning procedure.

The authors use a Gaussian prior centered on the algorithm’s expected output. This makes the prior depend on the data-generating distribution, a distinguishing feature of the analysis. Their main result bounds the risk of a randomized algorithm in terms of hypothesis stability coefficients, connecting a measure of learning sensitivity to a prediction-risk estimate.

The paper also derives a new bound for support vector machine classifiers and compares it experimentally with existing bounds. The authors describe theirs as apparently the first bound based on uniform hypothesis stability to yield non-trivial values. That qualification matters: the stated contribution concerns making this kind of theoretical risk estimate informative, with empirical comparisons supporting its usefulness for the SVM setting.
summary.tldr: Distribution-dependent Gaussian priors connect PAC-Bayes risk estimates with algorithmic stability and yield an informative SVM bound.

title: PAC-Bayes bounds for stable algorithms with instance-dependent priors

abstract: We study minimax convergence rates of nonparametric density estimation under a large class of loss functions called ``adversarial losses'', which, besides classical L^p losses, includes maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), Wasserstein distance, and total variation distance. These losses are closely related to the losses encoded by discriminator networks in generative adversarial networks (GANs). In a general framework, we study how the choice of loss and the assumed smoothness of the underlying density together determine the minimax rate. We also discuss implications for training GANs based on deep ReLU networks, and more general connections to learning implicit generative models in a minimax statistical sense.

paragraphs: Density estimation seeks to learn the distribution underlying observed data. Its difficulty depends partly on how error is measured: two estimated distributions can look close under one comparison and farther apart under another. This paper studies that dependence through a broad family of adversarial losses in a nonparametric setting.

The framework includes classical Lp losses, maximum mean discrepancy, Wasserstein distance, and total variation distance. The authors investigate how the selected loss and assumptions about the true density's smoothness jointly determine minimax convergence rates. These rates describe the best achievable worst-case statistical accuracy over the relevant class of densities as more observations become available.

Adversarial losses are closely connected to the comparisons made by discriminator networks in generative adversarial networks. The paper discusses implications for GANs built with deep ReLU networks and for implicit generative models more generally. Its contribution is a statistical framework for relating the chosen distribution-comparison objective to the fundamental difficulty of learning, rather than treating all such objectives as interchangeable.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes how adversarial loss choices and density smoothness jointly determine minimax rates for distribution estimation.

title: Nonparametric Density Estimation under Adversarial Losses

abstract: Previous works on sequential learning address the problem of forgetting in discriminative models. In this paper we consider the case of generative models. In particular, we investigate generative adversarial networks (GANs) in the task of learning new categories in a sequential fashion. We first show that sequential fine tuning renders the network unable to properly generate images from previous categories (i.e. forgetting). Addressing this problem, we propose Memory Replay GANs (MeRGANs), a conditional GAN framework that integrates a memory replay generator. We study two methods to prevent forgetting by leveraging these replays, namely joint training with replay and replay alignment. Qualitative and quantitative experimental results in MNIST, SVHN and LSUN datasets show that our memory replay approach can generate competitive images while significantly mitigating the forgetting of previous categories.

paragraphs: A generative model learning new categories sequentially can lose the ability to generate categories it learned earlier. This paper investigates that problem in generative adversarial networks. The authors first demonstrate that sequential fine-tuning leads to forgetting, extending a concern often studied in discriminative models to the quality of generated images.

Their solution, Memory Replay GANs, is a conditional GAN framework with a generator that provides memory replays. They study two ways to use those replays: joint training with replay and replay alignment. In both cases, replay supplies a mechanism for retaining earlier generative behavior while the model learns additional categories.

Qualitative and quantitative evaluations on MNIST, SVHN, and LSUN show that the approach produces competitive images while significantly reducing forgetting of previous categories. The stated outcome is mitigation rather than complete elimination of forgetting. The work establishes sequential category learning as a challenge for image generation and demonstrates that incorporating generated replays can help preserve earlier capabilities as the model's category repertoire grows.
summary.tldr: Memory Replay GANs use generated replays to learn new image categories while substantially reducing forgetting of earlier categories.

title: Memory Replay GANs: Learning to Generate New Categories without Forgetting

abstract: Current state-of-the-art approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) algorithms generate indices that must be stored in main memory for fast high-recall search. This makes them expensive and limits the size of the dataset. We present a new graph-based indexing and search system called DiskANN that can index, store, and search a billion point database on a single workstation with just 64GB RAM and an inexpensive solid-state drive (SSD). Contrary to current wisdom, we demonstrate that the SSD-based indices built by DiskANN can meet all three desiderata for large-scale ANNS: high-recall, low query latency and high density (points indexed per node). On the billion point SIFT1B bigann dataset, DiskANN serves > 5000 queries a second with < 3ms mean latency and 95%+ 1-recall@1 on a 16 core machine, where state-of-the-art billion-point ANNS algorithms with similar memory footprint like FAISS and IVFOADC+G+P plateau at around 50% 1-recall@1. Alternately, in the high recall regime, DiskANN can index and serve 5 − 10x more points per node compared to state-of-the-art graph- based methods such as HNSW and NSG. Finally, as part of our overall DiskANN system, we introduce Vamana, a new graph-based ANNS index that is more versatile than the graph indices even for in-memory indices.

DiskANN uses a graph-based index and an SSD to index, store, and search a billion points on one workstation with 64GB of RAM.

summary.tldr: DiskANN combines graph indexing with SSD storage to deliver fast, high-recall billion-point search on a single workstation.

title: DiskANN: Fast Accurate Billion-point Nearest Neighbor Search on a Single Node

abstract: Many decision-making problems naturally exhibit pronounced structures inherited from the characteristics of the underlying environment. In a Markov decision process model, for example, two distinct states can have inherently related semantics or encode resembling physical state configurations. This often implies locally correlated transition dynamics among the states. In order to complete a certain task in such environments, the operating agent usually needs to execute a series of temporally and spatially correlated actions. Though there exists a variety of approaches to capture these correlations in continuous state-action domains, a principled solution for discrete environments is missing. In this work, we present a Bayesian learning framework based on Pólya-Gamma augmentation that enables an analogous reasoning in such cases. We demonstrate the framework on a number of common decision-making related problems, such as imitation learning, subgoal extraction, system identification and Bayesian reinforcement learning. By explicitly modeling the underlying correlation structures of these problems, the proposed approach yields superior predictive performance compared to correlation-agnostic models, even when trained on data sets that are an order of magnitude smaller in size.

paragraphs: Decision-making environments often contain related states and coordinated sequences of actions. Two states may describe similar physical configurations, making their transition behavior related as well. This paper asks how a learning system for discrete environments can explicitly represent such correlations, instead of treating related parts of the problem as unrelated.

The authors introduce a Bayesian learning framework based on Pólya-Gamma augmentation. It is designed to incorporate correlation structure into reasoning about discrete decision problems. This matters because the structure of an environment can provide information beyond isolated observations: relationships among states or actions can help the model learn from the data it receives.

The framework is demonstrated on imitation learning, subgoal extraction, system identification, and Bayesian reinforcement learning. Across the reported applications, explicitly modeling correlations yields better predictive performance than models that ignore them, even with training datasets an order of magnitude smaller. These findings support the value of representing the relevant correlations in the studied problems, particularly when available observations are limited.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian framework models correlations in discrete decision problems to improve predictions with substantially less training data.

title: Correlation Priors for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Matrix Factorization is a popular non-convex optimization problem, for which alternating minimization schemes are mostly used. They usually suffer from the major drawback that the solution is biased towards one of the optimization variables. A remedy is non-alternating schemes. However, due to a lack of Lipschitz continuity of the gradient in matrix factorization problems, convergence cannot be guaranteed. A recently developed approach relies on the concept of Bregman distances, which generalizes the standard Euclidean distance. We exploit this theory by proposing a novel Bregman distance for matrix factorization problems, which, at the same time, allows for simple/closed form update steps. Therefore, for non-alternating schemes, such as the recently introduced Bregman Proximal Gradient (BPG) method and an inertial variant Convex--Concave Inertial BPG (CoCaIn BPG), convergence of the whole sequence to a stationary point is proved for Matrix Factorization. In several experiments, we observe a superior performance of our non-alternating schemes in terms of speed and objective value at the limit point.

The authors identify a drawback: this procedure can favor one optimization variable. Updating without alternation offers a remedy, but standard convergence arguments encounter a problem because the gradient lacks the Lipschitz continuity those arguments require.

The paper addresses this obstacle by constructing a Bregman distance tailored to matrix factorization. Bregman distances generalize ordinary Euclidean distance, giving the optimization method a different way to measure changes between iterates. The proposed choice also permits simple or closed-form updates, connecting the convergence analysis to steps that are practical to compute.

Using this construction, the authors prove convergence of the entire sequence to a stationary point for Bregman Proximal Gradient and its inertial CoCaIn BPG variant. A stationary point is the stated destination; the result does not claim a global optimum. In several experiments, the non-alternating methods achieve better speed and better final objective values, supporting the practical value of the tailored distance.
summary.tldr: A tailored Bregman distance enables simple non-alternating matrix-factorization updates with convergence to a stationary point and strong experimental performance.

title: Beyond Alternating Updates for Matrix Factorization with Inertial Bregman Proximal Gradient Algorithms

abstract: We present a causal view on the robustness of neural networks against input manipulations, which applies not only to traditional classification tasks but also to general measurement data. Based on this view, we design a deep causal manipulation augmented model (deep CAMA) which explicitly models possible manipulations on certain causes leading to changes in the observed effect. We further develop data augmentation and test-time fine-tuning methods to improve deep CAMA's robustness. When compared with discriminative deep neural networks, our proposed model shows superior robustness against unseen manipulations. As a by-product, our model achieves disentangled representation which separates the representation of manipulations from those of other latent causes.
