paragraphs: This paper studies robustness by asking how changes to underlying causes produce changes in observed inputs. Its scope includes both classification and more general measurement data. The central idea is to represent possible input manipulations within a causal model, so that the model explicitly accounts for how those manipulations affect what it observes.

The resulting system, deep CAMA, models manipulations of selected causes and their consequences for observed effects. The authors also develop data augmentation and fine-tuning at test time to improve its robustness. These methods accompany the causal representation, giving the approach both a way to describe manipulations and training or adaptation procedures intended to handle them.

In the reported comparison, deep CAMA is more robust to previously unseen manipulations than discriminative deep neural networks. It also learns representations that separate manipulation-related information from other hidden causes. This separation is a useful additional result: the learned representation distinguishes factors associated with manipulation from other factors contributing to the observation.
summary.tldr: Deep CAMA explicitly models causal manipulations and shows improved robustness to unseen manipulations while separating their representations from other latent causes.

title: A Causal View on Robustness of Neural Networks

abstract: Exploration policies in Bayesian bandits maximize the average reward over problem instances drawn from some distribution P. In this work, we learn such policies for an unknown distribution P using samples from P. Our approach is a form of meta-learning and exploits properties of P without making strong assumptions about its form. To do this, we parameterize our policies in a differentiable way and optimize them by policy gradients, an approach that is pleasantly general and easy to implement. We derive effective gradient estimators and propose novel variance reduction techniques. We also analyze and experiment with various bandit policy classes, including neural networks and a novel softmax policy. The latter has regret guarantees and is a natural starting point for our optimization. Our experiments show the versatility of our approach. We also observe that neural network policies can learn implicit biases expressed only through the sampled instances.

paragraphs: A useful exploration strategy can depend on which bandit problems an agent typically encounters. This paper learns policies that maximize average reward across problem instances drawn from an unknown distribution. Instead of specifying that distribution in a restrictive mathematical form, the approach uses sampled instances to learn exploration behavior suited to its structure.

The authors make policies differentiable and optimize them with policy gradients. This turns the design of exploration behavior into a meta-learning problem: training happens across bandit instances, while the learned policy acts within an instance. They derive gradient estimators and introduce variance-reduction techniques to make this optimization more effective.

The study covers several policy classes, including neural networks and a new softmax policy. The softmax policy has regret guarantees and provides a starting point for optimization; those guarantees are specific to that policy rather than automatically applying to every learned class. Experiments demonstrate versatility, and neural policies learn implicit biases conveyed only through the sampled problems. The results show how recurring problem structure can inform exploration without being explicitly encoded by the designer.
summary.tldr: Differentiable meta-learning trains bandit exploration policies to exploit structure in sampled problems from an unknown distribution.

title: Differentiable Meta-Learning of Bandit Policies

abstract: This article considers the problem of community detection in sparse dynamical graphs in which the community structure evolves over time. A fast spectral algorithm based on an extension of the Bethe-Hessian matrix is proposed, which benefits from the positive correlation in the class labels and in their temporal evolution and is designed to be applicable to any dynamical graph with a community structure. Under the dynamical degree-corrected stochastic block model, in the case of two classes of equal size, we demonstrate and support with extensive simulations that our proposed algorithm is capable of making non-trivial community reconstruction as soon as theoretically possible, thereby reaching the optimal detectability threshold and provably outperforming competing spectral methods.

paragraphs: Community detection seeks groups within a network, but sparse networks offer relatively little connection information. When the network changes over time, group membership can change as well. This paper develops a fast spectral method that uses both the network structure and the positive correlations present in community labels and their temporal evolution.

The algorithm extends the Bethe-Hessian matrix to the dynamic setting. This gives the spectral procedure a representation suited to communities that evolve across observations. The method is designed for broad use on dynamic graphs with community structure, allowing information from temporal relationships to contribute alongside information from individual graph observations.

Its strongest guarantee is established under a specific model: a dynamic degree-corrected stochastic block model with two equally sized classes. In that setting, the authors show that the algorithm achieves meaningful reconstruction as soon as theory permits, reaching the optimal detectability threshold and provably outperforming competing spectral methods. Extensive simulations support this result. Reaching that threshold concerns obtaining non-trivial community information, rather than claiming perfect reconstruction of every membership.
summary.tldr: A dynamic Bethe-Hessian spectral method reaches the optimal community detectability threshold under a model with two equally sized classes.

title: Community detection in sparse time-evolving graphs with a dynamical Bethe-Hessian

abstract: Deep learning (DL) frameworks take advantage of GPUs to improve the speed of DL inference and training. Ideally, DL frameworks should be able to fully utilize the computation power of GPUs such that the running time depends on the amount of computation assigned to GPUs. Yet, we observe that in scheduling GPU tasks, existing DL frameworks suffer from inefficiencies such as large scheduling overhead and unnecessary serial execution. To this end, we propose Nimble, a DL execution engine that runs GPU tasks in parallel with minimal scheduling overhead. Nimble introduces a novel technique called ahead-of-time (AoT) scheduling. Here, the scheduling procedure finishes before executing the GPU kernel, thereby removing most of the scheduling overhead during run time. Furthermore, Nimble automatically parallelizes the execution of GPU tasks by exploiting multiple GPU streams in a single GPU. Evaluation on a variety of neural networks shows that compared to PyTorch, Nimble speeds up inference and training by up to 22.34× and 3.61×, respectively. Moreover, Nimble outperforms state-of-the-art inference systems, TensorRT and TVM, by up to 2.81× and 1.70×, respectively.

paragraphs: Deep learning frameworks use GPUs for fast computation, but managing the work can itself consume time. The paper identifies two sources of inefficiency: substantial scheduling overhead and tasks being executed sequentially when they could run in parallel. Nimble is an execution engine designed to reduce both costs during neural network inference and training.

Its ahead-of-time scheduling technique completes scheduling before GPU kernels execute, removing most scheduling work from runtime. Nimble also automatically uses multiple streams on a single GPU to execute tasks in parallel. These mechanisms address different parts of execution time: one reduces the cost of organizing work, while the other exploits opportunities to perform work concurrently.

Across the evaluated neural networks, Nimble achieves speedups over PyTorch of up to 22.34 times for inference and 3.61 times for training. It also exceeds TensorRT and TVM inference performance by up to 2.81 and 1.70 times, respectively. These are maximum reported improvements across the evaluation, showing that scheduling choices can substantially affect realized GPU performance.
summary.tldr: Nimble reduces GPU scheduling overhead and automatically parallelizes tasks, delivering substantial maximum speedups in the evaluated networks.

title: Nimble: Lightweight and Parallel GPU Task Scheduling for Deep Learning

abstract: We consider neural networks with rational activation functions. The choice of the nonlinear activation function in deep learning architectures is crucial and heavily impacts the performance of a neural network. We establish optimal bounds in terms of network complexity and prove that rational neural networks approximate smooth functions more efficiently than ReLU networks with exponentially smaller depth. The flexibility and smoothness of rational activation functions make them an attractive alternative to ReLU, as we demonstrate with numerical experiments.
originalAbstract: We consider neural networks with rational activation functions. The flexibility and smoothness of rational activation functions make them an attractive alternative to ReLU, as we demonstrate with numerical experiments.

paragraphs: A neural network's activation function determines the nonlinear transformations it can build between layers. This paper studies rational activations, which are ratios of polynomials. Their flexibility and smoothness make them an alternative to ReLU activations, and the authors investigate how that choice changes the complexity needed to approximate functions.

The main theoretical contribution establishes optimal bounds on network complexity. For approximating smooth functions, the authors prove that rational networks can be more efficient than ReLU networks, with exponentially smaller depth. This connects activation design directly to how many layers a representation requires, rather than treating the activation as a minor implementation choice.

Numerical experiments further demonstrate the appeal of rational activations. The theoretical result is specifically about approximation of smooth functions, so its significance lies in the representational advantage established for that setting. Together, the analysis and experiments make a case for exploring rational activations when smoothness and approximation efficiency matter, showing that changing the form of each nonlinearity can substantially affect the network architecture needed.
summary.tldr: Rational activation functions enable provably more efficient approximation of smooth functions than ReLU networks, including exponentially smaller depth.

title: Rational neural networks

abstract: A fundamental difficulty of causal learning is that causal models can generally not be fully identified based on observational data only. Interventional data, that is, data originating from different experimental environments, improves identifiability. However, the improvement depends critically on the target and nature of the interventions carried out in each experiment. Since in real applications experiments tend to be costly, there is a need to perform the right interventions such that as few as possible are required. In this work we propose a new active learning (i.e. experiment selection) framework (A-ICP) based on Invariant Causal Prediction (ICP) (Peters et al. 2016). For general structural causal models, we characterize the effect of interventions on so-called stable sets, a notion introduced by Pfister et al. 2019. We leverage these results to propose several intervention selection policies for A-ICP which quickly reveal the direct causes of a response variable in the causal graph while maintaining the error control inherent in ICP. Empirically, we analyze the performance of the proposed policies in both population and finite-regime experiments.

paragraphs: Observational data generally cannot fully determine a causal model. Experiments can improve identification, but their value depends on what is changed and how. Because experiments can be costly, this paper studies how to select interventions that efficiently reveal the direct causes of a particular response variable.

The proposed framework, Active Invariant Causal Prediction, builds experiment selection around Invariant Causal Prediction. Its theoretical foundation characterizes how interventions affect stable sets in general structural causal models. These results provide a basis for deciding which intervention to perform, linking the choice of experiment to stability properties relevant to causal discovery.

The authors use this analysis to develop several intervention-selection policies that quickly reveal direct causes while retaining ICP's error control. They evaluate the policies in both population and finite-data experiments. The contribution connects experimental planning with controlled causal inference: the framework aims to make each intervention informative without abandoning the error guarantees of the underlying prediction method.
summary.tldr: A-ICP uses intervention-induced stability changes to select informative causal experiments while preserving ICP's error control.

title: Active Invariant Causal Prediction: Experiment Selection through Stability

abstract: Graphs have been commonly used to represent complex data structures. In models dealing with graph-structured data, multivariate parameters may not only exhibit sparse patterns but have structured sparsity and smoothness in the sense that both zero and non-zero parameters tend to cluster together. We propose a new prior for high-dimensional parameters with graphical relations, referred to as the Tree-based Low-rank Horseshoe (T-LoHo) model, that generalizes the popular univariate Bayesian horseshoe shrinkage prior to the multivariate setting to detect structured sparsity and smoothness simultaneously. The T-LoHo prior can be embedded in many high-dimensional hierarchical models. To illustrate its utility, we apply it to regularize a Bayesian high-dimensional regression problem where the regression coefficients are linked by a graph, so that the resulting clusters have flexible shapes and satisfy the cluster contiguity constraint with respect to the graph. We design an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that delivers full Bayesian inference with uncertainty measures for model parameters such as the number of clusters. We offer theoretical investigations of the clustering effects and posterior concentration results. Finally, we illustrate the performance of the model with simulation studies and a real data application for anomaly detection on a road network. The results indicate substantial improvements over other competing methods such as the sparse fused lasso.

Both zero and nonzero parameters can form connected groups, with related values varying smoothly. T-LoHo addresses this combination of structured sparsity and smoothness through a Bayesian prior for high-dimensional parameters linked by a graph.

The Tree-based Low-rank Horseshoe model extends the univariate horseshoe shrinkage prior to a multivariate setting. The authors demonstrate it in Bayesian regression with graph-linked coefficients, producing flexibly shaped clusters that remain contiguous on the graph. They also develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that provides full Bayesian inference, including uncertainty about quantities such as the number of clusters.

The paper investigates clustering behavior theoretically and provides posterior concentration results. Simulations and an application to road-network anomaly detection report substantial improvements over competing methods such as the sparse fused lasso. The approach brings together coefficient regularization, graph-respecting clustering, and uncertainty measurement, rather than treating the discovered grouping as a single fixed output without associated Bayesian uncertainty.
summary.tldr: T-LoHo models graph-connected sparsity and smoothness while providing Bayesian uncertainty about parameters and their clusters.

title: T-LoHo: A Bayesian Regularization Model for Structured Sparsity and Smoothness on Graphs

abstract: Background. Floods are the most common natural disaster in the world, affecting the lives of hundreds of millions. Flood forecasting is therefore a vitally important endeavor, typically achieved using physical water flow simulations, which rely on accurate terrain elevation maps. However, such simulations, based on solving partial differential equations, are computationally prohibitive on a large scale. This scalability issue is commonly alleviated using a coarse grid representation of the elevation map, though this representation may distort crucial terrain details, leading to significant inaccuracies in the simulation.\\Contributions. We train a deep neural network to perform physics-informed downsampling of the terrain map: we optimize the coarse grid representation of the terrain maps, so that the flood prediction will match the fine grid solution. For the learning process to succeed, we configure a dataset specifically for this task. We demonstrate that with this method, it is possible to achieve a significant reduction in computational cost, while maintaining an accurate solution. A reference implementation accompanies the paper as well as documentation and code for dataset reproduction.

paragraphs: Flood simulations depend on accurate terrain elevations because the shape of the ground influences water flow. Solving the underlying physical equations over a fine grid can be too expensive at large scales. Using a coarser terrain map reduces the computational burden, but may erase details that matter for the resulting flood prediction.

This paper trains a neural network to produce coarse terrain maps with the simulation outcome in mind. The training objective asks the flood prediction on the coarse representation to match the solution obtained on a fine grid. This makes downsampling sensitive to the physical task: the quality of the reduced map is judged through the water-flow prediction it supports.

The authors construct a dataset specifically for this learning problem and demonstrate that their method can substantially reduce computational cost while maintaining an accurate solution. The result supports learning the terrain representation as a way to make physical flood simulation more scalable. A reference implementation, together with documentation and dataset-reproduction code, accompanies the paper.
summary.tldr: A neural network learns coarse terrain maps that preserve fine-grid flood predictions while reducing simulation cost.

title: Physics-Aware Downsampling with Deep Learning for Scalable Flood Modeling

abstract: With the proliferation of machine learning applications in the real world, the demand for explaining machine learning predictions continues to grow especially in high-stakes fields. Recent studies have found that interpretation methods can be sensitive and unreliable, where the interpretations can be disturbed by perturbations or transformations of input data. To address this issue, we propose to learn robust interpretation through transformation equivariant regularization in a self-interpretable model. The resulting model is capable of capturing valid interpretation that is equivariant to geometric transformations. Moreover, since our model is self-interpretable, it enables faithful interpretations that reflect the true predictive mechanism. Unlike existing self-interpretable models, which usually sacrifice expressive power for the sake of interpretation quality, our model preserves the high expressive capability comparable to the state-of-the-art deep learning models in complex tasks, while providing visualizable and faithful high-quality interpretation. We compare with various related methods and validate the interpretation quality and consistency of our model.

paragraphs: An explanation of a model prediction can be unreliable if it changes unpredictably when the input is transformed. This paper addresses that problem by training a self-interpretable model with transformation-equivariant regularization. The goal is for geometric changes to an input to produce corresponding changes in its interpretation.

Equivariance gives explanation consistency a concrete training target: the interpretation should track the transformation applied to the data. Because the model is self-interpretable, its explanations are tied to its predictive mechanism. The authors aim to combine this faithfulness with robustness, so that a visually accessible explanation both reflects how the model predicts and behaves consistently under geometric transformations.

The paper reports that its model retains expressive capability comparable to state-of-the-art deep models on complex tasks while producing high-quality visual interpretations. Comparisons with related methods validate interpretation quality and consistency. These findings support the possibility of building explanatory structure into a powerful predictive model without the expressive-power sacrifice commonly associated with existing self-interpretable approaches.
summary.tldr: A self-interpretable model uses transformation-equivariant regularization to produce faithful, geometrically consistent explanations while retaining strong expressive capability.

title: Self-Interpretable Model with Transformation Equivariant Interpretation

abstract: Robust reinforcement learning (RL) is to find a policy that optimizes the worst-case performance over an uncertainty set of MDPs. In this paper, we focus on model-free robust RL, where the uncertainty set is defined to be centering at a misspecified MDP that generates samples, and is assumed to be unknown. We develop a sample-based approach to estimate the unknown uncertainty set, and design robust Q-learning algorithm (tabular case) and robust TDC algorithm (function approximation setting), which can be implemented in an online and incremental fashion. For the robust Q-learning algorithm, we prove that it converges to the optimal robust Q function, and for the robust TDC algorithm, we prove that it converges asymptotically to some stationary points. Unlike the results in [Roy et al., 2017], our algorithms do not need any additional conditions on the discount factor to guarantee the convergence. We further characterize the finite-time error bounds of the two algorithms, and show that both the robust Q-learning and robust TDC algorithms converge as fast as their vanilla counterparts (within a constant factor). Our numerical experiments further demonstrate the robustness of our algorithms. Our approach can be readily extended to robustify many other algorithms, e.g., TD, SARSA, and other GTD algorithms.

paragraphs: Robust reinforcement learning seeks a policy with good worst-case performance across a set of possible environments. This paper considers model-free learning when that uncertainty set is unknown and centered on a misspecified environment that supplies the observations. The learner must therefore estimate the uncertainty set from samples while learning robust behavior.

The authors develop an estimation approach and two online, incremental algorithms: robust Q-learning for tabular problems and robust TDC for function approximation. Their convergence results differ in strength. Robust Q-learning converges to the optimal robust Q function, while robust TDC converges asymptotically to stationary points. The latter result does not claim convergence to a global optimum.

The analysis avoids additional discount-factor conditions required by the cited earlier result. Finite-time bounds also show convergence as fast as the corresponding standard algorithms, within a constant factor. Numerical experiments further support robustness. The authors explain that the approach can extend to other methods, including TD and SARSA, making sample-based uncertainty estimation a potentially reusable component of online robust learning.
summary.tldr: Sample-based uncertainty estimation enables online robust reinforcement-learning algorithms with convergence guarantees and rates comparable to their standard counterparts.

title: Online Robust Reinforcement Learning with Model Uncertainty

abstract: Self-Driven Particles (SDP) describe a category of multi-agent systems common in everyday life, such as flocking birds and traffic flows. In a SDP system, each agent pursues its own goal and constantly changes its cooperative or competitive behaviors with its nearby agents. Manually designing the controllers for such SDP system is time-consuming, while the resulting emergent behaviors are often not realistic nor generalizable. Thus the realistic simulation of SDP systems remains challenging. Reinforcement learning provides an appealing alternative for automating the development of the controller for SDP. However, previous multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods define the agents to be teammates or enemies before hand, which fail to capture the essence of SDP where the role of each agent varies to be cooperative or competitive even within one episode. To simulate SDP with MARL, a key challenge is to coordinate agents' behaviors while still maximizing individual objectives. Taking traffic simulation as the testing bed, in this work we develop a novel MARL method called Coordinated Policy Optimization (CoPO), which incorporates social psychology principle to learn neural controller for SDP. Experiments show that the proposed method can achieve superior performance compared to MARL baselines in various metrics. Noticeably the trained vehicles exhibit complex and diverse social behaviors that improve performance and safety of the population as a whole. Demo video and source code are available at: https://decisionforce.github.io/CoPO/

paragraphs: Systems such as traffic and bird flocks contain agents pursuing individual goals while continually adjusting to nearby agents. Their relationships can shift between cooperation and competition within a single episode. This makes realistic simulation difficult for controllers designed manually or for learning methods that assign fixed teammate and opponent roles.

Coordinated Policy Optimization, or CoPO, addresses the challenge of coordinating behavior while preserving individual objectives. It uses a principle from social psychology within a multi-agent reinforcement learning method to train neural controllers. Traffic simulation serves as the testing environment, where vehicles must pursue their own objectives while interacting with the surrounding population.

The experiments report better performance than the compared multi-agent reinforcement learning baselines across various metrics. Trained vehicles exhibit complex and varied social behaviors that improve population-level performance and safety. The findings show that learning coordination can support useful collective outcomes even when participants have individual goals. They provide evidence for the approach in traffic simulation, the application used to evaluate the proposed method.
summary.tldr: CoPO learns traffic controllers that balance individual goals and coordination, producing diverse social behaviors and improved population outcomes in simulation.

title: Learning to Simulate Self-driven Particles System with Coordinated Policy Optimization

abstract: Machine-learning systems such as self-driving cars or virtual assistants are composed of a large number of machine-learning models that recognize image content, transcribe speech, analyze natural language, infer preferences, rank options, etc. Models in these systems are often developed and trained independently, which raises an obvious concern: Can improving a machine-learning model make the overall system worse? We answer this question affirmatively by showing that improving a model can deteriorate the performance of downstream models, even after those downstream models are retrained. Such self-defeating improvements are the result of entanglement between the models in the system. We perform an error decomposition of systems with multiple machine-learning models, which sheds light on the types of errors that can lead to self-defeating improvements. We also present the results of experiments which show that self-defeating improvements emerge in a realistic stereo-based detection system for cars and pedestrians.
originalAbstract: Machine-learning systems such as self-driving cars or virtual assistants are composed of a large number of machine-learning models that recognize image content, transcribe speech, analyze natural language, infer preferences, rank options, etc. Models in these systems are often developed and trained independently, which raises an obvious concern: Can improving a machine-learning model make the overall system worse? We answer this question affirmatively by showing that improving a model can deteriorate the performance of downstream models, even after those downstream models are retrained. Such self-defeating improvements are the result of entanglement between the models in the system. We perform an error decomposition of systems with multiple machine-learning models, which sheds light on the types of errors that can lead to self-defeating improvements. We also present the results of experiments which show that self-defeating improvements emerge in a realistic stereo-based detection system for cars and pedestrians.

paragraphs: Many machine-learning products combine several models, each handling a different part of a larger task. These components are often trained and evaluated independently. This paper asks whether improving one component can actually reduce the performance of the system that uses it, and shows that this can happen.

The problem arises from entanglement between models: downstream performance depends on the behavior of upstream components, not just their individual scores. The authors show that the damage can persist even after downstream models are retrained. They develop an error decomposition for systems containing multiple models to clarify which kinds of errors can produce these self-defeating improvements.

It establishes that a better component score alone is insufficient to guarantee a better overall result. The analysis makes the relationship between errors across components central to understanding whether an apparent improvement will help the complete system.
summary.tldr: Improving an individual model can worsen a larger machine-learning system, even after downstream components are retrained.

title: Fixes That Fail: Self-Defeating Improvements in Machine-Learning Systems

abstract: According to Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) theory~\cite{mcclelland1995there} in neuroscience, humans do effective \emph{continual learning} through two complementary systems: a fast learning system centered on the hippocampus for rapid learning of the specifics and individual experiences, and a slow learning system located in the neocortex for the gradual acquisition of structured knowledge about the environment. Motivated by this theory, we propose a novel continual learning framework named ``DualNet", which comprises a fast learning system for supervised learning of pattern-separated representation from specific tasks and a slow learning system for unsupervised representation learning of task-agnostic general representation via a Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) technique. The two fast and slow learning systems are complementary and work seamlessly in a holistic continual learning framework. Our extensive experiments on two challenging continual learning benchmarks of CORE50 and miniImageNet show that DualNet outperforms state-of-the-art continual learning methods by a large margin. We further conduct ablation studies of different SSL objectives to validate DualNet's efficacy, robustness, and scalability. Code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/phquang/DualNet}.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires a model to keep learning as it encounters tasks and experiences over time. DualNet takes inspiration from Complementary Learning Systems theory, which describes human learning through interacting fast and slow systems. The paper translates this motivation into a neural learning framework with two components assigned different representation-learning roles.

The fast component uses supervision to learn representations that distinguish patterns associated with specific tasks. The slow component uses self-supervised learning to acquire a more general representation that is not tied to any one task. Their intended complementarity comes from combining rapid learning of particular experiences with broader structure learned without task-specific supervision. Both operate within one continual learning framework.

Experiments on CORE50 and miniImageNet report that DualNet exceeds leading continual learning methods by a large margin. The authors also examine different self-supervised objectives through ablation studies to assess efficacy, robustness, and scalability. The findings support combining task-specific supervised learning with general self-supervised representation learning, with evidence drawn from the two evaluated benchmarks rather than a universal claim about continual learning.
summary.tldr: DualNet combines fast supervised task learning with slow self-supervised representation learning, improving performance on two continual learning benchmarks.

title: DualNet: Continual Learning, Fast and Slow

abstract: Deep learning (DL) systems are notoriously difficult to test and debug due to the lack of correctness proof and the huge test input space to cover. Given the ubiquitous unlabeled test data and high labeling cost, in this paper, we propose a novel test prioritization technique, namely TestRank, which aims at revealing more model failures with less labeling effort. TestRank brings order into the unlabeled test data according to their likelihood of being a failure, i.e., their failure-revealing capabilities. Different from existing solutions, TestRank leverages both intrinsic and contextual attributes of the unlabeled test data when prioritizing them. To be specific, we first build a similarity graph on both unlabeled test samples and labeled samples (e.g., training or previously labeled test samples). Then, we conduct graph-based semi-supervised learning to extract contextual features from the correctness of similar labeled samples. For a particular test instance, the contextual features extracted with the graph neural network and the intrinsic features obtained with the DL model itself are combined to predict its failure-revealing capability. Finally, TestRank prioritizes unlabeled test inputs in descending order of the above probability value. We evaluate TestRank on three popular image classification datasets, and results show that TestRank significantly outperforms existing test prioritization techniques.

paragraphs: Testing a deep-learning model can involve far more unlabeled inputs than people can afford to label. TestRank aims to make that labeling effort more productive by ordering inputs according to how likely they are to reveal a model failure. The goal is to find more mistakes with fewer labeled test examples.

The method combines information from each input with information about similar examples. It first builds a similarity graph containing both unlabeled samples and already labeled samples. Graph-based semi-supervised learning then extracts contextual features using whether the model was correct on similar labeled examples. These features supplement intrinsic features obtained from the model being tested.

TestRank combines the two feature sources to estimate each input's failure-revealing probability and ranks inputs from highest to lowest. Evaluations on three image-classification datasets show significant improvements over existing test-prioritization techniques. The result supports using the correctness of neighboring labeled examples as additional evidence when deciding which unknown cases deserve testing attention first.
summary.tldr: TestRank combines model features with graph-based context to prioritize unlabeled test inputs likely to expose failures.

title: TestRank: Bringing Order into Unlabeled Test Instances for Deep Learning Tasks

abstract: This paper considers the global geometry of general low-rank minimization problems via the Burer-Monterio factorization approach. For the rank-$1$ case, we prove that there is no spurious second-order critical point for both symmetric and asymmetric problems if the rank-$2$ RIP constant $\delta$ is less than $1/2$. Combining with a counterexample with $\delta=1/2$, we show that the derived bound is the sharpest possible. For the arbitrary rank-$r$ case, the same property is established when the rank-$2r$ RIP constant $\delta$ is at most $1/3$. We design a counterexample to show that the non-existence of spurious second-order critical points may not hold if $\delta$ is at least $1/2$. In addition, for any problem with $\delta$ between $1/3$ and $1/2$, we prove that all second-order critical points have a positive correlation to the ground truth. Finally, the strict saddle property, which can lead to the polynomial-time global convergence of various algorithms, is established for both the symmetric and asymmetric problems when the rank-$2r$ RIP constant $\delta$ is less than $1/3$. The results of this paper significantly extend several existing bounds in the literature.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix optimization can represent a matrix through smaller factors, but this creates a nonconvex optimization problem. The paper studies when its geometry avoids misleading second-order critical points: points that satisfy local derivative checks without solving the intended problem. Its guarantees depend on restricted isometry constants, which quantify a structural condition on the objective.

For rank one, the authors prove that symmetric and asymmetric problems have no such spurious points when the rank-two constant is below one-half. A counterexample at one-half makes this threshold sharp. Between one-third and one-half, every second-order critical point still has positive correlation with the ground truth. Below one-third, the authors also establish a strict saddle property for both problem types, which can support polynomial-time global convergence of various algorithms. These results distinguish exact recovery geometry from weaker alignment guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper sharpens structural conditions under which factored low-rank optimization avoids spurious second-order critical points and supports global convergence.

title: General Low-rank Matrix Optimization: Geometric Analysis and Sharper Bounds

abstract: We consider the problem of offline policy evaluation~(OPE) with Markov decision processes~(MDPs), where the goal is to estimate the utility of given decision-making policies based on static datasets. Recently, theoretical understanding of OPE has been rapidly advanced under (approximate) realizability assumptions, i.e., where the environments of interest are well approximated with the given hypothetical models. On the other hand, the OPE under unrealizability has not been well understood as much as in the realizable setting despite its importance in real-world applications.To address this issue, we study the behavior of a simple existing OPE method called the linear direct method~(DM) under the unrealizability. Consequently, we obtain an asymptotically exact characterization of the OPE error in a doubly robust form. Leveraging this result, we also establish the nonparametric consistency of the tile-coding estimators under quite mild assumptions.

paragraphs: Offline policy evaluation asks how useful a decision-making policy would be using only an existing dataset. Much of its theory assumes that the chosen model can represent, or closely approximate, the relevant environment. This paper examines the less understood situation where a linear model does not adequately represent that environment.

The authors analyze an existing estimator, the linear direct method, rather than introducing a new policy-learning procedure. Their main result characterizes its evaluation error asymptotically, meaning in the limit as the amount of data grows. The characterization is exact in that limit and has a doubly robust form, giving a structured account of error when model realizability cannot be assumed.

The authors then use this analysis to establish nonparametric consistency for tile-coding estimators under assumptions they describe as quite mild. Consistency means that estimation approaches the correct value as data grows under those conditions. The contribution therefore links an error analysis for misspecified linear evaluation to a positive convergence result for a particular family of estimators.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes the asymptotic error of linear offline policy evaluation under misspecification and establishes consistency for tile-coding estimators.

title: Asymptotically Exact Error Characterization of Offline Policy Evaluation with Misspecified Linear Models

abstract: Concept-based explanations permit to understand the predictions of a deep neural network (DNN) through the lens of concepts specified by users. Existing methods assume that the examples illustrating a concept are mapped in a fixed direction of the DNN's latent space. When this holds true, the concept can be represented by a concept activation vector (CAV) pointing in that direction. In this work, we propose to relax this assumption by allowing concept examples to be scattered across different clusters in the DNN's latent space. Each concept is then represented by a region of the DNN's latent space that includes these clusters and that we call concept activation region (CAR). To formalize this idea, we introduce an extension of the CAV formalism that is based on the kernel trick and support vector classifiers. This CAR formalism yields global concept-based explanations and local concept-based feature importance. We prove that CAR explanations built with radial kernels are invariant under latent space isometries. In this way, CAR assigns the same explanations to latent spaces that have the same geometry. We further demonstrate empirically that CARs offer (1) more accurate descriptions of how concepts are scattered in the DNN's latent space; (2) global explanations that are closer to human concept annotations and (3) concept-based feature importance that meaningfully relate concepts with each other. Finally, we use CARs to show that DNNs can autonomously rediscover known scientific concepts, such as the prostate cancer grading system.

This paper relaxes that assumption so a concept can occupy several separate clusters within that representation.

The proposed concept activation region, or CAR, covers those clusters rather than reducing the concept to one direction. The authors construct the framework using kernel methods and support vector classifiers. It produces both global concept-based explanations and local estimates of feature importance. They also prove that CAR explanations using radial kernels remain unchanged under transformations that preserve the geometry of the latent space.

Experiments show more accurate descriptions of concept distributions and global explanations that agree more closely with human annotations. The reported local explanations also meaningfully connect concepts with one another. Finally, the authors use CARs to demonstrate that networks can rediscover established scientific concepts, including prostate cancer grading concepts, through their learned representations.
summary.tldr: Concept activation regions explain neural networks using concepts that can span multiple clusters in their internal representations.

title: Concept Activation Regions: A Generalized Framework For Concept-Based Explanations

abstract: We study the problem of reward shaping to accelerate the training process of a reinforcement learning agent. Existing works have considered a number of different reward shaping formulations; however, they either require external domain knowledge or fail in environments with extremely sparse rewards. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, Exploration-Guided Reward Shaping (ExploRS), that operates in a fully self-supervised manner and can accelerate an agent's learning even in sparse-reward environments. The key idea of ExploRS is to learn an intrinsic reward function in combination with exploration-based bonuses to maximize the agent's utility w.r.t. extrinsic rewards. We theoretically showcase the usefulness of our reward shaping framework in a special family of MDPs. Experimental results on several environments with sparse/noisy reward signals demonstrate the effectiveness of ExploRS.

paragraphs: When useful rewards arrive rarely, a reinforcement learning agent receives little guidance about which behavior to develop. Reward shaping supplies additional learning signals to accelerate training. The paper argues that existing formulations can require outside domain knowledge or fail when the original reward signal is extremely sparse.

Exploration-Guided Reward Shaping, or ExploRS, combines a learned intrinsic reward function with exploration bonuses. The intrinsic reward is learned to improve the agent’s utility under the environment’s extrinsic rewards. This connects the additional training signal to the original task objective while retaining incentives to explore. The framework operates in a fully self-supervised manner.

The authors theoretically demonstrate the usefulness of this construction for a special family of Markov decision processes. Experiments in several environments with sparse or noisy rewards also demonstrate its effectiveness. Together, these results support the idea that exploration bonuses and learned reward shaping can complement each other. The theoretical result is specific to the analyzed family, while the broader practical evidence comes from the reported environments.
summary.tldr: ExploRS combines learned intrinsic rewards with exploration bonuses to accelerate learning from sparse or noisy task rewards.

title: Exploration-Guided Reward Shaping for Reinforcement Learning under Sparse Rewards

abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) produce good probabilistic models of functions, but most GP kernels require $O((n+m)n^2)$ time, where $n$ is the number of data points and $m$ the number of predictive locations. We present a new kernel that allows for Gaussian process regression in $O((n+m)\log(n+m))$ time. Our "binary tree" kernel places all data points on the leaves of a binary tree, with the kernel depending only on the depth of the deepest common ancestor. We can store the resulting kernel matrix in $O(n)$ space in $O(n \log n)$ time, as a sum of sparse rank-one matrices, and approximately invert the kernel matrix in $O(n)$ time. Sparse GP methods also offer linear run time, but they predict less well than higher dimensional kernels. On a classic suite of regression tasks, we compare our kernel against Mat\'ern, sparse, and sparse variational kernels. The binary tree GP assigns the highest likelihood to the test data on a plurality of datasets, usually achieves lower mean squared error than the sparse methods, and often ties or beats the Mat\'ern GP. On large datasets, the binary tree GP is fastest, and much faster than a Mat\'ern GP.

title: Log-Linear-Time Gaussian Processes Using Binary Tree Kernels

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated their superiority in practice. Arguably, the rapid development of DNNs is largely benefited from high-quality (open-sourced) datasets, based on which researchers and developers can easily evaluate and improve their learning methods. Since the data collection is usually time-consuming or even expensive, how to protect their copyrights is of great significance and worth further exploration. In this paper, we revisit dataset ownership verification. We find that existing verification methods introduced new security risks in DNNs trained on the protected dataset, due to the targeted nature of poison-only backdoor watermarks. To alleviate this problem, in this work, we explore the untargeted backdoor watermarking scheme, where the abnormal model behaviors are not deterministic. Specifically, we introduce two dispersibilities and prove their correlation, based on which we design the untargeted backdoor watermark under both poisoned-label and clean-label settings. We also discuss how to use the proposed untargeted backdoor watermark for dataset ownership verification. Experiments on benchmark datasets verify the effectiveness of our methods and their resistance to existing backdoor defenses.

paragraphs: Creating useful datasets can require substantial time and expense, motivating methods for verifying ownership. One approach embeds a watermark that affects models trained on the protected data. The paper finds that existing poison-only backdoor watermarks introduce security risks because they induce targeted behavior, tying ownership verification to a particular abnormal model response.

The authors investigate untargeted backdoor watermarking, where abnormal behavior is not deterministic. They introduce two dispersibility quantities, prove a relationship between them, and use that relationship to design watermarks. The proposed designs cover both poisoned-label and clean-label settings, allowing the ownership-verification approach to be studied with and without changes to training labels.

Experiments on benchmark datasets support the methods' effectiveness and their resistance to existing backdoor defenses. The paper also discusses how the watermarks can be used to verify dataset ownership. Its contribution is a scheme intended to alleviate risks associated with targeted watermark behavior; the stated experimental findings establish effectiveness and resistance in the tested settings rather than universal harmlessness.
summary.tldr: Untargeted backdoor watermarks support dataset ownership verification while aiming to reduce risks from deterministic targeted behavior.

title: Untargeted Backdoor Watermark: Towards Harmless and Stealthy Dataset Copyright Protection

abstract: We study the Combinatorial Thompson Sampling policy (CTS) for combinatorial multi-armed bandit problems (CMAB), within an approximation regret setting. Although CTS has attracted a lot of interest, it has a drawback that other usual CMAB policies do not have when considering non-exact oracles: for some oracles, CTS has a poor approximation regret (scaling linearly with the time horizon $T$) [Wang and Chen, 2018]. A study is then necessary to discriminate the oracles on which CTS could learn. This study was started by Kong et al. [2021]: they gave the first approximation regret analysis of CTS for the greedy oracle, obtaining an upper bound of order $\mathcal{O}{\left(\log(T)/\Delta^2\right)}$, where $\Delta$ is some minimal reward gap. In this paper, our objective is to push this study further than the simple case of the greedy oracle. We provide the first $\mathcal{O}{\left(\log(T)/\Delta\right)}$ approximation regret upper bound for CTS, obtained under a specific condition on the approximation oracle, allowing a reduction to the exact oracle analysis. We thus term this condition Reduce2Exact, and observe that it is satisfied in many concrete examples. Moreover, it can be extended to the probabilistically triggered arms setting, thus capturing even more problems, such as online influence maximization.

paragraphs: Combinatorial Thompson Sampling chooses combinations of actions while learning their rewards. When finding an exact best combination is difficult, it can rely on an approximation oracle. But this substitution can undermine learning: for some oracles, approximation regret grows linearly with time. This paper asks which oracle properties permit a stronger learning guarantee.

The authors introduce a condition called Reduce2Exact that allows analysis with an approximate oracle to be reduced to exact-oracle analysis. Under that condition, they prove an O(log(T)/Delta) upper bound on approximation regret, where T is the time horizon and Delta is a minimal reward gap. This improves the gap dependence over an earlier O(log(T)/Delta²) bound established for the greedy oracle.

The condition holds in many concrete examples and extends to settings where actions trigger arms probabilistically, including online influence maximization. Its importance is that the guarantee covers an identifiable class of approximation procedures beyond the greedy case. The result remains conditional: it does not claim that an arbitrary approximate oracle makes Thompson Sampling learn effectively.
summary.tldr: The Reduce2Exact oracle condition yields an O(log(T)/Delta) approximation-regret bound for Combinatorial Thompson Sampling.

title: When Combinatorial Thompson Sampling meets Approximation Regret

abstract: Data-Augmentation (DA) is known to improve performance across tasks and datasets. We propose a method to theoretically analyze the effect of DA and study questions such as: how many augmented samples are needed to correctly estimate the information encoded by that DA? How does the augmentation policy impact the final parameters of a model? We derive several quantities in close-form, such as the expectation and variance of an image, loss, and model's output under a given DA distribution. Up to our knowledge, we obtain the first explicit regularizer that corresponds to using DA during training for non-trivial transformations such as affine transformations, color jittering, or Gaussian blur. Those derivations open new avenues to quantify the benefits and limitations of DA. For example, given a loss at hand, we find that common DAs require tens of thousands of samples for the loss to be correctly estimated and for the model training to converge. We then show that for a training loss to have reduced variance under DA sampling, the model's saliency map (gradient of the loss with respect to the model's input) must align with the smallest eigenvector of the sample's covariance matrix under the considered DA augmentation; this is exactly the quantity estimated and regularized by TangentProp. Those findings also hint at a possible explanation on why models tend to shift their focus from edges to textures when specific DAs are employed.

We derive several quantities in close-form, such as the expectation and variance of an image, loss, and model's output under a given DA distribution. Up to our knowledge, we obtain the first explicit regularizer that corresponds to using DA during training for non-trivial transformations such as affine transformations, color jittering, or Gaussian blur. Those derivations open new avenues to quantify the benefits and limitations of DA. For example, given a loss at hand, we find that common DAs require tens of thousands of samples for the loss to be correctly estimated and for the model training to converge. We then show that for a training loss to have reduced variance under DA sampling, the model's saliency map (gradient of the loss with respect to the model's input) must align with the smallest eigenvector of the sample's covariance matrix under the considered DA augmentation; this is exactly the quantity estimated and regularized by TangentProp. Those findings also hint at a possible explanation on why models tend to shift their focus from edges to textures when specific DAs are employed.

paragraphs: Data augmentation trains a model on transformed versions of its inputs, but the information supplied by those transformations can be difficult to quantify. This paper develops an analytical approach to studying that information. It derives closed-form expectations and variances for augmented images, model outputs, and losses under a specified augmentation distribution.

These calculations connect augmentation to explicit regularization for transformations including affine changes, color jittering, and Gaussian blur. They also address how many randomly augmented samples are needed to estimate a loss accurately. For the losses and common augmentations considered, the authors find that this can require tens of thousands of samples, showing why sampling variability matters for training.

The analysis further identifies an alignment requirement for reducing loss variance: the input gradient of the loss must align with the smallest-eigenvalue direction of the augmented sample covariance. This connects the result to what TangentProp estimates and regularizes. The findings also suggest a possible explanation for shifts from edge-based to texture-based attention under particular augmentations.
summary.tldr: Closed-form analysis connects data augmentation to regularization, sampling requirements, and the directions of input sensitivity that reduce loss variance.

title: A Data-Augmentation Is Worth A Thousand Samples: Analytical Moments And Sampling-Free Training

abstract: Selecting subsets of features that differentiate between two conditions is a key task in a broad range of scientific domains. In many applications, the features of interest form clusters with similar effects on the data at hand. To recover such clusters we develop DiSC, a data-driven approach for detecting groups of features that differentiate between conditions. For each condition, we construct a graph whose nodes correspond to the features and whose weights are functions of the similarity between them for that condition. We then apply a spectral approach to compute subsets of nodes whose connectivity pattern differs significantly between the condition-specific feature graphs. On the theoretical front, we analyze our approach with a toy example based on the stochastic block model. We evaluate DiSC on a variety of datasets, including MNIST, hyperspectral imaging, simulated scRNA-seq and task fMRI, and demonstrate that DiSC uncovers features that better differentiate between conditions compared to competing methods.

paragraphs: When comparing two conditions, useful differences may involve groups of related features rather than isolated measurements. DiSC is designed to find such groups. Its central idea is to examine how relationships among features change between conditions, using those changes to identify subsets that distinguish the conditions.

The method builds a separate graph for each condition. Each node represents a feature, and connections are weighted according to feature similarity within that condition. A spectral procedure then searches for groups of nodes whose connection patterns differ substantially between the two graphs. This makes the organization of features part of the selection process, rather than considering only individual features independently.

The authors analyze the approach through a simplified example based on the stochastic block model. They also test it on MNIST, hyperspectral images, simulated single-cell RNA sequencing data, and task-based functional MRI. Across these evaluations, DiSC identifies features that distinguish conditions better than competing methods. The results support comparing condition-specific feature relationships as a useful route to discovering informative groups.
summary.tldr: DiSC finds groups of discriminative features by comparing their similarity graphs across two conditions.

title: DiSC: Differential Spectral Clustering of Features

abstract: We study two of the most popular performance metrics in medical image segmentation, Accuracy and Dice, when the target labels are noisy. For both metrics, several statements related to characterization and volume properties of the set of optimal segmentations are proved, and associated experiments are provided. Our main insights are: (i) the volume of the solutions to both metrics may deviate significantly from the expected volume of the target, (ii) the volume of a solution to Accuracy is always less than or equal to the volume of a solution to Dice and (iii) the optimal solutions to both of these metrics coincide when the set of feasible segmentations is constrained to the set of segmentations with the volume equal to the expected volume of the target.

paragraphs: Medical image segmentation assigns parts of an image to a target region, whose volume can be an important property of the result. This paper studies optimal segmentations under two common evaluation metrics, Accuracy and Dice, when target labels are noisy. It examines both what the optimal solutions look like and how much volume they contain.

The authors prove that optimizing either metric can produce a volume substantially different from the expected target volume. They also establish an ordering: an Accuracy-optimal solution has volume no greater than a Dice-optimal solution. Thus, the choice of metric has a systematic relationship with predicted volume, even when each solution is optimal for its own criterion.

A further result identifies a condition under which the metrics agree. If feasible segmentations must have volume equal to the expected target volume, their optimal solutions coincide. Experiments accompany the theoretical statements. Together, the findings show why metric optimality alone does not ensure volume agreement with a noisy target, and how a specific volume constraint reconciles the two objectives.
summary.tldr: With noisy segmentation labels, Accuracy and Dice can favor different volumes, but their optima coincide under an expected-target-volume constraint.

title: On Image Segmentation With Noisy Labels: Characterization and Volume Properties of the Optimal Solutions to Accuracy and Dice

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning methods hold the promise of learning policies from pre-collected datasets without the need to query the environment for new samples. This setting is particularly well-suited for continuous control robotic applications for which online data collection based on trial-and-error is costly and potentially unsafe. In practice, offline datasets are often heterogeneous, i.e., collected in a variety of scenarios, such as data from several human demonstrators or from policies that act with different purposes. Unfortunately, such datasets often contain action distributions with multiple modes and, in some cases, lack a sufficient number of high-reward trajectories, which render offline policy training inefficient. To address this challenge, we propose to leverage latent-variable generative model to represent high-advantage state-action pairs leading to better adherence to data distributions that contributes to solving the task, while maximizing reward via a policy over the latent variable. As we empirically show on a range of simulated locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tasks, our method referred to as latent-variable advantage-weighted policy optimization (LAPO), improves the average performance of the next best-performing offline reinforcement learning methods by 49\% on heterogeneous datasets, and by 8\% on datasets with narrow and biased distributions.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning builds policies from previously collected data without requesting new environmental interactions. LAPO targets datasets assembled from different demonstrators or policies, which can contain several distinct patterns of action. Such datasets may also include too few high-reward trajectories, making policy learning difficult.

The method uses a latent-variable generative model to represent state-action pairs with high advantage. This emphasizes parts of the observed behavior that contribute to solving the task while accommodating varied action patterns. A policy operating over the latent variable then seeks higher rewards through that representation.

The authors evaluate LAPO on simulated locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tasks. They report average performance improvements over the next best-performing offline methods of 49% on heterogeneous datasets and 8% on datasets with narrow, biased distributions. These results support the proposed combination of expressive action modeling and advantage-based emphasis in the evaluated settings. The reported gains concern learning from existing datasets, consistent with the method's offline objective.
summary.tldr: LAPO uses an advantage-weighted latent action model to improve offline policy learning, especially on the evaluated heterogeneous datasets.

title: LAPO: Latent-Variable Advantage-Weighted Policy Optimization for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) is an inference algorithm for state space models that approximates the posterior by sampling from a sequence of target distributions. The target distributions are often chosen to be the filtering distributions, but these ignore information from future observations, leading to practical and theoretical limitations in inference and model learning. We introduce SIXO, a method that instead learns target distributions that approximate the smoothing distributions, incorporating information from all observations. The key idea is to use density ratio estimation to fit functions that warp the filtering distributions into the smoothing distributions. We then use SMC with these learned targets to define a variational objective for model and proposal learning. SIXO yields provably tighter log marginal lower bounds and offers more accurate posterior inferences and parameter estimates in a variety of domains.

paragraphs: Sequential Monte Carlo approximates hidden-state distributions by sampling through a sequence of targets. Those targets commonly use filtering distributions, which incorporate observations only up to the current point. SIXO instead seeks targets resembling smoothing distributions, allowing later observations to inform inference about earlier hidden states.

The method learns functions that transform filtering targets toward smoothing targets through density-ratio estimation. Intuitively, the learned functions adjust how states are weighted so that the target reflects information from the full observation sequence. The authors then use Sequential Monte Carlo with these learned targets to construct a variational objective for learning both the model and its sampling proposals.

The paper establishes tighter lower bounds on the log marginal likelihood and reports more accurate posterior inference and parameter estimates across several domains. These contributions connect better use of observations with both inference and learning: changing the intermediate targets can improve the approximation of hidden states and the objective used to fit the underlying model.
summary.tldr: SIXO learns smoothing-aware sampling targets that incorporate future observations, yielding tighter likelihood bounds and improved inference and parameter estimation.

title: SIXO: Smoothing Inference with Twisted Objectives

abstract: Recommender systems (RS) have to select the top-N items from a massive item set. For the sake of efficient recommendation, RS usually represents user and item as latent embeddings, and relies on approximate nearest neighbour search (ANNs) to retrieve the recommendation result. Despite the reduction of running time, the representation learning is independent of ANNs index construction; thus, the two operations can be incompatible, which results in potential loss of recommendation accuracy. To overcome the above problem, we propose the Recommender Forest (a.k.a., RecForest), which jointly learns latent embedding and index for efficient and high-fidelity recommendation. RecForest consists of multiple k-ary trees, each of which is a partition of the item set via hierarchical balanced clustering such that each item is uniquely represented by a path from the root to a leaf. Given such a data structure, an encoder-decoder based routing network is developed: it first encodes the context, i.e., user information, into hidden states; then, leveraging a transformer-based decoder, it identifies the top-N items via beam search. Compared with the existing methods, RecForest brings in the following advantages: 1) the false partition of the boundary items can be effectively alleviated by the use of multiple trees; 2) the routing operation becomes much more accurate thanks to the powerful transformer decoder; 3) the tree parameters are shared across different tree levels, making the index to be extremely memory-efficient. The experimental studies are performed on five popular recommendation datasets: with a significantly simplified training cost, RecForest outperforms competitive baseline approaches in terms of both recommendation accuracy and efficiency.

paragraphs: Large recommender systems must retrieve a small number of useful items from enormous collections. A common approach learns user and item embeddings, then builds an approximate nearest-neighbor index separately. RecForest addresses the possible mismatch between those stages by learning the representations and retrieval index together, aiming for both efficient search and accurate recommendations.

The index contains multiple branching trees built through hierarchical balanced clustering of items. Within each tree, an item corresponds to a unique route from the root to a leaf. A routing network encodes user information and uses a Transformer decoder with beam search to identify promising items. Multiple trees help alleviate errors involving items near partition boundaries.

Parameters are shared across tree levels to reduce index memory requirements. The authors evaluate RecForest on five recommendation datasets and report better accuracy and efficiency than competitive baselines, along with substantially simplified training cost. The results support treating retrieval structure as part of the learning problem, so that the model’s representations and the routes used to access items develop together.
summary.tldr: RecForest jointly learns item representations and a multi-tree retrieval index, improving recommendation accuracy and efficiency in five dataset evaluations.

title: Recommender Forest for Efficient Retrieval

abstract: Transfer-based attacks generate adversarial examples on the surrogate model, which can mislead other black-box models without access, making it promising to attack real-world applications. Recently, several works have been proposed to boost adversarial transferability, in which the surrogate model is usually overlooked. In this work, we identify that non-linear layers (e.g., ReLU, max-pooling, etc.) truncate the gradient during backward propagation, making the gradient w.r.t. input image imprecise to the loss function. We hypothesize and empirically validate that such truncation undermines the transferability of adversarial examples. Based on these findings, we propose a novel method called Backward Propagation Attack (BPA) to increase the relevance between the gradient w.r.t. input image and loss function so as to generate adversarial examples with higher transferability. Specifically, BPA adopts a non-monotonic function as the derivative of ReLU and incorporates softmax with temperature to smooth the derivative of max-pooling, thereby mitigating the information loss during the backward propagation of gradients. Empirical results on the ImageNet dataset demonstrate that not only does our method substantially boost the adversarial transferability, but it is also general to existing transfer-based attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/Trustworthy-AI-Group/RPA.

paragraphs: Transfer-based adversarial attacks create examples using a surrogate model and then apply them to other models without accessing those targets. This paper investigates how the surrogate’s backward computation affects that transfer. The authors focus on nonlinear layers that truncate gradients, including ReLU and max-pooling.

They hypothesize that this truncation weakens the relationship between input gradients and the loss, thereby reducing adversarial transferability, and report empirical support for that hypothesis. Their Backward Propagation Attack changes the backward rules: it uses a non-monotonic function in place of the ReLU derivative and temperature-controlled softmax to smooth the max-pooling derivative.

These modifications aim to preserve more information as gradients propagate backward through the surrogate. Experiments on ImageNet show substantially improved transferability, and the method can be used with existing transfer-based attacks. The contribution identifies backward propagation as an important component of transfer performance and supplies a concrete way to alter it, with the effectiveness established empirically in the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: BPA modifies surrogate-model backward rules to reduce gradient information loss and empirically improve adversarial transferability.

title: Rethinking the Backward Propagation for Adversarial Transferability

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit in-context learning abilities which enable the same model to perform several tasks without any task-specific training. In contrast, traditional adaptation approaches, such as fine-tuning, modify the underlying models for each specific task. In-context learning, however, consistently underperforms task-specific tuning approaches even when presented with the same examples. While most existing approaches (e.g., prompt engineering) focus on the LLM's learned representations to patch this performance gap, our experiments actually reveal that LLM representations contain sufficient information to make good predictions. As such, we focus on the LLM's reasoning abilities and demonstrate that this performance gap exists due to their inability to perform simple probabilistic reasoning tasks. This raises an intriguing question: Are LLMs actually capable of learning how to reason in a task-agnostic manner? We answer this in the affirmative and, as a proof of concept, propose TART which generically improves an LLM's reasoning abilities using a synthetically trained reasoning module. TART trains this Transformer-based reasoning module in a task-agnostic manner using only synthetic logistic regression tasks and composes it with an arbitrary real-world pre-trained model without any additional training. With a single inference module, TART improves performance across different model families (GPT-Neo, Pythia, Bloom), model sizes (100M - 6B), tasks (14 NLP classification tasks), and even across different modalities (audio and vision). On the RAFT Benchmark, TART improves GPT-Neo (125M)'s performance such that it outperforms Bloom (176B), and is within $4$% of GPT-3.

summary.tldr: TART learns a reusable reasoning module from synthetic logistic-regression tasks and improves predictions across tested pretrained models, tasks, and modalities.

title: TART: A plug-and-play Transformer module for task-agnostic reasoning

abstract: Hyperbolic spaces have been quite popular in the recent past for representing hierarchically organized data. Further, several classification algorithms for data in these spaces have been proposed in the literature. These algorithms mainly use either hyperplanes or geodesics for decision boundaries in a large margin classifiers setting leading to a non-convex optimization problem. In this paper, we propose a novel large margin classifier based on horospherical decision boundaries that leads to a geodesically convex optimization problem that can be optimized using any Riemannian gradient descent technique guaranteeing a globally optimal solution. We present several experiments depicting the competitive performance of our classifier in comparison to SOTA.
originalAbstract: Hyperbolic spaces have been quite popular in the recent past for representing hierarchically organized data. Further, several classification algorithms for data in these spaces have been proposed in the literature. These algorithms mainly use either hyperplanes or geodesics for decision boundaries in a large margin classifiers setting leading to a non-convex optimization problem. In this paper, we propose a novel large margin classifier based on horospherical decision boundaries that leads to a geodesically convex optimization problem that can be optimized using any Riemannian gradient descent technique guaranteeing a globally optimal solution. We present several experiments depicting the competitive performance of our classifier in comparison to SOTA.

paragraphs: Hyperbolic spaces are useful for representing hierarchically organized data, but building a classifier in those spaces also requires choosing an appropriate decision boundary. Existing large-margin approaches often use hyperplanes or geodesics. According to the paper, these choices lead to nonconvex optimization problems, making the training objective itself a central difficulty.

The authors propose using horospherical decision boundaries instead. The key consequence is geometric: the resulting optimization problem is geodesically convex, meaning convexity is expressed along paths appropriate to the curved space. This gives the proposed classifier a globally optimal solution guarantee through Riemannian gradient descent techniques, as stated in the abstract.

Experiments show competitive performance against state-of-the-art classifiers. The significance lies in pairing that empirical competitiveness with a more favorable optimization formulation. The guarantee concerns optimizing the proposed classifier's objective; the reported predictive finding is competitive performance, rather than universal superiority over other classifiers. The work illustrates how changing the boundary geometry can improve the mathematical structure of learning in a non-Euclidean representation.
summary.tldr: Horospherical boundaries make a hyperbolic large-margin classifier geodesically convex while retaining competitive empirical performance.

title: Horospherical Decision Boundaries for Large Margin Classification in Hyperbolic Space

abstract: Even though trained mainly on images, we discover that pretrained diffusion models show impressive power in guiding sketch synthesis. In this paper, we present DiffSketcher, an innovative algorithm that creates \textit{vectorized} free-hand sketches using natural language input. DiffSketcher is developed based on a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion model. It performs the task by directly optimizing a set of Bézier curves with an extended version of the score distillation sampling (SDS) loss, which allows us to use a raster-level diffusion model as a prior for optimizing a parametric vectorized sketch generator. Furthermore, we explore attention maps embedded in the diffusion model for effective stroke initialization to speed up the generation process. The generated sketches demonstrate multiple levels of abstraction while maintaining recognizability, underlying structure, and essential visual details of the subject drawn. Our experiments show that DiffSketcher achieves greater quality than prior work. The code and demo of DiffSketcher can be found at https://ximinng.github.io/DiffSketcher-project/.
