paragraphs: DiffSketcher turns a natural-language description into a vector sketch using a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model. The central observation is that a model trained mainly on images can still provide useful guidance for drawing. The output is represented by curves, allowing the synthesis process to work directly with the strokes that form the sketch.

The method optimizes a collection of Bézier curves through an extended score distillation sampling loss. This connects an image-based diffusion prior to a parametric vector sketch generator: the diffusion model supplies guidance while the optimized representation remains a set of curves. The authors also use attention maps inside the diffusion model to initialize strokes more effectively and accelerate generation.

The resulting sketches exhibit different degrees of abstraction while retaining recognizable subjects, underlying structure, and essential details. Experiments report higher sketch quality than prior work. The approach matters because it transfers the guidance available in a pretrained image model into a different visual representation, without making raster pixels the final representation being optimized.
summary.tldr: DiffSketcher uses a pretrained diffusion model to guide direct optimization of vector strokes into recognizable text-prompted sketches.

title: DiffSketcher: Text Guided Vector Sketch Synthesis through Latent Diffusion Models

abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance as few-shot learners. However, their security risks under such settings are largely unexplored. In this work, we conduct a pilot study showing that PLMs as few-shot learners are highly vulnerable to backdoor attacks while existing defenses are inadequate due to the unique challenges of few-shot scenarios. To address such challenges, we advocate MDP, a novel lightweight, pluggable, and effective defense for PLMs as few-shot learners. Specifically, MDP leverages the gap between the masking-sensitivity of poisoned and clean samples: with reference to the limited few-shot data as distributional anchors, it compares the representations of given samples under varying masking and identifies poisoned samples as ones with significant variations. We show analytically that MDP creates an interesting dilemma for the attacker to choose between attack effectiveness and detection evasiveness. The empirical evaluation using benchmark datasets and representative attacks validates the efficacy of MDP. The code of MDP is publicly available.

paragraphs: Language models can learn tasks from very few examples, but that limited-data setting also creates challenges for detecting backdoor attacks. The paper begins with a pilot study finding that pretrained language models used as few-shot learners are highly vulnerable and that existing defenses are inadequate for the particular demands of this setting.

The proposed defense, MDP, examines how a sample’s internal representation changes when different parts of it are masked. It uses the small set of available few-shot examples as reference points for the data distribution. Samples whose representations vary substantially under masking are identified as poisoned, exploiting a difference in masking sensitivity between clean and poisoned inputs.

The authors analytically show that this detection strategy creates a trade-off for attackers between maintaining attack effectiveness and avoiding detection. Evaluations with benchmark datasets and representative attacks support the defense’s effectiveness. MDP is presented as lightweight and pluggable, making the main contribution a detection mechanism suited to scarce reference data rather than a requirement to build a separate defense around abundant examples.
summary.tldr: MDP detects backdoor-poisoned inputs in few-shot language learning by measuring representation changes under masking.

title: Defending Pre-trained Language Models as Few-shot Learners against Backdoor Attacks

abstract: We consider contextual bandit problems with knapsacks [CBwK], a problem where at each round, a scalar reward is obtained and vector-valued costs are suffered. The learner aims to maximize the cumulative rewards while ensuring that the cumulative costs are lower than some predetermined cost constraints. We assume that contexts come from a continuous set, that costs can be signed, and that the expected reward and cost functions, while unknown, may be uniformly estimated---a typical assumption in the literature. In this setting, total cost constraints had so far to be at least of order $T^{3/4}$, where $T$ is the number of rounds, and were even typically assumed to depend linearly on $T$. We are however motivated to use CBwK to impose a fairness constraint of equalized average costs between groups: the budget associated with the corresponding cost constraints should be as close as possible to the natural deviations, of order $\sqrt{T}$. To that end, we introduce a dual strategy based on projected-gradient-descent updates, that is able to deal with total-cost constraints of the order of $\sqrt{T}$ up to poly-logarithmic terms. This strategy is more direct and simpler than existing strategies in the literature. It relies on a careful, adaptive, tuning of the step size.

title: Small Total-Cost Constraints in Contextual Bandits with Knapsacks, with Application to Fairness

abstract: Applying reinforcement learning (RL) to combinatorial optimization problems is attractive as it removes the need for expert knowledge or pre-solved instances. However, it is unrealistic to expect an agent to solve these (often NP-)hard problems in a single shot at inference due to their inherent complexity. Thus, leading approaches often implement additional search strategies, from stochastic sampling and beam-search to explicit fine-tuning. In this paper, we argue for the benefits of learning a population of complementary policies, which can be simultaneously rolled out at inference. To this end, we introduce Poppy, a simple training procedure for populations. Instead of relying on a predefined or hand-crafted notion of diversity, Poppy induces an unsupervised specialization targeted solely at maximizing the performance of the population. We show that Poppy produces a set of complementary policies, and obtains state-of-the-art RL results on three popular NP-hard problems: traveling salesman, capacitated vehicle routing, and job-shop scheduling.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can produce combinatorial optimization policies without requiring expert-designed solutions or pre-solved training instances. Yet difficult optimization problems often need more than a single attempt at inference. This paper proposes learning a population of complementary policies whose solutions can be generated simultaneously.

The training procedure, Poppy, encourages specialization through the performance of the population as a whole. It does not require a manually specified definition of diversity. The motivation is that policies should differ in ways that improve collective solution quality, allowing different members to contribute useful behavior across the problems they encounter.

Experiments show that Poppy learns complementary policies and achieves state-of-the-art reinforcement-learning results on traveling salesman, capacitated vehicle routing, and job-shop scheduling problems. These findings support population training as an effective way to prepare multiple solution attempts for inference. The reported advances concern reinforcement-learning approaches on those three NP-hard problem families, where coordinated specialization provides a useful alternative source of solution diversity.
summary.tldr: Poppy trains complementary policy populations through collective performance, achieving leading reinforcement-learning results on three combinatorial optimization problems.

title: Winner Takes It All: Training Performant RL Populations for Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: Privacy-preserving instance encoding aims to encode raw data into feature vectors without revealing their privacy-sensitive information. When designed properly, these encodings can be used for downstream ML applications such as training and inference with limited privacy risk. However, the vast majority of existing schemes do not theoretically justify that their encoding is non-invertible, and their privacy-enhancing properties are only validated empirically against a limited set of attacks. In this paper, we propose a theoretically-principled measure for the invertibility of instance encoding based on Fisher information that is broadly applicable to a wide range of popular encoders. We show that dFIL can be used to bound the invertibility of encodings both theoretically and empirically, providing an intuitive interpretation of the privacy of instance encoding.

paragraphs: Privacy-preserving instance encoding converts raw inputs into feature vectors intended to support machine learning without revealing sensitive information. Its usefulness depends partly on how difficult it is to recover the original input from its encoding. The paper focuses on giving that recovery question a theoretical basis.

Many existing encoding schemes support their privacy claims by testing a limited collection of reconstruction attacks. Such evaluations show how those attacks perform, but do not themselves theoretically establish non-invertibility. The authors introduce a measure based on Fisher information, called dFIL, to characterize the invertibility of an encoding. They describe the measure as broadly applicable across popular encoders.

The paper shows theoretically and empirically that dFIL can bound invertibility. This gives a principled way to interpret reconstruction-related privacy, beyond observing whether particular tested attacks succeed. The contribution concerns the recoverability of encoded instances: it provides an interpretable quantity for assessing that aspect of an encoder while preserving the motivation of using encoded data for downstream training and inference.
summary.tldr: A Fisher-information-based measure provides theoretical and empirical bounds on how invertible privacy-preserving instance encodings are.

title: Bounding the Invertibility of Privacy-preserving Instance Encoding using Fisher Information

abstract: We study the maximin share (MMS) fair allocation of $m$ indivisible tasks to $n$ agents who have costs for completing the assigned tasks.It is known that exact MMS fairness cannot be guaranteed, and so far the best-known approximation for additive cost functions is $\frac{13}{11}$ by Huang and Segal-Halevi [EC, 2023]; however, beyond additivity, very little is known. In this work, we first prove that no algorithm can ensure better than $\min\{n,\frac{\log m}{\log \log m}\}$-approximation if the cost functions are submodular. This result also shows a sharp contrast with the allocation of goods where constant approximations exist as shown by Barman and Krishnamurthy [TEAC, 2020] and Ghodsi et al. [AIJ, 2022]. We then prove that for subadditive costs, there always exists an allocation that is $\min\{n,\lceil\log m\rceil\}$-approximation, and thus the approximation ratio is asymptotically tight.Besides multiplicative approximation, we also consider the ordinal relaxation, 1-out-of-$d$ MMS, which was recently proposed by Hosseini et al. [JAIR and AAMAS, 2022]. Our impossibility result implies that for any $d\ge 2$, a 1-out-of-$d$ MMS allocation may not exist.Due to these hardness results for general subadditive costs, we turn to studying two specific subadditive costs, namely, bin packing and job scheduling. For both settings, we show that constant approximate allocations exist for both multiplicative and ordinal relaxations of MMS.

paragraphs: This paper studies fairness when indivisible chores must be distributed among people whose costs for bundles need not equal the sum of individual task costs. It uses maximin share fairness as the benchmark. Because exact fairness cannot always be achieved, the question is how closely an allocation can approximate that benchmark under different cost structures.

For submodular costs, the authors prove that no algorithm can guarantee an approximation better than the smaller of n and log(m)/log(log(m)), where n counts agents and m counts tasks. For subadditive costs, they establish existence of an allocation with factor min(n, ceil(log(m))). They also show that the ordinal relaxation called 1-out-of-d MMS can fail to exist for any d of at least two.

The picture improves for two structured applications: bin packing and job scheduling. Both admit constant approximations under multiplicative and ordinal fairness relaxations. The results therefore distinguish broad nonadditive cost classes, where strong fairness guarantees face serious barriers, from specific task structures where useful guarantees remain possible.
summary.tldr: Strong fairness guarantees face barriers for general nonadditive chores, while bin packing and job scheduling admit constant approximations.

title: Fair Allocation of Indivisible Chores: Beyond Additive Costs

abstract: We develop new sub-optimality bounds for gradient descent (GD) that depend on the conditioning of the objective along the path of optimization, rather than on global, worst-case constants. Key to our proofs is directional smoothness, a measure of gradient variation that we use to develop upper-bounds on the objective. Minimizing these upper-bounds requires solving implicit equations to obtain a sequence of strongly adapted step-sizes; we show that these equations are straightforward to solve for convex quadratics and lead to new guarantees for two classical step-sizes. For general functions, we prove that the Polyak step-size and normalized GD obtain fast, path-dependent rates despite using no knowledge of the directional smoothness. Experiments on logistic regression show our convergence guarantees are tighter than the classical theory based on $L$-smoothness.

Key to our proofs is directional smoothness, a measure of gradient variation that we use to develop upper-bounds on the objective. Minimizing these upper-bounds requires solving implicit equations to obtain a sequence of strongly adapted step-sizes; we show that these equations are straightforward to solve for convex quadratics and lead to new guarantees for two classical step-sizes. For general functions, we prove that the Polyak step-size and normalized GD obtain fast, path-dependent rates despite using no knowledge of the directional smoothness. paragraphs: Standard analyses of gradient descent often describe an objective using a global worst-case measure of how quickly its gradient can change. Such a measure may poorly reflect the regions that optimization actually visits. This paper develops bounds on remaining optimization error that instead depend on the conditioning encountered along the optimization path.

The key quantity is directional smoothness, which measures gradient variation in a relevant direction. The authors use it to construct upper bounds on the objective. Minimizing those bounds produces implicit equations for strongly adapted step sizes. For convex quadratic objectives, these equations are straightforward to solve and provide new guarantees for two classical step-size choices.

The analysis also covers the Polyak step size and normalized gradient descent for general functions, proving fast path-dependent rates without requiring knowledge of directional smoothness. Logistic-regression experiments show tighter convergence guarantees than classical smoothness-based theory. The contribution is therefore both explanatory and analytical: familiar optimization methods can receive guarantees that better reflect the geometry they actually encounter during a run.
summary.tldr: Directional smoothness yields gradient-descent guarantees that reflect the optimization path rather than global worst-case behavior.

title: Directional Smoothness and Gradient Methods: Convergence and Adaptivity

abstract: Success in collaborative and competitive environments, where agents must work with or against each other, requires individuals to encode the position and trajectory of themselves and others. Decades of neurophysiological experiments have shed light on how brain regions [e.g., medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), hippocampus] encode the self's position and trajectory. However, it has only recently been discovered that MEC and hippocampus are modulated by the positions and trajectories of others. To understand how encoding spatial information of multiple agents shapes neural representations, we train a recurrent neural network (RNN) model that captures properties of MEC to path integrate trajectories of two agents simultaneously navigating the same environment. We find significant differences between these RNNs and those trained to path integrate only a single agent. At the individual unit level, RNNs trained to path integrate more than one agent develop weaker grid responses, stronger border responses, and tuning for the relative position of the two agents. At the population level, they develop more distributed and robust representations, with changes in network dynamics and manifold topology. Our results provide testable predictions and open new directions with which to study the neural computations supporting spatial navigation.

paragraphs: Navigating around other agents requires keeping track of their locations and movement as well as one's own. This paper investigates how that additional demand changes learned spatial representations. It trains recurrent neural networks that capture properties of the medial entorhinal cortex to integrate the trajectories of two agents sharing an environment.

The resulting networks differ substantially from networks trained to track a single agent. Individual units show weaker grid responses, stronger responses associated with borders, and sensitivity to the relative positions of the two agents. These changes suggest that adding another agent reorganizes what individual units represent, beyond simply duplicating a single-agent spatial code.

At the population level, the networks develop more distributed and robust representations, accompanied by changes in network dynamics and the topology of their representation manifolds. The findings come from trained RNN models and provide testable predictions for neuroscience. Their significance is that the demands of tracking multiple agents can alter both individual-unit responses and the collective organization of spatial information, opening further questions about neural navigation mechanisms.
summary.tldr: RNNs trained to track two agents develop weaker grid responses and more distributed spatial representations than networks trained to track one.

title: Not so griddy: Internal representations of RNNs path integrating more than one agent

abstract: Neural operators, serving as physics surrogate models, have recently gained increased interest. With ever increasing problem complexity, the natural question arises: what is an efficient way to scale neural operators to larger and more complex simulations - most importantly by taking into account different types of simulation datasets. This is of special interest since, akin to their numerical counterparts, different techniques are used across applications, even if the underlying dynamics of the systems are similar. Whereas the flexibility of transformers has enabled unified architectures across domains, neural operators mostly follow a problem specific design, where GNNs are commonly used for Lagrangian simulations and grid-based models predominate Eulerian simulations. We introduce Universal Physics Transformers (UPTs), an efficient and unified learning paradigm for a wide range of spatio-temporal problems. UPTs operate without grid- or particle-based latent structures, enabling flexibility and scalability across meshes and particles. UPTs efficiently propagate dynamics in the latent space, emphasized by inverse encoding and decoding techniques. Finally, UPTs allow for queries of the latent space representation at any point in space-time. We demonstrate diverse applicability and efficacy of UPTs in mesh-based fluid simulations, and steady-state Reynolds averaged Navier-Stokes simulations, and Lagrangian-based dynamics.

paragraphs: Universal Physics Transformers address the challenge of scaling learned physics surrogates across different simulation representations. Neural operators often use designs tied to their problem: graph networks are common for Lagrangian simulations, while grid-based models dominate Eulerian settings. This specialization complicates a unified approach even when underlying dynamics are similar.

UPTs use a latent representation that is not organized as a grid or a collection of particles. They propagate dynamics within that latent space, supported by inverse encoding and decoding techniques. The representation can also be queried at any point in space-time, separating where predictions are requested from the structure used internally to evolve the system.

The authors demonstrate the framework on mesh-based fluid simulations, steady-state Reynolds averaged Navier-Stokes simulations, and Lagrangian dynamics. These applications support its stated flexibility across meshes and particles. The contribution is an efficient, shared learning framework for varied spatio-temporal problems, with the demonstrations showing applicability across several simulation types rather than establishing coverage of every physical system.
summary.tldr: UPTs evolve physics in a flexible latent space to support simulation learning across mesh-based and particle-based settings.

title: Universal Physics Transformers: A Framework For Efficiently Scaling Neural Operators

abstract: Influential and popular benchmarks in AI are largely irrelevant to developing NLP tools for low-resource, Indigenous languages. With the primary goal of measuring the performance of general-purpose AI systems, these benchmarks fail to give due consideration and care to individual language communities, especially low-resource languages. The datasets contain numerous grammatical and orthographic errors, poor pronunciation, limited vocabulary, and the content lacks cultural relevance to the language community. To overcome the issues with these benchmarks, we have created a dataset for te reo Māori (the Indigenous language of Aotearoa/New Zealand) to pursue NLP tools that are ‘fit-for-our-purpose’. This paper demonstrates how low-resourced, Indigenous languages can develop tailored, high-quality benchmarks that; i. Consider the impact of colonisation on their language; ii. Reflect the diversity of speakers in the language community; iii. Support the aspirations for the tools they are developing and their language revitalisation efforts.

paragraphs: The paper argues that widely used AI benchmarks often fail to serve the development of language tools for Indigenous communities. Their emphasis on general-purpose systems can overlook the needs of particular languages. The authors identify problems including grammatical and spelling errors, poor pronunciation, restricted vocabulary, and content that lacks relevance to the community’s culture.

They create a dataset for te reo Māori, the Indigenous language of Aotearoa/New Zealand, with the aim of evaluating tools against community purposes. The work presents tailored benchmark development as a way to connect data quality and evaluation choices with the language tools that a community actually wants to build.

The proposed approach considers the effects of colonisation, represents diversity among speakers, and supports community aspirations for tools and language revitalisation. Its contribution is a demonstration of how a low-resource Indigenous language can develop a high-quality benchmark around those priorities. Evaluation becomes a means of supporting a language community’s goals, with success defined in relation to those goals.
summary.tldr: A te reo Māori dataset demonstrates benchmark design centered on Indigenous language communities, speaker diversity, and revitalisation goals.

title: Fit for our purpose, not yours: Benchmark for a low-resource, Indigenous language

abstract: Self-supervised large language models have demonstrated the ability to perform various tasks via in-context learning, but little is known about where the model locates the task with respect to prompt instructions and demonstration examples. In this work, we attempt to characterize the region where large language models transition from recognizing the task to performing the task. Through a series of layer-wise context-masking experiments on GPTNeo2.7B, Bloom3B, Starcoder2-7B, Llama3.1-8B, Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, on Machine Translation and Code generation, we demonstrate evidence of a "task recognition" point where the task is encoded into the input representations and attention to context is no longer necessary. Taking advantage of this redundancy results in 45% computational savings when prompting with 5 examples, and task recognition achieved at layer 14 / 32 using an example with Machine Translation. Our findings also have implications for resource and parameter efficient fine-tuning; we observe a correspondence between strong fine-tuning performance of individual LoRA layers and the task recognition layers.

paragraphs: This paper investigates where a language model moves from identifying a task in its prompt to carrying out that task. In-context learning supplies instructions or demonstrations without changing model weights. The authors ask whether continued attention to that context remains necessary throughout the network once the task has been recognized.

They run layer-wise context-masking experiments across several language models on machine translation and code generation. The results provide evidence for a task-recognition point: task information has become encoded in the input representations, and attention to the original context is no longer necessary in the tested setting. A machine-translation example places this point at layer 14 of 32.

Exploiting the observed redundancy produces reported computational savings of 45% when prompting with five examples. The study also finds a correspondence between task-recognition layers and individual layers that perform strongly when fine-tuned with LoRA. These findings connect the location of task processing with both inference efficiency and targeted fine-tuning, while presenting the recognition point as experimental evidence rather than a universal layer shared by all tasks and models.
summary.tldr: Context-masking experiments identify task-recognition layers after which continued context attention can become redundant, enabling reported inference savings.

title: Where does In-context Learning Happen in Large Language Models?

abstract: Proteins are essential for almost all biological processes and derive their diverse functions from complex $3 \rm D$ structures, which are in turn determined by their amino acid sequences. In this paper, we exploit the rich biological inductive bias of amino acid sequences and introduce FoldFlow++, a novel sequence-conditioned $\text{SE}(3)$-equivariant flow matching model for protein structure generation. FoldFlow++ presents substantial new architectural features over the previous FoldFlow family of models including a protein large language model to encode sequence, a new multi-modal fusion trunk that combines structure and sequence representations, and a geometric transformer based decoder. To increase diversity and novelty of generated samples -- crucial for de-novo drug design -- wetrain FoldFlow++ at scale on a new dataset that is an order of magnitude larger than PDB datasets of prior works, containing both known proteins in PDB and high-quality synthetic structures achieved through filtering. We further demonstrate the ability to align FoldFlow++ to arbitrary rewards, e.g. increasing secondary structures diversity, by introducing a Reinforced Finetuning (ReFT) objective. We empirically observe that FoldFlow++ outperforms previous state-of-the-art protein structure-based generative models, improving over RFDiffusion in terms of unconditional generation across all metrics including designability, diversity, and novelty across all protein lengths, as well as exhibiting generalization on the task of equilibrium conformation sampling. Finally, we demonstrate that a fine-tuned FoldFlow++ makes progress on challenging conditional design tasks such as designing scaffolds for the VHH nanobody.

Its SE(3)-equivariant design respects rotations and translations of three-dimensional structures. A protein language model encodes sequences, a multimodal fusion component combines sequence and structure representations, and a geometric transformer decodes the resulting information.

summary.tldr: FoldFlow++ combines sequence information, geometric flow matching, and scaled training to improve protein structure generation and support reward-guided design.

title: Sequence-Augmented SE(3)-Flow Matching For Conditional Protein Generation

abstract: Leveraging the model’s outputs, specifically the logits, is a common approach to estimating the test accuracy of a pre-trained neural network on out-of-distribution (OOD) samples without requiring access to the corresponding ground-truth labels.Despite their ease of implementation and computational efficiency, current logit-based methods are vulnerable to overconfidence issues, leading to prediction bias, especially under the natural shift. In this work, we first study the relationship between logits and generalization performance from the view of low-density separation assumption. Our findings motivate our proposed method \method{} that \textbf{(1)}~applies a data-dependent normalization on the logits to reduce prediction bias, and \textbf{(2)} takes the $L_p$ norm of the matrix of normalized logits as the estimation score. Our theoretical analysis highlights the connection between the provided score and the model's uncertainty. We conduct an extensive empirical study on common unsupervised accuracy estimation benchmarks and demonstrate that \method{} achieves state-of-the-art performance across various architectures in the presence of synthetic, natural, or subpopulation shifts. The code is available at https://github.com/Renchunzi-Xie/MaNo.

The code is available at https://github.com/Renchunzi-Xie/MaNo.

paragraphs: When a trained model encounters shifted data, its accuracy may change even though no labels are available to measure that change. MaNo estimates accuracy from the model's output scores, or logits. The paper addresses a weakness of existing logit-based methods: overconfidence can bias their estimates, particularly under natural distribution shifts.

MaNo then gathers the normalized logits into a matrix and uses its Lp norm as an estimation score. The theoretical analysis connects this score to model uncertainty.

The method matters because it extracts an accuracy signal from outputs already available at prediction time. Its contribution combines a normalization step addressing overconfidence with a matrix-level summary, and the experiments support that combination across the tested forms of distribution change.

title: MaNo: Exploiting Matrix Norm for Unsupervised Accuracy Estimation Under Distribution Shifts

abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) are non-parametric probabilistic regression models that are popular due to their flexibility, data efficiency, and well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. However, standard GP models assume homoskedastic Gaussian noise, while many real-world applications are subject to non-Gaussian corruptions. Variants of GPs that are more robust to alternative noise models have been proposed, and entail significant trade-offs between accuracy and robustness, and between computational requirements and theoretical guarantees. In this work, we propose and study a GP model that achieves robustness against sparse outliers by inferring data-point-specific noise levels with a sequential selection procedure maximizing the log marginal likelihood that we refer to as relevance pursuit. We show, surprisingly, that the model can be parameterized such that the associated log marginal likelihood is strongly concave in the data-point-specific noise variances, a property rarely found in either robust regression objectives or GP marginal likelihoods. This in turn implies the weak submodularity of the corresponding subset selection problem, and thereby proves approximation guarantees for the proposed algorithm. We compare the model’s performance relative to other approaches on diverse regression and Bayesian optimization tasks, including the challenging but common setting of sparse corruptions of the labels within or close to the function range.

paragraphs: Standard Gaussian processes assume Gaussian observation noise with the same variance across data points. Sparse corrupted observations can violate that assumption. This paper develops a robust Gaussian process that assigns noise levels to individual observations, allowing the model to account for unusually unreliable points within an otherwise useful dataset.

The authors show that a suitable parameterization makes this objective strongly concave in the point-specific noise variances. It includes sparse label corruptions that fall within or near the function’s normal range, a setting where corrupted values can resemble plausible observations. The central contribution combines a model aimed at sparse-outlier robustness with an optimization structure that supports formal guarantees; the abstract describes these comparisons without asserting uniform empirical superiority.
summary.tldr: Relevance pursuit gives Gaussian processes point-specific noise levels for sparse-outlier robustness, with approximation guarantees derived from the optimization structure.

title: Robust Gaussian Processes via Relevance Pursuit

abstract: While diffusion models have demonstrated impressive performance, there is a growing need for generating samples tailored to specific user-defined concepts. The customized requirements promote the development of few-shot diffusion models, which use limited $n_{ta}$ target samples to fine-tune a pre-trained diffusion model trained on $n_s$ source samples. Despite the empirical success, no theoretical work specifically analyzes few-shot diffusion models. Moreover, the existing results for diffusion models without a fine-tuning phase can not explain why few-shot models generate great samples due to the curse of dimensionality. In this work, we analyze few-shot diffusion models under a linear structure distribution with a latent dimension $d$. From the approximation perspective, we prove that few-shot models have a $\widetilde{O}(n_s^{-2/d}+n_{ta}^{-1/2})$ bound to approximate the target score function, which is better than $n_{ta}^{-2/d}$ results. From the optimization perspective, we consider a latent Gaussian special case and prove that the optimization problem has a closed-form minimizer. This means few-shot models can directly obtain an approximated minimizer without a complex optimization process. Furthermore, we also provide the accuracy bound $\widetilde{O}(1/n_{ta}+1/\sqrt{n_s})$ for the empirical solution, which still has better dependence on $n_{ta}$ compared to $n_s$. The results of the real-world experiments also show that the models obtained by only fine-tuning the encoder and decoder specific to the target distribution can produce novel images with the target feature, which supports our theoretical results.

paragraphs: Few-shot diffusion adapts a pretrained generator to a user-defined concept using limited target examples. This paper analyzes why pretraining can make that adaptation effective under a linear distribution structure with latent dimension d. It separates the contribution of source samples, n_s, from the contribution of target samples, n_ta.

summary.tldr: Under a linear latent structure, few-shot diffusion has favorable target-sample error bounds that help explain efficient adaptation.

title: Few-Shot Diffusion Models Escape the Curse of Dimensionality

abstract: Event-based cameras are attracting significant interest as they provide rich edge information, high dynamic range, and high temporal resolution. Many state-of-the-art event-based algorithms rely on splitting the events into fixed groups, resulting in the omission of crucial temporal information, particularly when dealing with diverse motion scenarios (e.g., high/low speed). In this work, we propose SpikeSlicer, a novel-designed event processing framework capable of splitting events stream adaptively. SpikeSlicer utilizes a low-energy spiking neural network (SNN) to trigger event slicing. To guide the SNN to fire spikes at optimal time steps, we propose the Spiking Position-aware Loss (SPA-Loss) to modulate the neuron's state. Additionally, we develop a Feedback-Update training strategy that refines the slicing decisions using feedback from the downstream artificial neural network (ANN). Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method yields significant performance improvements in event-based object tracking and recognition. Notably, SpikeSlicer provides a brand-new SNN-ANN cooperation paradigm, where the SNN acts as an efficient, low-energy data processor to assist the ANN in improving downstream performance, injecting new perspectives and potential avenues of exploration.

paragraphs: SpikeSlicer improves how event-camera data are grouped before downstream processing. This is especially relevant when motion varies between fast and slow regimes, making one fixed grouping strategy poorly matched to different inputs.

The framework uses a low-energy spiking neural network to decide when to cut the event stream into slices. A proposed Spiking Position-aware Loss adjusts the neuron’s state to encourage spikes at suitable times. The slicing decisions are also refined through a Feedback-Update training strategy that uses feedback from the downstream artificial neural network.

The contribution is a cooperative arrangement between two kinds of networks: the spiking network performs efficient adaptive data preparation, while the artificial neural network handles the downstream task. Feedback ties the preparation stage to task performance, making the grouping of incoming events a learned part of the overall processing framework.
summary.tldr: SpikeSlicer uses a spiking network and downstream feedback to adapt event-stream grouping, improving tracking and recognition.

title: Spiking Neural Network as Adaptive Event Stream Slicer

abstract: Variational inequalities represent a broad class of problems, including minimization and min-max problems, commonly found in machine learning. Existing second-order and high-order methods for variational inequalities require precise computation of derivatives, often resulting in prohibitively high iteration costs. In this work, we study the impact of Jacobian inaccuracy on second-order methods. For the smooth and monotone case, we establish a lower bound with explicit dependence on the level of Jacobian inaccuracy and propose an optimal algorithm for this key setting. When derivatives are exact, our method converges at the same rate as exact optimal second-order methods. To reduce the cost of solving the auxiliary problem, which arises in all high-order methods with global convergence, we introduce several Quasi-Newton approximations. Our method with Quasi-Newton updates achieves a global sublinear convergence rate. We extend our approach with a tensor generalization for inexact high-order derivatives and support the theory with experiments.

paragraphs: Variational inequalities encompass optimization problems such as minimization and min-max learning. Methods that use higher-order derivative information can have expensive iterations because they demand precise derivative calculations. This paper studies how inaccurate Jacobians affect second-order methods, making the accuracy of derivative information an explicit part of the analysis.

summary.tldr: The paper characterizes how Jacobian errors affect second-order optimization and develops optimal and Quasi-Newton methods with stated convergence guarantees.

title: Exploring Jacobian Inexactness in Second-Order Methods for Variational Inequalities: Lower Bounds, Optimal Algorithms and Quasi-Newton Approximations

abstract: Visual Place Recognition (VPR) is essential for mobile robots as it enables them to retrieve images from a database closest to their current location. The progress of Visual Foundation Models (VFMs) has significantly advanced VPR by capturing representative descriptors in images. However, existing fine-tuning efforts for VFMs often overlook the crucial role of probing in effectively adapting these descriptors for improved image representation. In this paper, we propose the Centroid-Free Probing (CFP) stage, making novel use of second-order features for more effective use of descriptors from VFMs. Moreover, to control the preservation of task-specific information adaptively based on the context of the VPR, we introduce the Dynamic Power Normalization (DPN) module in both the recalibration and CFP stages, forming a novel Parameter Efficiency Fine-Tuning (PEFT) pipeline (EMVP) tailored for the VPR task. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of the proposed CFP over existing probing methods. Moreover, the EMVP pipeline can further enhance fine-tuning performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Specifically, it achieves 93.9\%, 96.5\%, and 94.6\% Recall@1 on the MSLS Validation, Pitts250k-test, and SPED datasets, respectively, while saving 64.3\% of trainable parameters compared with the existing SOTA PEFT method.

title: EMVP: Embracing Visual Foundation Model for Visual Place Recognition with Centroid-Free Probing

abstract: The Passive-Aggressive (PA) method is widely used in online regression problems for handling large-scale streaming data, typically updating model parameters in a passive-aggressive manner based on whether the error exceeds a predefined threshold. However, this approach struggles with determining optimal thresholds and adapting to complex scenarios with side information, where tracking accuracy is not the sole metric in the regression model. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel adaptive framework that allows finer adjustments to the weight vector in PA using side information. This framework adaptively selects the threshold parameter in PA, theoretically ensuring convergence to the optimal setting. Additionally, we present an efficient implementation of our algorithm that significantly reduces computational complexity. Numerical experiments show that our model achieves outstanding performance associated with the side information while maintaining low tracking error, demonstrating marked improvements over traditional PA methods across various scenarios.

paragraphs: Online regression updates a prediction model as streaming observations arrive. The Passive-Aggressive method controls these updates using an error threshold: whether the prediction error crosses that threshold affects the response. Selecting the threshold is difficult, particularly when the model must account for side information and prediction tracking is only one part of the objective.

This paper introduces an adaptive framework that uses side information to make finer adjustments to the model's weight vector. It also selects the threshold adaptively, with a theoretical guarantee of convergence to the optimal setting. The contribution connects adjustment of the model itself with adjustment of the rule governing its updates.

The authors additionally provide an efficient implementation that substantially reduces computational complexity. Their numerical experiments report improved performance on criteria associated with the side information while keeping tracking error low. These results matter because they show that adapting to additional requirements can coexist with accurate tracking in the tested scenarios, extending the practical scope of the traditional Passive-Aggressive approach.
summary.tldr: An adaptive Passive-Aggressive regression framework uses side information to refine updates and automatically select its error threshold.

title: Adaptive Passive-Aggressive Framework for Online Regression with Side Information

abstract: How can diffusion models process 3D geometries in a coarse-to-fine manner, akin to our multiscale view of the world?In this paper, we address the question by focusing on a fundamental biochemical problem of generating 3D molecular conformers conditioned on molecular graphs in a multiscale manner. Our approach consists of two hierarchical stages: i) generation of coarse-grained fragment-level 3D structure from the molecular graph, and ii) generation of fine atomic details from the coarse-grained approximated structure while allowing the latter to be adjusted simultaneously.For the challenging second stage, which demands preserving coarse-grained information while ensuring SE(3) equivariance, we introduce a novel generative model termed Equivariant Blurring Diffusion (EBD), which defines a forward process that moves towards the fragment-level coarse-grained structure by blurring the fine atomic details of conformers, and a reverse process that performs the opposite operation using equivariant networks.We demonstrate the effectiveness of EBD by geometric and chemical comparison to state-of-the-art denoising diffusion models on a benchmark of drug-like molecules.Ablation studies draw insights on the design of EBD by thoroughly analyzing its architecture, which includes the design of the loss function and the data corruption process.Codes are released at https://github.com/Shen-Lab/EBD.

paragraphs: A molecular conformer describes a molecule's three-dimensional arrangement. This paper generates conformers from molecular graphs through a coarse-to-fine process. It first constructs a rough arrangement at the level of molecular fragments, then generates individual atomic details while allowing the initial fragment arrangement to change.

The second stage must retain useful coarse structure while handling three-dimensional geometry consistently. Equivariant Blurring Diffusion addresses this with a forward process that progressively blurs atomic detail toward the fragment-level structure. Its reverse process reconstructs the details using equivariant networks. SE(3) equivariance means that rotating or translating the input geometry produces corresponding changes in the output geometry.

This design makes the coarse approximation a guide that can be refined alongside the atomic coordinates. The authors assess geometric and chemical quality against state-of-the-art denoising diffusion models on a benchmark of drug-like molecules and report effective generation. They also use ablations to investigate architectural choices, including the loss function and corruption process, providing evidence about how the model's design contributes to its behavior.
summary.tldr: Equivariant Blurring Diffusion generates molecular conformers by refining fragment-level geometry into atomic detail while preserving geometric equivariance.

title: Equivariant Blurring Diffusion for Hierarchical Molecular Conformer Generation

abstract: Scaling has been a critical factor in improving model performance and generalization across various fields of machine learning.It involves how a model’s performance changes with increases in model size or input data, as well as how efficiently computational resources are utilized to support this growth. Despite successes in scaling other types of machine learning models, the study of scaling in Neural Network Interatomic Potentials (NNIPs) remains limited. NNIPs act as surrogate models for ab initio quantum mechanical calculations, predicting the energy and forces between atoms in molecules and materials based on atomic configurations. The dominant paradigm in this field is to incorporate numerous physical domain constraints into the model, such as symmetry constraints like rotational equivariance. We contend that these increasingly complex domain constraints inhibit the scaling ability of NNIPs, and such strategies are likely to cause model performance to plateau in the long run. In this work, we take an alternative approach and start by systematically studying NNIP scaling properties and strategies. Our findings indicate that scaling the model through attention mechanisms is both efficient and improves model expressivity. These insights motivate us to develop an NNIP architecture designed for scalability: the Efficiently Scaled Attention Interatomic Potential (EScAIP). EScAIP leverages a novel multi-head self-attention formulation within graph neural networks, applying attention at the neighbor-level representations.Implemented with highly-optimized attention GPU kernels, EScAIP achieves substantial gains in efficiency---at least 10x speed up in inference time, 5x less in memory usage---compared to existing NNIP models. EScAIP also achieves state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of datasets including catalysts (OC20 and OC22), molecules (SPICE), and materials (MPTrj). After training EScAIP, we test its ability to learn rotational equivariance by predicting forces on new, unseen atomistic systems before and after rotation. The model's force predictions exactly match the rotated forces, suggesting that it has precisely learned rotational equivariance.Finally, we emphasize that our approach should be thought of as a philosophy rather than a specific model, representing a proof-of-concept towards developing general-purpose NNIPs that achieve better expressivity through scaling, and continue to scale efficiently with increased computational resources and training data.

abstract: Explicit, momentum-based dynamics that optimize functions defined on Lie groups can be constructed via variational optimization and momentum trivialization. Structure preserving time discretizations can then turn this dynamics into optimization algorithms. This article investigates two types of discretization, Lie Heavy-Ball, which is a known splitting scheme, and Lie NAG-SC, which is newly proposed. Their convergence rates are explicitly quantified under $L$-smoothness and \emph{local} strong convexity assumptions. Lie NAG-SC provides acceleration over the momentumless case, i.e. Riemannian gradient descent, but Lie Heavy-Ball does not. When compared to existing accelerated optimizers for general manifolds, both Lie Heavy-Ball and Lie NAG-SC are computationally cheaper and easier to implement, thanks to their utilization of group structure. Only gradient oracle and exponential map are required, but not logarithm map or parallel transport which are computational costly.

paragraphs: Optimization on Lie groups must respect the structure of the space in which the variables live. This paper studies momentum-based optimization dynamics and algorithms obtained by discretizing those dynamics while preserving that structure. It analyzes an existing scheme, Lie Heavy-Ball, and introduces a new one, Lie NAG-SC.

The authors explicitly quantify convergence rates under smoothness and local strong convexity assumptions. Within this analysis, Lie NAG-SC accelerates convergence relative to Riemannian gradient descent, the momentumless comparison. Lie Heavy-Ball does not provide that acceleration. The distinction shows that adding momentum alone does not establish the same rate improvement for both discretizations.

Both algorithms use the group structure to simplify computation compared with existing accelerated methods for general manifolds. They require a gradient oracle and an exponential map, avoiding logarithm maps and parallel transport, which the abstract identifies as costly. The contribution therefore combines conditional convergence guarantees with simpler computational requirements, while tying the acceleration result specifically to Lie NAG-SC under the stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: Under smoothness and local strong convexity, Lie NAG-SC achieves accelerated convergence using Lie-group structure and relatively simple operations.

title: Quantitative Convergences of Lie Group Momentum Optimizers

abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) for music generation is undergoing rapid developments, with recent symbolic models leveraging sophisticated deep learning and diffusion model algorithms. One drawback with existing models is that they lack structural cohesion, particularly on harmonic-melodic structure. Furthermore, such existing models are largely "black-box" in nature and are not musically interpretable. This paper addresses these limitations via a novel generative music framework that incorporates concepts of Schenkerian analysis (SchA) in concert with a diffusion modeling framework. This framework, which we call ProGress ([Pro]longation-enhanced Di[Gress]), adapts state-of-the-art deep models for discrete diffusion (in particular, the DiGress model of Vignac et al., 2023) for interpretable and structured music generation. Concretely, our contributions include 1) novel adaptations of the DiGress model for music generation, 2) a novel SchA-inspired phrase fusion methodology, and 3) a framework allowing users to control various aspects of the generation process to create coherent musical compositions. Results from human experiments suggest superior performance to existing state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: ProGress addresses structural coherence and interpretability in symbolic music generation. The authors focus particularly on relationships between harmony and melody, arguing that existing generative systems often fail to organize these relationships coherently. Their approach brings concepts from Schenkerian musical analysis into a diffusion-based generation framework.

The system adapts DiGress, a discrete diffusion model, for music generation. It also introduces a phrase-fusion method inspired by Schenkerian analysis, connecting the assembly of musical phrases with a structured analytical perspective. User controls over aspects of generation are included as part of the framework, making human influence an explicit component of composition.

Together, these elements aim to produce music whose organization is both coherent and musically interpretable. Human experiments suggest stronger performance than existing state-of-the-art methods. The stated result supports combining learned generation with music-theoretic structure in the evaluated setting. The broader contribution is a framework that connects generative modeling, phrase organization, and user control within the same compositional process.
summary.tldr: ProGress combines discrete diffusion, hierarchical musical analysis, and user controls to support coherent, interpretable music generation.

title: ProGress: Structured Music Generation via Graph Diffusion and Hierarchical Music Analysis

abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have emerged as powerful tools for modeling complex data distributions and generating realistic new samples. Over the years, advanced architectures and sampling methods have been developed to make these models practically usable. However, certain synthesis process decisions still rely on heuristics without a solid theoretical foundation. In our work, we offer a novel analysis of the DM's inference process, introducing a comprehensive frequency response perspective. Specifically, by relying on Gaussianity assumption, we present the inference process as a closed-form spectral transfer function, capturing how the generated signal evolves in response to the initial noise. We demonstrate how the proposed analysis can be leveraged to design a noise schedule that aligns effectively with the characteristics of the data. The spectral perspective also provides insights into the underlying dynamics and sheds light on the relationship between spectral properties and noise schedule structure. Our results lead to scheduling curves that are dependent on the spectral content of the data, offering a theoretical justification for some of the heuristics taken by practitioners.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate samples through a sequence of noise-removal steps, and the chosen noise schedule helps determine how that process unfolds. Some scheduling decisions remain heuristic. This paper develops a frequency-based analysis of inference to explain the relationship between the schedule and the spectral characteristics of the data.

Under a Gaussianity assumption, the authors express inference as a closed-form spectral transfer function. This describes how the generated signal evolves from the initial noise across spectral components. The formulation supplies a mathematical view of the synthesis process, making it possible to connect schedule structure with properties of the distribution being modeled.

The authors use this analysis to design noise schedules that depend on the data's spectral content. The resulting scheduling curves also provide theoretical justification for some existing practitioner heuristics. The Gaussianity assumption is central to the closed-form analysis, so its explanatory claims belong to that setting. The contribution gives schedule design a data-dependent theoretical basis and offers insight into the dynamics of diffusion inference.
summary.tldr: Under a Gaussianity assumption, a spectral analysis of diffusion inference yields data-dependent noise schedules and explains some scheduling heuristics.

title: Spectral Analysis of Diffusion Models with Application to Schedule Design

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at natural language processing tasks, but their massive size leads to high computational and storage demands. Recent works have sought to reduce their model size through layer-wise structured pruning. However, they tend to ignore retaining the capabilities in the pruned part. In this work, we re-examine structured pruning paradigms and uncover several key limitations: 1) notable performance degradation due to direct layer removal, 2) incompetent linear weighted layer aggregation, and 3) the lack of effective post-training recovery mechanisms. To address these limitations, we propose CoMe, including a progressive layer pruning framework with a Concatenation-based Merging technology and a hierarchical distillation post-training process. Specifically, we introduce a channel sensitivity metric that utilizes activation intensity and weight norms for fine-grained channel selection. Subsequently, we employ a concatenation-based layer merging method to fuse the most critical channels in the adjacent layers, enabling a progressive model size reduction. Finally, we propose a hierarchical distillation protocol, which leverages the correspondences between the original and pruned model layers established during pruning, enabling efficient knowledge transfer. Experiments on seven benchmarks show that CoMe achieves state-of-the-art performance; when pruning 30% of LLaMA-2-7b's parameters, the pruned model retains 83% of its original average accuracy.

paragraphs: Removing layers makes a language model smaller, but can also discard useful capabilities. This paper identifies weaknesses in direct layer removal, linear weighted layer aggregation, and existing recovery procedures. It then concatenates selected channels from adjacent layers to merge their useful content as compression proceeds. After pruning, hierarchical distillation transfers knowledge from the original model to the smaller one, using layer correspondences established during the pruning process.

That figure expresses retained accuracy relative to the original model, rather than an absolute accuracy score. The findings support compression that combines selective merging with targeted recovery, allowing the smaller model to retain some capabilities that straightforward layer deletion would lose.
summary.tldr: CoMe compresses language models by merging important channels across adjacent layers and then transferring knowledge through hierarchical distillation.

title: Layer as Puzzle Pieces: Compressing Large Language Models through Layer Concatenation

abstract: Current state-of-the-art generative models map noise to data distributions by matching flows or scores. A key limitation of these models is their inability to readily integrate available partial observations and additional priors. In contrast, energy-based models (EBMs) address this by incorporating corresponding scalar energy terms. Here, we propose Energy Matching, a framework that endows flow-based approaches with the flexibility of EBMs. Far from the data manifold, samples move from noise to data along irrotational, optimal transport paths. As they approach the data manifold, an entropic energy term guides the system into a Boltzmann equilibrium distribution, explicitly capturing the underlying likelihood structure of the data. We parameterize these dynamics with a single time-independent scalar field, which serves as both a powerful generator and a flexible prior for effective regularization of inverse problems. The present method substantially outperforms existing EBMs on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet generation in terms of fidelity, while retaining simulation-free training of transport-based approaches away from the data manifold. Furthermore, we leverage the flexibility of the method to introduce an interaction energy that supports the exploration of diverse modes, which we demonstrate in a controlled protein generation setting. This approach learns a scalar potential energy, without time conditioning, auxiliary generators, or additional networks, marking a significant departure from recent EBM methods. We believe this simplified yet rigorous formulation significantly advances EBMs capabilities and paves the way for their wider adoption in generative modeling in diverse domains.

title: Energy Matching: Unifying Flow Matching and Energy-Based Models for Generative Modeling

abstract: We explore if it is possible to learn data structures end-to-end with neural networks, with a focus on the problem of nearest-neighbor (NN) search. We introduce a framework for data structure discovery, which adapts to the underlying data distribution and provides fine-grained control over query and space complexity. Crucially, the data structure is learned from scratch, and does not require careful initialization or seeding with candidate data structures. In several settings, we are able to reverse-engineer the learned data structures and query algorithms. For 1D nearest neighbor search, the model discovers optimal distribution (in)dependent algorithms such as binary search and variants of interpolation search. In higher dimensions, the model learns solutions that resemble k-d trees in some regimes, while in others, elements of locality-sensitive hashing emerge. Additionally, the model learns useful representations of high-dimensional data such as images and exploits them to design effective data structures. Beyond NN search, we believe the framework could be a powerful tool for data structure discovery for other problems and adapt our framework to the problem of estimating frequencies over a data stream. To encourage future work in this direction, we conclude with a discussion on some of the opportunities and remaining challenges of learning data structures end-to-end.

paragraphs: A data structure determines how information is organized and how efficiently queries can be answered. This paper asks whether neural networks can learn both that organization and its query procedure from scratch. The framework focuses on nearest-neighbor search and allows fine-grained control over storage requirements and query complexity.

The learned structures adapt to the underlying data distribution without being initialized from candidate structures. In several settings, the authors can reverse-engineer what the model discovers. For one-dimensional search, these discoveries include optimal algorithms such as binary search and variants of interpolation search. In higher dimensions, some solutions resemble k-d trees, while others exhibit elements of locality-sensitive hashing.

The framework also learns representations of high-dimensional inputs such as images and uses those representations to build effective search structures. The authors extend it to estimating frequencies in a data stream, providing another application beyond nearest-neighbor search. Their findings show that end-to-end learning can recover recognizable algorithmic ideas and adapt structures to data, while broader use across other problems remains a proposed opportunity.
summary.tldr: An end-to-end learning framework discovers data structures and query algorithms, including recognizable nearest-neighbor search strategies.

title: Discovering Data Structures: Nearest Neighbor Search and Beyond

abstract: Audio is inherently temporal and closely synchronized with the visual world, making it a naturally aligned and expressive control signal for controllable video generation (e.g., movies). Beyond control, directly translating audio into video is essential for understanding and visualizing rich audio narratives (e.g., Podcasts or historical recordings). However, existing approaches fall short in generating high-quality videos with precise audio-visual synchronization, especially across diverse and complex audio types. In this work, we introduce MTV, a versatile framework for audio-sync video generation. MTV explicitly separates audios into speech, effects, and music tracks, enabling disentangled control over lip motion, event timing, and visual mood, respectively—resulting in fine-grained and semantically aligned video generation. To support the framework, we additionally present DEMIX, a dataset comprising high-quality cinematic videos and demixed audio tracks. DEMIX is structured into five overlapped subsets, enabling scalable multi-stage training for diverse generation scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MTV achieves state-of-the-art performance across six standard metrics spanning video quality, text-video consistency, and audio-video alignment.

paragraphs: Audio provides several kinds of guidance for video generation at once. Speech suggests how lips should move, sound effects indicate when events occur, and music helps establish mood. MTV is a framework that separates these signals so video generation can respond to their different roles, addressing the difficulty of synchronizing visuals with complex audio.

The framework explicitly divides audio into speech, effects, and music tracks. Each stream controls a corresponding aspect of the video: lip movement, event timing, or visual atmosphere. This separation gives the generator more specific temporal and semantic guidance than an undifferentiated audio signal. The authors also introduce DEMIX, a dataset pairing cinematic videos with separated audio tracks. Its five overlapping subsets support training in multiple stages for different generation scenarios.

The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art results across six metrics covering video quality, agreement with text, and audio-video alignment. These findings support separating audio by function as a useful way to improve both visual content and its synchronization with sound.
summary.tldr: MTV separates speech, effects, and music to control video lip motion, event timing, and mood, improving audiovisual generation.

title: Audio-Sync Video Generation with Multi-Stream Temporal Control

abstract: Information seeking demands iterative evidence gathering and reflective reasoning, yet large language models (LLMs) still struggle with it in open-web question answering. Existing prompting and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) methods remain fixed by prompt rules or training corpora, and are usually benchmarked only on well-structured wiki sources, limiting real-world adaptability. We introduce $\textbf{WebPuzzle}$, a 24k-sample training and 275-sample test benchmark that evaluates information seeking on the live internet, across both wiki and open-domain queries. Leveraging 7k WebPuzzle instances, we develop $\textbf{DeepDiver}$, a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that cultivates $\textbf{Search Intensity Scaling (SIS)}$—an emergent ability to escalate search frequency and depth instead of settling on overconfident, under-evidenced answers. With SIS, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Pangu-7B-Reasoner attain performance on real-web tasks comparable to the 671B-parameter DeepSeek-R1. We detail DeepDiver’s curriculum from cold-start SFT to a well designed RL procedure, and show that its seeking policy generalized from closed-ended queries to open-ended generation such as long-form writing. Our results advance adaptive information seeking in LLMs and provide a rigorous benchmark for future work.

paragraphs: DeepDiver addresses information seeking on the live web, where answering a question can require repeated searches and reconsideration of the evidence. The paper introduces WebPuzzle, containing 24,000 training samples and 275 test samples across wiki and open-domain queries. This provides a setting for studying search behavior beyond well-structured wiki sources.

Using 7,000 WebPuzzle instances, the authors train models through an initial supervised fine-tuning stage followed by reinforcement learning. The resulting behavior, called Search Intensity Scaling, increases search frequency and depth instead of prematurely settling on an answer with insufficient evidence. The focus is on learning how much information gathering a response requires.

The learned seeking policy also transfers from closed-ended questions to open-ended generation, including long-form writing. These findings support adaptive search as a useful learned capability in the evaluated settings, alongside the contribution of a live-internet benchmark.
summary.tldr: DeepDiver uses reinforcement learning to teach language models to increase web-search effort when gathering evidence.

title: DeepDiver: Adaptive Web-Search Intensity Scaling via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We investigate fingerprints in pretraining datasets for large language models (LLMs) through dataset classification experiments. Building on prior work demonstrating the existence of fingerprints or biases in popular computer vision datasets, we analyze popular open-source pretraining datasets for LLMs derived from CommonCrawl including C4, RefinedWeb, DolmaCC, RedPajama-V2, FineWeb, and DCLM-Baseline. Despite those datasets being obtained with similar curation steps, neural networks can classify surprisingly well which dataset a single text sequence belongs to, significantly better than a human can. This indicates that small differences in filtering and processing pipelines induce fingerprints, that we find are evident in formatting, vocabulary, and content distributions. Such fingerprints can negatively impact cross-dataset generalization. Additionally, we show that these fingerprints propagate through training: sequences generated by models trained on those datasets can be accurately classified by a classifier trained on the original datasets. This can offer insights into data characteristics that are typically undisclosed by LLM developers, including pretraining mixture proportions and finetuning data sources.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether text datasets retain recognizable signatures of how they were curated, even when they originate from the same web crawl. It examines several open-source language-model pretraining datasets derived from CommonCrawl. The central experiment trains neural networks to identify which dataset supplied a single text sequence, treating dataset identity as a classification target.

The classifiers perform surprisingly well and significantly better than humans, despite similarities in the datasets’ curation processes. The authors locate these fingerprints in formatting, vocabulary, and content distributions. Their findings indicate that small filtering and processing differences leave systematic traces, and that such traces can negatively affect generalization between datasets.

The study then tests whether those signatures survive model training. A classifier trained on original dataset text can accurately classify sequences generated by models trained on those datasets. This suggests that generated outputs can reveal aspects of training-data characteristics. The authors identify possible applications to understanding otherwise undisclosed pretraining mixture proportions and fine-tuning sources, rather than establishing universal recovery of training data.
summary.tldr: Web-text curation leaves recognizable dataset fingerprints that can persist in the outputs of language models trained on that text.

title: Measuring Fingerprints of Web-filtered Text Datasets and Fingerprint Propagation Through Training

abstract: Transformers have become the de facto architecture for a wide range of machine learning tasks, particularly in large language models (LLMs). Despite their remarkable performance, many challenges remain in training deep transformer networks, especially regarding the position of the layer normalization. While Pre-Norm structures facilitate more stable training owing to their stronger identity path, they often lead to suboptimal performance compared to Post-Norm. In this paper, we propose **HybridNorm**, a simple yet effective hybrid normalization strategy that integrates the advantages of both Pre-Norm and Post-Norm. Specifically, HybridNorm employs QKV normalization within the attention mechanism and Post-Norm in the feed-forward network (FFN) of each transformer block. We provide both theoretical insights and empirical evidence to demonstrate that HybridNorm improves the gradient flow and the model robustness. Extensive experiments on large-scale transformer models, including both dense and sparse variants, show that HybridNorm consistently outperforms both Pre-Norm and Post-Norm approaches across multiple benchmarks. These findings highlight the potential of HybridNorm as a more stable and effective technique for improving the training and performance of deep transformer models. Code is available at https://github.com/BryceZhuo/HybridNorm.

paragraphs: Where normalization is placed inside a Transformer affects how easily a deep model trains and how well it ultimately performs. Pre-Norm structures support stable training through a stronger identity path, but often deliver weaker performance than Post-Norm structures. HybridNorm seeks to combine advantages of these arrangements within each Transformer block.

The method normalizes the query, key, and value representations inside attention, while using Post-Norm in the feed-forward network. This gives the two main parts of the block different normalization treatments. The paper provides theoretical insights and empirical evidence that the combination improves gradient flow and model robustness, connecting its architectural choice to how learning signals move through a deep network.

Experiments on large-scale Transformers include both dense and sparse model variants. Across the reported benchmarks, HybridNorm consistently outperforms the Pre-Norm and Post-Norm approaches. These findings support the hybrid arrangement as a promising way to improve deep Transformer training and performance. Its contribution is a targeted change to normalization placement, supported by analysis and comparisons across multiple model settings.
summary.tldr: HybridNorm combines normalization inside attention with Post-Norm feed-forward layers to improve Transformer training and benchmark performance.

title: HybridNorm: Towards Stable and Efficient Transformer Training via Hybrid Normalization

abstract: We address the challenge of training diffusion models to sample from unnormalized energy distributions in the absence of data, the so-called diffusion samplers. Although these approaches have shown promise, they struggle to scale in more demanding scenarios where energy evaluations are expensive and the sampling space is high-dimensional. To address this limitation, we propose a scalable and sample-efficient framework that properly harmonizes the powerful classical sampling method and the diffusion sampler. Specifically, we utilize Monte Carlo Markov chain (MCMC) samplers with a novelty-based auxiliary energy as a Searcher to collect off-policy samples, using an auxiliary energy function to compensate for exploring modes the diffusion sampler rarely visits. These off-policy samples are then combined with on-policy data to train the diffusion sampler, thereby expanding its coverage of the energy landscape. Furthermore, we identify primacy bias, i.e., the preference of samplers for early experience during training, as the main cause of mode collapse during training, and introduce a periodic re-initialization trick to resolve this issue. Our method significantly improves sample efficiency on standard benchmarks for diffusion samplers and also excels at higher-dimensional problems and real-world molecular conformer generation.
