Furthermore, we identify primacy bias, i.e., the preference of samplers for early experience during training, as the main cause of mode collapse during training, and introduce a periodic re-initialization trick to resolve this issue. Our method significantly improves sample efficiency on standard benchmarks for diffusion samplers and also excels at higher-dimensional problems and real-world molecular conformer generation.

paragraphs: Diffusion samplers learn to draw samples from energy-defined distributions without a supplied training dataset. This becomes difficult when evaluating the energy is costly or the sampling space has many dimensions. The paper combines a diffusion sampler with a classical Markov chain Monte Carlo search process to improve exploration and make training samples more useful.

The search process uses an auxiliary energy based on novelty to seek modes that the diffusion sampler rarely reaches. Its off-policy samples are mixed with samples generated by the current diffusion sampler. Training therefore receives information from both the sampler's existing behavior and a complementary search mechanism directed toward underexplored regions.

The authors also identify primacy bias, a preference for early training experience, as the main cause of mode collapse in their study. They introduce periodic reinitialization to address it. Experiments report substantially improved sample efficiency on standard diffusion-sampler benchmarks, along with strong results in higher-dimensional settings and molecular conformer generation. The approach links broader exploration with a mechanism for preventing early experience from dominating later learning.
summary.tldr: A novelty-guided MCMC searcher and periodic reinitialization improve the exploration and training efficiency of diffusion samplers.

title: On scalable and efficient training of diffusion samplers

abstract: The alignment of vision-language representations endows current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) with strong multi-modal reasoning capabilities. However, the interpretability of the alignment component remains uninvestigated due to the difficulty in mapping the semantics of multi-modal representations into a unified concept set. To address this problem, we propose VL-SAE, a sparse autoencoder that encodes vision-language representations into its hidden activations. Each neuron in the hidden layer correlates to a concept represented by semantically similar images and texts, thereby interpreting these representations with a unified concept set. To establish the neuron-concept correlation, we encourage semantically similar representations to exhibit consistent neuron activations during self-supervised training. First, to measure the semantic similarity of multi-modal representations, we perform their alignment in an explicit form based on cosine similarity. Second, we construct the VL-SAE with a distance-based encoder and two modality-specific decoders to ensure the activation consistency of semantically similar representations. Experiments across multiple VLMs (e.g., CLIP, LLaVA) demonstrate the superior capability of VL-SAE in interpreting and enhancing the vision-language alignment. For interpretation, the alignment between vision and language representations can be understood by comparing their semantics with concepts. For enhancement, the alignment can be strengthened by aligning vision-language representations at the concept level, contributing to performance improvements in downstream tasks, including zero-shot image classification and hallucination elimination. Codes are provided in the supplementary and will be released to GitHub.

paragraphs: Vision-language models rely on alignment between image and text representations, but understanding that alignment requires a shared language for their meanings. VL-SAE proposes a sparse autoencoder whose hidden neurons correspond to concepts represented by semantically similar images and texts. During self-supervised training, the method encourages semantically similar representations to activate the same neurons. It first makes cross-modal alignment explicit using cosine similarity. The architecture is designed to make shared meaning visible in the hidden representation.

Experiments with models including CLIP and LLaVA report improved interpretation and enhancement of alignment. Comparing image and text representations through their concepts helps explain their relationship, while aligning at the concept level improves downstream tasks such as zero-shot image classification and hallucination elimination. The contribution thus links an interpretable representation to a practical way of improving the alignment it describes.
summary.tldr: VL-SAE maps image and text representations into shared interpretable concepts and uses concept-level alignment to improve downstream performance.

title: VL-SAE: Interpreting and Enhancing Vision-Language Alignment with a Unified Concept Set

abstract: We investigate the semi-discrete Optimal Transport (OT) problem, where a continuous source measure $\mu$ is transported to a discrete target measure $\nu$, with particular attention to the OT map approximation. In this setting, Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) based solvers have demonstrated strong empirical performance in recent machine learning applications, yet their theoretical guarantee to approximate the OT map is an open question. In this work, we answer it positively by providing both computational and statistical convergence guarantees of SGD. Specifically, we show that SGD methods can estimate the OT map with a minimax convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{n})$, where $n$ is the number of samples drawn from $\mu$. To establish this result, we study the averaged projected SGD algorithm, and identify a suitable projection set that contains a minimizer of the objective, even when the source measure is not compactly supported. Our analysis holds under mild assumptions on the source measure and applies to MTW cost functions,whic include $\|\cdot\|^p$ for $p \in (1, \infty)$. We finally provide numerical evidence for our theoretical results.

paragraphs: Semi-discrete optimal transport moves a continuous source distribution onto a discrete target distribution. The paper focuses on estimating the transport map itself. Stochastic gradient methods have performed well empirically in this setting, but a theoretical guarantee for how accurately they approximate that map had remained unresolved.

The authors analyze averaged projected stochastic gradient descent and establish computational and statistical convergence guarantees. A key step is identifying a projection set that contains an objective minimizer even when the source distribution is not compactly supported. This lets the analysis accommodate source distributions whose support need not be confined to a bounded region.

Under mild source-distribution assumptions and for the stated MTW cost family, including power costs with exponent greater than one, the map estimate achieves a minimax rate of order one over the square root of the sample count. Numerical evidence supports the theory. The result connects an empirically effective solver with an optimal statistical rate in the analyzed setting.
summary.tldr: Averaged projected SGD achieves a minimax 1/√n rate for semi-discrete transport map estimation under the paper’s distribution and cost assumptions.

title: Stochastic Optimization in Semi-Discrete Optimal Transport: Convergence Analysis and Minimax Rate

abstract: Robotic suturing is a prototypical long-horizon dexterous manipulation task, requiring coordinated needle grasping, precise tissue penetration, and secure knot tying. Despite numerous efforts toward end-to-end autonomy, a fully autonomous suturing pipeline has yet to be demonstrated on physical hardware. We introduce SutureBot: an autonomous suturing benchmark on the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK), spanning needle pickup, tissue insertion, and knot tying. To ensure repeatability, we release a high-fidelity dataset comprising 1,890 suturing demonstrations. Furthermore, we propose a goal-conditioned framework that explicitly optimizes insertion-point precision, improving targeting accuracy by 59\%-74\% over a task-only baseline. To establish this task as a benchmark for dexterous imitation learning, we evaluate state-of-the-art vision-language-action (VLA) models, including $\pi_0$, GR00T N1, OpenVLA-OFT, and multitask ACT, each augmented with a high-level task-prediction policy. Autonomous suturing is a key milestone toward achieving robotic autonomy in surgery. These contributions support reproducible evaluation and development of precision-focused, long-horizon dexterous manipulation policies necessary for end-to-end suturing. Dataset is available at: \href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/jchen396/suturebot}{Hugging Face}

paragraphs: Suturing requires a robot to coordinate several precise actions over an extended sequence: grasping a needle, inserting it into tissue, and tying a knot. SutureBot creates a benchmark for studying these connected stages on the da Vinci Research Kit. The work targets reproducible evaluation of policies for this demanding manipulation task.

The authors release 1,890 suturing demonstrations and propose a goal-conditioned framework that explicitly optimizes the precision of the insertion point. Compared with a baseline driven only by the task, this framework improves targeting accuracy by 59%–74%. The result emphasizes the value of making spatial precision an explicit training objective.

The benchmark also evaluates several vision-language-action models and multitask ACT, each supplemented with a policy that predicts the high-level task. Together, the dataset, framework, and evaluations support research on long-horizon imitation learning. The abstract positions these contributions as steps toward end-to-end suturing autonomy, while its concrete reported improvement concerns targeting accuracy rather than a claimed demonstration of fully autonomous surgery.
summary.tldr: SutureBot supplies a robotic suturing benchmark and demonstrations, with explicit precision optimization improving insertion targeting accuracy by 59%–74%.

title: SutureBot: A Precision Framework & Benchmark For Autonomous End-to-End Suturing

abstract: Comprehending natural language and following human instructions are critical capabilities for intelligent agents. However, the flexibility of linguistic instructions induces substantial ambiguity across language-conditioned tasks, severely degrading algorithmic performance. To address these limitations, we present a novel method named DAIL (Distributional Aligned Learning), featuring two key components: distributional policy and semantic alignment. Specifically, we provide theoretical results that the value distribution estimation mechanism enhances task differentiability. Meanwhile, the semantic alignment module captures the correspondence between trajectories and linguistic instructions. Extensive experimental results on both structured and visual observation benchmarks demonstrate that DAIL effectively resolves instruction ambiguities, achieving superior performance to baseline methods. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/RunpengXie/Distributional-Aligned-Learning.

paragraphs: An agent following natural-language instructions must connect what a person says to the task it should perform. Flexible wording can create ambiguity across tasks and degrade reinforcement learning performance. DAIL, short for Distributional Aligned Learning, addresses this problem with two components that help distinguish tasks and connect language to behavior.

The first component is a distributional policy. The authors provide theoretical results showing that its value-distribution estimation mechanism improves task differentiability, meaning the ability to distinguish tasks. The second component performs semantic alignment by capturing relationships between trajectories and instructions. Together, these components address both how tasks are represented through their outcomes and how observed behavior corresponds to linguistic descriptions.

Experiments on benchmarks with structured observations and visual observations show better performance than baseline methods. The authors interpret these results as evidence that DAIL effectively resolves instruction ambiguities in the evaluated settings. The contribution is a combined treatment of task distinction and language-behavior correspondence within language-conditioned reinforcement learning, supported by both theoretical analysis and experimental evaluation.
summary.tldr: DAIL combines value-distribution estimation and instruction-trajectory alignment to reduce ambiguity in language-conditioned reinforcement learning.

title: DAIL: Beyond Task Ambiguity for Language-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Geometric models like DUSt3R have shown great advances in understanding the geometry of a scene from pairs of photos. However, they fail when the inputs are from vastly different viewpoints (e.g., aerial vs.\ ground) or modalities (e.g., photos vs.\ abstract drawings) compared to what was observed during training. This paper addresses a challenging version of this problem: predicting correspondences between ground-level photos and floor plans. Current datasets for joint photo--floor plan reasoning are limited, either lacking in varying modalities (VIGOR) or lacking in correspondences (WAFFLE). To address these limitations, we introduce a new dataset, C3, created by first reconstructing a number of scenes in 3D from Internet photo collections via structure-from-motion, then manually registering the reconstructions to floor plans gathered from the Internet, from which we can derive correspondence between images and floor plans. C3 contains 90K paired floor plans and photos across 597 scenes with 153M pixel-level correspondences and 85K camera poses. We find that state-of-the-art correspondence models struggle on this task. By training on our new data, we can improve on the best performing method by 34\% in RMSE. We also identify open challenges in cross-modal geometric reasoning that our dataset aims to help address. Our project website is available at: \url{https://c3po-correspondence.github.io/}.

paragraphs: Matching a ground-level photograph to a floor plan requires connecting views that differ in both perspective and visual representation. The paper examines this difficult correspondence problem, where geometric models successful on pairs of photographs can struggle. Existing datasets leave important gaps, either in modality variation or in the correspondence annotations needed to learn and evaluate these connections.

The authors construct C3 by reconstructing scenes in three dimensions from Internet photo collections using structure-from-motion. They then manually align those reconstructions with floor plans collected online. That alignment allows them to derive matches between photograph pixels and floor-plan locations. Evaluations show that leading correspondence models struggle on this task. Training with the new data yields a reported 34% improvement in root mean squared error over the best-performing method. This supports the value of dedicated photo–floor-plan supervision, while the paper also identifies remaining challenges in geometric reasoning across different visual modalities.
summary.tldr: C3 supplies dense photo–floor-plan correspondences that improve performance on a difficult cross-view, cross-modality matching task.

title: C3Po: Cross-View Cross-Modality Correspondence by Pointmap Prediction

abstract: Neural PDE solvers offer a powerful tool for modeling complex dynamical systems, but often struggle with error accumulation over long time horizons and maintaining stability and physical consistency. We introduce a multiscale implicit neural emulator that enhances long-term prediction accuracy by conditioning on a hierarchy of lower-dimensional future state representations. Drawing inspiration from the stability properties of numerical implicit time-stepping methods, our approach leverages predictions several steps ahead in time at increasing compression rates for next-timestep refinements. By actively adjusting the temporal downsampling ratios, our design enables the model to capture dynamics across multiple granularities and enforce long-range temporal coherence. Experiments on turbulent fluid dynamics show that our method achieves high short-term accuracy and produces long-term stable forecasts, significantly outperforming autoregressive baselines while adding minimal computational overhead.

paragraphs: Neural models of dynamical systems can make accurate short-term predictions yet accumulate errors as their forecasts extend into the future. This paper introduces an implicit neural emulator that uses a hierarchy of compressed future-state predictions to refine the next time step. The aim is to keep immediate predictions connected to longer-term behavior.

The design draws inspiration from the stability of numerical implicit time-stepping methods. Predictions farther ahead are represented at increasing levels of compression, providing future context at several scales. By adjusting temporal downsampling ratios, the model captures dynamics at different time granularities and encourages coherence over longer horizons. These future representations are predictions used for conditioning, not observed future states.

Experiments on turbulent fluid dynamics show high short-term accuracy together with stable long-term forecasts. The method significantly outperforms autoregressive baselines while introducing minimal computational overhead. The stated result supports using compact, multiscale future context to reduce the weaknesses of repeatedly predicting one step ahead, without giving up accuracy at the immediate next step.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical implicit emulators use compressed predictions of future states to improve short-term accuracy and long-term stability in turbulent-flow forecasting.

title: Hierarchical Implicit Neural Emulators

abstract: Understanding and predicting emotions from videos has gathered significant attention in recent studies, driven by advancements in video large language models (VideoLLMs). While advanced methods have made progress in video emotion analysis, the intrinsic nature of emotions—characterized by their open-set, dynamic, and context-dependent properties—poses challenge in understanding complex and evolving emotional states with reasonable rationale. To tackle these challenges, we propose a novel affective cues-guided reasoning framework that unifies fundamental attribute perception, expression analysis, and high-level emotional understanding in a stage-wise manner. At the core of our approach is a family of video emotion foundation models (VidEmo), specifically designed for emotion reasoning and instruction-following. These models undergo a two-stage tuning process: first, curriculum emotion learning for injecting emotion knowledge, followed by affective-tree reinforcement learning for emotion reasoning. Moreover, we establish a foundational data infrastructure and introduce a emotion-centric fine-grained dataset (Emo-CFG) consisting of 2.1M diverse instruction-based samples. Emo-CFG includes explainable emotional question-answering, fine-grained captions, and associated rationales, providing essential resources for advancing emotion understanding tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive performance, setting a new milestone across 15 face perception tasks.

paragraphs: VidEmo addresses emotion understanding in videos, where emotional states evolve, depend on context, and need not fit a closed set of categories. The paper proposes a staged reasoning framework guided by affective cues. It connects basic attribute perception to expression analysis and then to higher-level emotional understanding.

The resulting family of video models is designed for emotion reasoning and instruction-following. Training has two stages: curriculum emotion learning introduces emotion knowledge, and affective-tree reinforcement learning develops reasoning. This separates the acquisition of relevant knowledge from the subsequent training intended to improve how that knowledge supports emotional interpretations.

The work also introduces Emo-CFG, a dataset with 2.1 million instruction-based samples. It includes emotional question-answering with explanations, detailed captions, and associated rationales. Experiments report competitive performance across 15 face perception tasks. The contribution combines a staged model-training approach with a substantial data resource, supporting the goal of producing emotional interpretations accompanied by reasons rather than relying on an emotion label alone.
summary.tldr: VidEmo combines staged emotion learning, affective-tree reinforcement learning, and a large instruction dataset for reasoned video emotion understanding.

title: VidEmo: Affective-Tree Reasoning for Emotion-Centric Video Foundation Models

abstract: Computer-Aided Design (CAD) is pivotal in industrial manufacturing, with orthographic projection reasoning foundational to its entire workflow—encompassing design, manufacturing, and simulation. However, prevailing deep-learning approaches employ standard 3D reconstruction pipelines as an alternative, which often introduce imprecise dimensions and limit the parametric editability required for CAD workflows. Recently, some researchers adopt vision–language models (VLMs), particularly supervised fine-tuning (SFT), to tackle CAD-related challenges. SFT shows promise but often devolves into pattern memorization, resulting in poor out-of-distribution (OOD) performance on complex reasoning tasks. To tackle these limitations, we introduce CReFT-CAD, a two-stage fine-tuning paradigm: first, a curriculum-driven reinforcement learning stage with difficulty-aware rewards to steadily build reasoning abilities; second, supervised post-tuning to refine instruction following and semantic extraction. Complementing this, we release TriView2CAD, the first large-scale, open-source benchmark for orthographic projection reasoning, comprising 200,000 synthetic and 3,000 real-world orthographic projections with precise dimensional annotations and six interoperable data modalities. Benchmarking leading VLMs on orthographic projection reasoning, we show that CReFT-CAD significantly improves reasoning accuracy and OOD generalizability in real-world scenarios, providing valuable insights to advance CAD reasoning research. The code and adopted datasets are available at \url{https://github.com/KeNiu042/CReFT-CAD}.

paragraphs: Reasoning from orthographic projections is central to CAD workflows, where precise dimensions and editable parameters matter. Standard 3D reconstruction approaches can lose these properties. Vision-language models offer another route, but supervised fine-tuning can encourage memorization of familiar patterns and leave models struggling with unfamiliar, complex reasoning problems.

CReFT-CAD uses two training stages in a specific order. It first applies reinforcement learning with a curriculum and rewards that account for task difficulty, aiming to build reasoning abilities progressively. Supervised post-tuning then refines instruction following and the extraction of relevant meaning. This separates the development of reasoning behavior from later refinement of how the model interprets and follows requests.

The paper also introduces TriView2CAD, a benchmark containing 200,000 synthetic and 3,000 real-world orthographic projections, precise dimensional annotations, and six interoperable data modalities. Evaluations of leading vision-language models show that CReFT-CAD improves reasoning accuracy and generalization to unfamiliar real-world cases. The training method and benchmark together target the dimensional reasoning needed for practical CAD work.
summary.tldr: CReFT-CAD combines curriculum-based reinforcement learning with supervised post-tuning to improve CAD projection reasoning and generalization.

title: CReFT-CAD: Boosting Orthographic Projection Reasoning for CAD via Reinforcement Fine-Tuning

abstract: Crossmodal matching in single-cell omics is essential for explaining biological regulatory mechanisms and enhancing downstream analyses. However, current single-cell crossmodal models often suffer from three limitations: sparse modality signals, underutilization of biological attributes, and insufficient modeling of regulatory interactions. These challenges hinder generalization in data-scarce settings and restrict the ability to uncover fine-grained biologically meaningful crossmodal relationships. Here, we present a novel framework which reformulates crossmodal matching as a graph classification task on Attributed Bipartite Graphs (ABGs). It models single-cell ATAC-RNA data as an ABG, where each expressed ATAC and RNA is treated as a distinct node with unique IDs and biological features. To model crossmodal interaction patterns on the constructed ABG, we propose $\text{Bi}^2\text{Former}$, a **bi**ologically-driven **bi**partite graph trans**former** that learns interpretable attention over ATAC–RNA pairs. This design enables the model to effectively learn and explain biological regulatory relationships between ATAC and RNA modalities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that $\text{Bi}^2\text{Former}$ achieves state-of-the-art performance in crossmodal matching across diverse datasets, remains robust under sparse training data, generalizes to unseen cell types and datasets, and reveals biologically meaningful regulatory patterns. This work pioneers an ABG-based approach for single-cell crossmodal matching, offering a powerful framework for uncovering regulatory interactions at the single-cell omics. Our code is available at: https://github.com/wangxiaotang0906/Bi2Former.

paragraphs: Single-cell crossmodal matching must connect sparse measurements while preserving biologically meaningful relationships. This paper represents paired ATAC and RNA observations as an attributed bipartite graph, with distinct nodes carrying identifiers and biological features.

Bi²Former, a biologically driven bipartite-graph Transformer, learns attention over crossmodal pairs. Framing matching as graph classification allows the model to use attributes and interaction patterns jointly, rather than comparing only two compressed modality summaries.

Across diverse datasets, the method achieves state-of-the-art matching, remains robust with sparse training data, and transfers to unseen cell types and datasets. Its learned interactions also reveal biologically meaningful patterns. Those patterns provide an interpretable basis for further biological investigation, while matching performance and attention structure alone do not establish that every highlighted relationship is causally regulatory.
summary.tldr: Bi²Former models ATAC–RNA matching as classification of biologically attributed bipartite graphs.

title: Learning Crossmodal Interaction Patterns via Attributed Bipartite Graphs for Single-Cell Omics

abstract: Existing Embodied Question Answering (EQA) benchmarks primarily focus on household environments, often overlooking safety-critical aspects and reasoning processes pertinent to industrial settings. This drawback limits the evaluation of agent readiness for real-world industrial applications. To bridge this, we introduce IndustryEQA, the first benchmark dedicated to evaluating embodied agent capabilities within safety-critical industrial warehouse scenarios. Built upon the NVIDIA Isaac Sim platform, IndustryEQA provides high-fidelity episodic memory videos featuring diverse industrial assets, dynamic human agents, and carefully designed hazardous situations inspired by real-world safety guidelines. The benchmark includes rich annotations covering six categories: equipment safety, human safety, object recognition, attribute recognition, temporal understanding, and spatial understanding. Besides, it also provides extra reasoning evaluation based on these categories. Specifically, it comprises 971 question-answer pairs generated from small warehouse scenarios and 373 pairs from large ones, incorporating scenarios with and without human. We further propose a comprehensive evaluation framework, including various baseline models, to assess their general perception and reasoning abilities in industrial environments. IndustryEQA aims to steer EQA research towards developing more robust, safety-aware, and practically applicable embodied agents for complex industrial environments.

abstract: The fine-tuning of pre-trained large language models (LLMs) using reinforcement learning (RL) is generally formulated as direct policy optimization. This approach was naturally favored as it efficiently improves a pretrained LLM with simple gradient updates. Another RL paradigm, Q-learning methods, has received far less attention in the LLM community while demonstrating major success in various non-LLM RL tasks. In particular, Q-learning effectiveness stems from its sample efficiency and ability to learn offline, which is particularly valuable given the high computational cost of sampling with LLM. However, naively applying a Q-learning–style update to the model’s logits is ineffective due to the specificity of LLMs. Our contribution is to derive theoretically grounded loss functions from Bellman equations to adapt Q-learning methods to LLMs. To do so, we interpret LLM logits as Q-values and carefully adapt insights from the RL literature to account for LLM-specific characteristics. It thereby ensures that the logits become reliable Q-value estimates. We then use this loss to build a practical algorithm, ShiQ for Shifted-Q, that supports off-policy, token-wise learning while remaining simple to implement. Finally, ShiQ is evaluated on both synthetic data and real-world benchmarks, e.g., UltraFeedback, BFCL-V3, demonstrating its effectiveness in both single-turn and multi-turn LLM settings.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning for language models usually updates the policy directly. ShiQ explores Q-learning, an alternative that learns values associated with choices and has advantages for sample-efficient and offline learning. Those properties are attractive when generating new language-model samples is computationally expensive, but straightforward Q-learning updates to token logits are ineffective.

Evaluations on synthetic data and real-world benchmarks, including UltraFeedback and BFCL-V3, demonstrate effectiveness in single-turn and multi-turn settings. The contribution is a theoretically grounded adaptation that makes Q-learning usable for language-model fine-tuning while remaining simple to implement.
summary.tldr: ShiQ derives Bellman-based losses that turn language-model logits into useful Q-value estimates for off-policy, token-level learning.

title: ShiQ: Bringing back Bellman to LLMs

abstract: Stochastic Natural Gradient Variational Inference (NGVI) is a widely used method for approximating posterior distribution in probabilistic models. Despite its empirical success and foundational role in variational inference, its theoretical underpinnings remain limited, particularly in the case of non-conjugate likelihoods. While NGVI has been shown to be a special instance of Stochastic Mirror Descent, and recent work has provided convergence guarantees using relative smoothness and strong convexity for conjugate models, these results do not extend to the non-conjugate setting, where the variational loss becomes non-convex and harder to analyze. In this work, we focus on mean-field parameterization and advance the theoretical understanding of NGVI in three key directions. First, we derive sufficient conditions under which the variational loss satisfies relative smoothness with respect to a suitable mirror map. Second, leveraging this structure, we propose a modified NGVI algorithm incorporating non-Euclidean projections and prove its global non-asymptotic convergence to a stationary point. Finally, under additional structural assumptions about the likelihood, we uncover hidden convexity properties of the variational loss and establish fast global convergence of NGVI to a global optimum. These results provide new insights into the geometry and convergence behavior of NGVI in challenging inference settings.

paragraphs: Natural Gradient Variational Inference approximates posterior distributions by optimizing a simpler distribution. Although widely used, its convergence theory is less developed for non-conjugate models, where the objective can be non-convex. This paper studies that setting under a mean-field parameterization, which structures the approximate distribution into separate components.

The authors first derive sufficient conditions for relative smoothness: a way to control how the objective changes using geometry defined by a suitable mirror map. They then modify the algorithm with non-Euclidean projections. Using this structure, they prove a finite-iteration convergence guarantee toward a stationary point. Such a point need not be a global optimum in a non-convex problem.

A stronger result requires additional structural assumptions on the likelihood. Under those assumptions, the authors identify hidden convexity and establish fast global convergence to a global optimum. The paper therefore separates two levels of guarantee, showing how the available mathematical structure determines whether convergence reaches stationarity or the best possible objective value.
summary.tldr: The paper gives conditional convergence guarantees for non-conjugate natural-gradient variational inference, with global optimality requiring additional likelihood structure.

title: Natural Gradient VI: Guarantees for Non-Conjugate Models

abstract: Boosting methods often achieve excellent classification accuracy, but can experience notable performance degradation in the presence of label noise. Existing robust methods for boosting provide theoretical robustness guarantees for certain types of label noise, and can exhibit only moderate performance degradation. However, previous theoretical results do not account for realistic types of noise and finite training sizes, and existing robust methods can provide unsatisfactory accuracies, even without noise. This paper presents methods for robust minimax boosting (RMBoost) that minimize worst-case error probabilities and are robust to general types of label noise. In addition, we provide finite-sample performance guarantees for RMBoost with respect to the error obtained without noise and with respect to the best possible error (Bayes risk). The experimental results corroborate that RMBoost is not only resilient to label noise but can also provide strong classification accuracy.

paragraphs: RMBoost addresses the loss of classification accuracy that boosting methods can experience when training labels are wrong. Existing robust approaches offer guarantees for some noise types, but the paper identifies gaps around realistic noise and finite datasets. It also notes that robustness methods can deliver unsatisfactory accuracy even when labels are clean.

The proposed robust minimax boosting methods minimize worst-case error probabilities and address general types of label noise. Their theoretical analysis provides finite-sample guarantees, making the number of available training examples part of the performance statement. The guarantees relate performance both to the error achieved without label noise and to Bayes risk, the best possible error.

These two reference points connect resistance to corrupted labels with the broader goal of accurate classification. Experiments support the theoretical direction: RMBoost remains resilient to label noise while also providing strong classification accuracy. The contribution combines a worst-case optimization approach with guarantees relevant to finite training sets and empirical evidence that robustness can accompany effective prediction.
summary.tldr: RMBoost minimizes worst-case classification error and provides finite-sample guarantees for learning with general label noise.

title: Robust Minimax Boosting with Performance Guarantees

abstract: Conformal prediction offers a distribution-free framework for constructing prediction sets with coverage guarantees. In practice, multiple valid conformal prediction sets may be available, arising from different models or methodologies. However, selecting the most desirable set, such as the smallest, can invalidate the coverage guarantees. To address this challenge, we propose a stability-based approach that ensures coverage for the selected prediction set. We extend our results to the online conformal setting, propose several refinements in settings where additional structure is available, and demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments.
originalAbstract: Conformal prediction offers a distribution-free framework for constructing prediction sets with coverage guarantees. In practice, multiple valid conformal prediction sets may be available, arising from different models or methodologies. However, selecting the most desirable set, such as the smallest, can invalidate the coverage guarantees. We extend our results to the online conformal setting, propose several refinements in settings where additional structure is available, and demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction produces sets of possible answers with coverage guarantees. In practice, several models or methods may each provide a valid set, creating a natural desire to choose the most useful one. This paper addresses a subtle problem: selecting among individually valid sets, for example by choosing the smallest, can destroy the coverage guarantee.

The authors propose a stability-based approach that ensures coverage for the selected prediction set. The key contribution is to account for the selection step itself. Having a guarantee for every candidate separately is insufficient to justify the final choice, so the method makes validity after selection the object of the analysis.

The results also extend to online conformal prediction, and the paper develops refinements for settings with additional structure. Experiments demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. This work matters whenever practical preferences guide a choice among prediction sets: it provides a way to accommodate that choice while retaining a coverage guarantee, rather than evaluating validity only before the selection takes place.
summary.tldr: A stability-based method preserves conformal coverage when choosing among multiple prediction sets, including extensions to online settings.

title: Valid Selection among Conformal Sets

abstract: We study the repeated, non-atomic routing game, in which selfish players make a sequence of routing decisions. We consider a model in which players use regret-minimizing algorithms as the learning mechanism, and study the resulting dynamics. We are concerned in particular with the convergence to the set of Nash equilibria of the routing game. No-regret learning algorithms are known to guarantee convergence of a subsequence of population strategies. We are concerned with convergence of the actual sequence. We show that convergence holds for a large class of online learning algorithms, inspired from the continuous-time replicator dynamics. In particular, the discounted Hedge algorithm is proved to belong to this class, which guarantees its convergence.

paragraphs: The paper studies repeated routing decisions by selfish players in a non-atomic game, where individual players have negligible influence on overall traffic. Players choose routes using regret-minimizing learning algorithms. The question is whether the resulting population behavior approaches the set of Nash equilibria as learning continues.

Previously known no-regret guarantees establish convergence for a subsequence of population strategies. That leaves open what happens along the complete sequence of decisions. The authors focus on this stronger requirement: whether the actual sequence converges to the equilibrium set, rather than only selected points along the learning process.

They prove full-sequence convergence for a large class of online learning algorithms inspired by continuous-time replicator dynamics. They also prove that discounted Hedge belongs to this class, establishing its convergence in the studied routing setting. The result connects a concrete learning algorithm to stable long-run population behavior while keeping the guarantee specific to the algorithm class and game model analyzed.
summary.tldr: A broad class of no-regret algorithms, including discounted Hedge, has full-sequence convergence to Nash equilibria in repeated non-atomic routing.

title: On the convergence of no-regret learning in selfish routing

abstract: This paper introduces AdaSDCA: an adaptive variant of stochastic dual coordinate ascent (SDCA) for solving the regularized empirical risk minimization problems. Our modification consists in allowing the method adaptively change the probability distribution over the dual variables throughout the iterative process. AdaSDCA achieves provably better complexity bound than SDCA with the best fixed probability distribution, known as importance sampling. However, it is of a theoretical character as it is expensive to implement. We also propose AdaSDCA+: a practical variant which in our experiments outperforms existing non-adaptive methods.
originalAbstract: This paper introduces AdaSDCA: an adaptive variant of stochastic dual coordinate ascent (SDCA) for solving the regularized empirical risk minimization problems. Our modification consists in allowing the method adaptively change the probability distribution over the dual variables throughout the iterative process. AdaSDCA achieves provably better complexity bound than SDCA with the best fixed probability distribution, known as importance sampling. However, it is of a theoretical character as it is expensive to implement. We also propose AdaSDCA+: a practical variant which in our experiments outperforms existing non-adaptive methods.

paragraphs: Stochastic dual coordinate ascent solves regularized empirical-risk minimization problems by iteratively updating dual variables. This paper asks whether the probabilities used to choose those variables should change as optimization proceeds. Its AdaSDCA method makes that sampling distribution adaptive, allowing the selection rule to evolve throughout the iterative process.

The theoretical result is a better complexity bound than SDCA using the best fixed probability distribution, known as importance sampling. This comparison is meaningful because the advantage is over an optimized fixed sampling rule. However, the authors explicitly describe AdaSDCA as expensive to implement, so the improved bound does not by itself establish a practical computational advantage.

To address that cost, they introduce AdaSDCA+, a practical variant. In the reported experiments, it outperforms existing nonadaptive methods. The paper thus separates two contributions: a theoretical case for changing sampling probabilities during optimization and an implementable method with empirical benefits. The abstract gives the stronger complexity claim for AdaSDCA and the experimental performance claim for AdaSDCA+.
summary.tldr: Adaptive coordinate sampling improves SDCA’s theoretical complexity, while a practical variant outperforms nonadaptive methods in experiments.

title: Stochastic Dual Coordinate Ascent with Adaptive Probabilities

abstract: Second-order optimization methods, such as natural gradient, are difficult to apply to high-dimensional problems, because they require approximately solving large linear systems. We present FActorized Natural Gradient (FANG), an approximation to natural gradient descent where the Fisher matrix is approximated with a Gaussian graphical model whose precision matrix can be computed efficiently. We analyze the Fisher matrix for a small RBM and derive an extremely sparse graphical model which is a good match to the covariance of the sufficient statistics. Our experiments indicate that FANG allows RBMs to be trained more efficiently compared with stochastic gradient descent. Additionally, our analysis yields insight into the surprisingly good performance of the “centering trick” for training RBMs.

We analyze the Fisher matrix for a small RBM and derive an extremely sparse graphical model which is a good match to the covariance of the sufficient statistics. Our experiments indicate that FANG allows RBMs to be trained more efficiently compared with stochastic gradient descent. Additionally, our analysis yields insight into the surprisingly good performance of the “centering trick” for training RBMs.

paragraphs: Natural-gradient methods become difficult to apply in high dimensions because their updates require approximately solving large linear systems. This paper introduces FActorized Natural Gradient, or FANG, to make those updates cheaper. The approach approximates the Fisher information matrix through a Gaussian graphical model whose precision matrix can be computed efficiently.

The authors study the Fisher matrix of a small restricted Boltzmann machine and derive an extremely sparse graphical model. That model closely matches the covariance of the sufficient statistics examined in their analysis. The important design idea is to exploit structure in the approximation so that the matrix operation needed for natural-gradient learning becomes more manageable.

Experiments indicate that FANG trains restricted Boltzmann machines more efficiently than stochastic gradient descent. The analysis also provides insight into why the centering trick works surprisingly well for RBM training. Together, these contributions offer both an approximate optimization method and an explanation of an existing training practice, grounded in the structure of the Fisher matrix investigated in the paper.
summary.tldr: FANG uses a sparse graphical approximation to make natural-gradient RBM training more efficient in reported experiments.

title: Scaling up Natural Gradient by Sparsely Factorizing the Inverse Fisher Matrix

abstract: In compressed sensing, a small number of linear measurements can be used to reconstruct an unknown signal. Existing approaches leverage assumptions on the structure of these signals, such as sparsity or the availability of a generative model. A domain-specific generative model can provide a stronger prior and thus allow for recovery with far fewer measurements. However, unlike sparsity-based approaches, existing methods based on generative models guarantee exact recovery only over their support, which is typically only a small subset of the space on which the signals are defined. We propose Sparse-Gen, a framework that allows for sparse deviations from the support set, thereby achieving the best of both worlds by using a domain specific prior and allowing reconstruction over the full space of signals. Theoretically, our framework provides a new class of signals that can be acquired using compressed sensing, reducing classic sparse vector recovery to a special case and avoiding the restrictive support due to a generative model prior. Empirically, we observe consistent improvements in reconstruction accuracy over competing approaches, especially in the more practical setting of transfer compressed sensing where a generative model for a data-rich, source domain aids sensing on a data-scarce, target domain.

paragraphs: Compressed sensing reconstructs a signal from a small number of linear measurements by exploiting assumptions about its structure. A domain-specific generative model can supply a strong prior and reduce the measurements needed. However, existing generative approaches guarantee exact recovery only for signals within the model's support, which may cover little of the overall signal space.

Sparse-Gen allows a signal to deviate sparsely from that support. It therefore combines a domain-specific generative prior with a way to represent departures from what the generator can produce. This expands the reconstruction framework beyond the generator's support without discarding the structure supplied by the model.

The theoretical framework introduces a class of signals suitable for compressed sensing and includes classical sparse-vector recovery as a special case. Experiments report consistent reconstruction improvements over competing approaches, especially in transfer compressed sensing. In that setting, a generator learned from a data-rich source domain helps sensing in a data-scarce target domain, where allowing deviations from the source model is particularly useful.
summary.tldr: Sparse-Gen combines generative priors with sparse deviations to broaden compressed-sensing reconstruction beyond a generator's support.

title: Modeling Sparse Deviations for Compressed Sensing using Generative Models

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful technique to train an agent to perform a task; however, an agent that is trained using RL is only capable of achieving the single task that is specified via its reward function. Such an approach does not scale well to settings in which an agent needs to perform a diverse set of tasks, such as navigating to varying positions in a room or moving objects to varying locations. Instead, we propose a method that allows an agent to automatically discover the range of tasks that it is capable of performing in its environment. We use a generator network to propose tasks for the agent to try to accomplish, each task being specified as reaching a certain parametrized subset of the state-space. The generator network is optimized using adversarial training to produce tasks that are always at the appropriate level of difficulty for the agent, thus automatically producing a curriculum. We show that, by using this framework, an agent can efficiently and automatically learn to perform a wide set of tasks without requiring any prior knowledge of its environment, even when only sparse rewards are available. Videos and code available at https://sites.google.com/view/goalgeneration4rl.

Videos and code available at https://sites.google.com/view/goalgeneration4rl.

paragraphs: Training a reinforcement learning agent around one reward-defined task does not directly provide a way to learn a diverse collection of tasks. This paper tackles the problem of discovering what an agent can accomplish in its environment. Its motivating examples include reaching different positions and moving objects to different locations.

A generator network proposes goals for the agent, with each goal expressed as reaching a parameterized subset of possible states. Adversarial training adjusts the generator to produce tasks at a suitable difficulty for the agent. The resulting sequence of goals acts as an automatically produced curriculum, linking task selection to the agent's developing capabilities.

The authors show that this framework can efficiently learn a broad set of tasks without prior knowledge of the environment, including settings with sparse rewards. The significance is that choosing learning goals becomes part of the learning process itself. The method supplies both tasks to attempt and a mechanism for keeping those tasks aligned with the agent's progress.
summary.tldr: An adversarially trained goal generator creates an adaptive curriculum that helps reinforcement learning agents discover and learn many tasks.

title: Automatic Goal Generation for Reinforcement Learning Agents

abstract: Model-free deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have been demonstrated on a range of challenging decision making and control tasks. However, these methods typically suffer from two major challenges: very high sample complexity and brittle convergence properties, which necessitate meticulous hyperparameter tuning. Both of these challenges severely limit the applicability of such methods to complex, real-world domains. In this paper, we propose soft actor-critic, an off-policy actor-critic deep RL algorithm based on the maximum entropy reinforcement learning framework. In this framework, the actor aims to maximize expected reward while also maximizing entropy. That is, to succeed at the task while acting as randomly as possible. Prior deep RL methods based on this framework have been formulated as Q-learning methods. By combining off-policy updates with a stable stochastic actor-critic formulation, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on a range of continuous control benchmark tasks, outperforming prior on-policy and off-policy methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, in contrast to other off-policy algorithms, our approach is very stable, achieving very similar performance across different random seeds.

In this framework, the actor aims to maximize expected reward while also maximizing entropy. That is, to succeed at the task while acting as randomly as possible. paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can require many samples and careful hyperparameter choices to train reliably. Soft actor-critic addresses these challenges through an off-policy actor-critic algorithm built around maximum-entropy reinforcement learning. Its actor seeks high expected reward while also retaining as much randomness in its behavior as the objective encourages.

The method combines off-policy updates with a stable stochastic actor-critic formulation. This brings an explicit stochastic actor into a maximum-entropy framework that prior deep methods had formulated through Q-learning. The approach makes behavioral randomness part of the learning objective alongside task success, rather than treating reward as the sole quantity being maximized.

On a range of continuous-control benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance, exceeding the prior on-policy and off-policy methods they evaluate. They also find very similar performance across different random seeds, supporting the claim of stable learning in those experiments. The findings connect competitive control performance with reproducibility across training runs, addressing both effectiveness and the brittleness motivating the method.
summary.tldr: Soft actor-critic combines off-policy learning with a maximum-entropy stochastic actor to deliver strong, stable continuous-control benchmark performance.

title: Soft Actor-Critic: Off-Policy Maximum Entropy Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Stochastic Actor

abstract: The Cox process is a flexible event model that can account for uncertainty of the intensity function in the Poisson process. However, previous approaches make strong assumptions in terms of time stationarity, potentially failing to generalize when the data do not conform to the assumed stationarity conditions. In this paper we bring up two most popular Cox models representing two extremes, and propose a novel semi-stationary Cox process model that can take benefits from both models. Our model has a set of Gaussian process latent functions governed by a latent stationary Markov process where we provide analytic derivations for the variational inference. Empirical evaluations on several synthetic and real-world events data including the football shot attempts and daily earthquakes, demonstrate that the proposed model is promising, can yield improved generalization performance over existing approaches.

In this paper we bring up two most popular Cox models representing two extremes, and propose a novel semi-stationary Cox process model that can take benefits from both models. Our model has a set of Gaussian process latent functions governed by a latent stationary Markov process where we provide analytic derivations for the variational inference. paragraphs: Event models describe how frequently occurrences happen over time. A Cox process allows uncertainty in the event intensity, or rate, of a Poisson process. This paper addresses the concern that existing Cox approaches impose strong stationarity assumptions and may generalize poorly when the observed event data do not follow those assumptions.

The authors propose a semi-stationary model intended to combine benefits from two popular Cox models representing different extremes. Their construction uses several latent Gaussian-process functions governed by a hidden stationary Markov process. This arrangement gives the model a way to represent event intensity through multiple latent functions within a common probabilistic framework.

The paper provides analytic derivations for variational inference in this model and evaluates it on synthetic and real-world event data. The real-world examples include football shot attempts and daily earthquakes. The reported results are promising and show that the approach can improve generalization over existing methods, supporting its use when the stationarity assumptions of those methods are unsuitable.
summary.tldr: A semi-stationary Cox model combines Gaussian-process functions under a latent Markov process and shows promising event-prediction generalization.

title: Markov Modulated Gaussian Cox Processes for Semi-Stationary Intensity Modeling of Events Data

abstract: The convolutional layers are core building blocks of neural network architectures. In general, a convolutional filter applies to the entire frequency spectrum of the input data. We explore artificially constraining the frequency spectra of these filters and data, called band-limiting, during training. The frequency domain constraints apply to both the feed-forward and back-propagation steps. Experimentally, we observe that Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are resilient to this compression scheme and results suggest that CNNs learn to leverage lower-frequency components. In particular, we found: (1) band-limited training can effectively control the resource usage (GPU and memory); (2) models trained with band-limited layers retain high prediction accuracy; and (3) requires no modification to existing training algorithms or neural network architectures to use unlike other compression schemes.

Training therefore takes place with the compression already present. The authors report that using these layers requires no changes to the surrounding network architecture or existing training algorithms, making the approach applicable within established training procedures.

The results suggest that networks learn to use lower-frequency information effectively. That interpretation is an empirical finding about the investigated approach, rather than a claim that higher-frequency information is always unnecessary.
summary.tldr: Restricting convolutional computations to selected frequencies can control resource use while retaining high accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: Band-limited Training and Inference for Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: We initiate the study of coresets for clustering in graph metrics, i.e., the shortest-path metric of edge-weighted graphs. Such clustering problems are essential to data analysis and used for example in road networks and data visualization. A coreset is a compact summary of the data that approximately preserves the clustering objective for every possible center set, and it offers significant efficiency improvements in terms of running time, storage, and communication, including in streaming and distributed settings. Our main result is a near-linear time construction of a coreset for k-Median in a general graph $G$, with size $O_{\epsilon, k}(\mathrm{tw}(G))$ where $\mathrm{tw}(G)$ is the treewidth of $G$, and we complement the construction with a nearly-tight size lower bound. The construction is based on the framework of Feldman and Langberg [STOC 2011], and our main technical contribution, as required by this framework, is a uniform bound of $O(\mathrm{tw}(G))$ on the shattering dimension under any point weights. We validate our coreset on real-world road networks, and our scalable algorithm constructs tiny coresets with high accuracy, which translates to a massive speedup of existing approximation algorithms such as local search for graph k-Median.

paragraphs: Clustering on a road network or another weighted graph uses shortest-path distances rather than ordinary straight-line distances. This paper studies how to compress such clustering problems using a coreset: a small summary that approximately preserves the clustering objective for every possible choice of centers. Preserving all center choices makes the summary useful throughout the search for a good clustering.

For graph k-Median, the authors construct a coreset in near-linear time. With the accuracy requirement and number of centers fixed, its size grows linearly with the graph's treewidth. A nearly matching lower bound shows that the size dependence is close to unavoidable. The key technical step bounds a complexity measure called shattering dimension by treewidth, uniformly over point weights.

On real road networks, the method produces very small coresets with high accuracy and substantially speeds up existing approximation algorithms, including local search. The theoretical result connects compressibility to graph structure, while the experiments show how that compression can translate into faster clustering. Coresets also provide a route to reducing storage and communication requirements.
summary.tldr: Graph k-Median coresets can be constructed in near-linear time with size controlled by treewidth, yielding substantial clustering speedups on road networks.

title: Coresets for Clustering in Graphs of Bounded Treewidth

abstract: Federated learning is a key scenario in modern large-scale machine learning where the data remains distributed over a large number of clients and the task is to learn a centralized model without transmitting the client data. The standard optimization algorithm used in this setting is Federated Averaging (FedAvg) due to its low communication cost. We obtain a tight characterization of the convergence of FedAvg and prove that heterogeneity (non-iid-ness) in the client’s data results in a ‘drift’ in the local updates resulting in poor performance. As a solution, we propose a new algorithm (SCAFFOLD) which uses control variates (variance reduction) to correct for the ‘client drift’. We prove that SCAFFOLD requires significantly fewer communication rounds and is not affected by data heterogeneity or client sampling. Further, we show that (for quadratics) SCAFFOLD can take advantage of similarity in the client’s data yielding even faster convergence. The latter is the first result to quantify the usefulness of local-steps in distributed optimization.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains a shared model while leaving data distributed across clients. Federated Averaging is attractive because it limits communication, but clients may hold different data distributions. This paper gives a tight convergence characterization of Federated Averaging and shows how those differences cause local updates to drift, harming performance.

SCAFFOLD corrects this client drift using control variates, a variance-reduction mechanism. The authors prove that it requires substantially fewer communication rounds and that its convergence guarantees are not affected by data heterogeneity or client sampling in the analyzed setting. The correction directly addresses the failure mechanism identified in the analysis of local updates.

For quadratic objectives, the paper further shows that SCAFFOLD can exploit similarities between clients' data to converge faster. This result quantifies when local optimization steps provide an advantage in distributed learning. Together, the results explain both a source of difficulty with local training and how corrected local steps can reduce communication while benefiting from shared structure.
summary.tldr: SCAFFOLD uses control variates to correct federated client drift and provides stronger convergence and communication guarantees.

title: SCAFFOLD: Stochastic Controlled Averaging for Federated Learning

abstract: We build four new test sets for the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) and evaluate the ability of question-answering systems to generalize to new data. Our first test set is from the original Wikipedia domain and measures the extent to which existing systems overfit the original test set. Despite several years of heavy test set re-use, we find no evidence of adaptive overfitting. The remaining three test sets are constructed from New York Times articles, Reddit posts, and Amazon product reviews and measure robustness to natural distribution shifts. Across a broad range of models, we observe average performance drops of 3.8, 14.0, and 17.4 F1 points, respectively. In contrast, a strong human baseline matches or exceeds the performance of SQuAD models on the original domain and exhibits little to no drop in new domains. Taken together, our results confirm the surprising resilience of the holdout method and emphasize the need to move towards evaluation metrics that incorporate robustness to natural distribution shifts.

paragraphs: A strong benchmark score can leave two questions unresolved: whether repeated use has encouraged overfitting to the test set, and whether the model works on different kinds of text. This paper separates those questions by constructing four new test sets for SQuAD question-answering systems.

One test set uses Wikipedia, matching the original domain. Despite extensive reuse of the original test set, the authors find no evidence of adaptive overfitting. The other sets use New York Times articles, Reddit posts, and Amazon product reviews. Across a broad collection of models, average performance falls by 3.8, 14.0, and 17.4 F1 points, respectively, on those domains.

A strong human baseline matches or exceeds model performance in the original domain and shows little or no decline on the new domains. This contrast indicates that the observed model drops are not mirrored by comparable human deterioration. The results support the resilience of holdout evaluation in the studied setting while motivating evaluations that explicitly measure robustness to natural changes in data.
summary.tldr: New SQuAD tests find no evidence of adaptive test-set overfitting but substantial model performance drops across naturally different text domains.

title: The Effect of Natural Distribution Shift on Question Answering Models

abstract: In a standard setting of Bayesian optimization (BO), the objective function evaluation is assumed to be highly expensive. Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) accelerates BO by incorporating lower fidelity observations available with a lower sampling cost. We propose a novel information-theoretic approach to MFBO, called multi-fidelity max-value entropy search (MF-MES), that enables us to obtain a more reliable evaluation of the information gain compared with existing information-based methods for MFBO. Further, we also propose a parallelization of MF-MES mainly for the asynchronous setting because queries typically occur asynchronously in MFBO due to a variety of sampling costs. We show that most of computations in our acquisition functions can be derived analytically, except for at most only two dimensional numerical integration that can be performed efficiently by simple approximations. We demonstrate effectiveness of our approach by using benchmark datasets and a real-world application to materials science data.

paragraphs: When evaluating an objective is expensive, Bayesian optimization tries to choose informative evaluations carefully. Multi-fidelity optimization also uses cheaper, lower-fidelity observations to accelerate this search. The challenge is deciding which observations are worth acquiring when their costs and usefulness differ.

The paper proposes multi-fidelity max-value entropy search, or MF-MES, an information-based approach centered on the maximum objective value. The authors report a more reliable evaluation of information gain than existing information-based multi-fidelity methods. Most acquisition-function calculations can be derived analytically; the remaining numerical integration is at most two-dimensional and can be handled efficiently with simple approximations.

The method is also extended to parallel evaluation, particularly when queries finish asynchronously. That setting is relevant because different fidelity levels have different sampling costs. Experiments on benchmark datasets and materials science data demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution connects information-guided evaluation choices with computationally manageable acquisition calculations and parallel execution suited to unequal evaluation times.
summary.tldr: MF-MES selects informative evaluations across fidelity levels using tractable entropy calculations and supports asynchronous parallel optimization.

title: Multi-fidelity Bayesian Optimization with Max-value Entropy Search and its Parallelization

abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) leverages unlabeled data when training a model with insufficient labeled data. A common strategy for SSL is to enforce the consistency of model outputs between similar samples, e.g., neighbors or data augmentations of the same sample. However, model outputs can vary dramatically on unlabeled data over different training stages, e.g., when using large learning rates. This can introduce harmful noises and inconsistent objectives over time that may lead to concept drift and catastrophic forgetting. In this paper, we study the dynamics of neural net outputs in SSL and show that selecting and using first the unlabeled samples with more consistent outputs over the course of training (i.e., "time-consistency") can improve the final test accuracy and save computation. Under the time-consistent data selection, we design an SSL objective composed of two self-supervised losses, i.e., a consistency loss between a sample and its augmentation, and a contrastive loss encouraging different samples to have different outputs. Our approach achieves SOTA on several SSL benchmarks with much fewer computations.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled examples alongside limited labeled data. A common approach asks the model to produce consistent outputs for similar examples or augmentations. This paper points out that predictions on an unlabeled example can change substantially across training stages, creating noisy or conflicting objectives that may contribute to concept drift and catastrophic forgetting.

The proposed approach gives priority to unlabeled examples whose outputs remain more consistent over time. Under this selection rule, training combines two self-supervised losses. A consistency loss aligns an example with its augmentation, while a contrastive loss encourages different examples to have different outputs. Temporal stability thus guides which unlabeled examples are used first.

The authors show that this time-consistent selection can improve final test accuracy while reducing computation. Their complete method achieves state-of-the-art results on several semi-supervised benchmarks with substantially less computation. The findings make training dynamics part of the data-selection strategy: the usefulness of an unlabeled example depends partly on how reliably the model treats it over the course of learning.
summary.tldr: Prioritizing unlabeled examples with stable predictions over time improves semi-supervised accuracy and reduces computation in the reported benchmarks.

title: Time-Consistent Self-Supervision for Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: We provide an approximation algorithm for k-means clustering in the \emph{one-round} (aka \emph{non-interactive}) local model of differential privacy (DP). Our algorithm achieves an approximation ratio arbitrarily close to the best \emph{non private} approximation algorithm, improving upon previously known algorithms that only guarantee large (constant) approximation ratios. Furthermore, ours is the first constant-factor approximation algorithm for k-means that requires only \emph{one} round of communication in the local DP model, positively resolving an open question of Stemmer (SODA 2020). Our algorithmic framework is quite flexible; we demonstrate this by showing that it also yields a similar near-optimal approximation algorithm in the (one-round) shuffle DP model.

paragraphs: This paper studies k-means clustering under local differential privacy with only one round of communication. The non-interactive requirement rules out repeated exchanges as the clustering procedure develops. The central question is whether strong clustering approximations remain possible while meeting both this communication restriction and the local privacy requirement.

The authors provide an algorithm whose approximation ratio can be made arbitrarily close to that of the best non-private approximation algorithm. This improves on previously known methods with large constant approximation ratios. They also establish the first constant-factor approximation for k-means using a single round in the local privacy model, resolving the stated open question.

The result concerns approximation quality relative to non-private algorithms, rather than a claim of always recovering the exact optimal clustering. The same framework also yields a similar near-optimal approximation in the one-round shuffle privacy model. This extension shows that the underlying approach can support strong clustering guarantees across more than one privacy setting while retaining a non-interactive communication structure.
summary.tldr: A one-round private k-means algorithm approaches the approximation ratio of the best non-private algorithm.

title: Locally Private k-Means in One Round

abstract: In this paper, we revisit the classic CountSketch method, which is a sparse, random projection that transforms a (high-dimensional) Euclidean vector $v$ to a vector of dimension $(2t-1) s$, where $t, s > 0$ are integer parameters. It is known that a CountSketch allows estimating coordinates of $v$ with variance bounded by $\|v\|_2^2/s$. For $t > 1$, the estimator takes the median of $2t-1$ independent estimates, and the probability that the estimate is off by more than $2 \|v\|_2/\sqrt{s}$ is exponentially small in $t$. This suggests choosing $t$ to be logarithmic in a desired inverse failure probability. However, implementations of CountSketch often use a small, constant $t$. Previous work only predicts a constant factor improvement in this setting. Our main contribution is a new analysis of CountSketch, showing an improvement in variance to $O(\min\{\|v\|_1^2/s^2,\|v\|_2^2/s\})$ when $t > 1$. That is, the variance decreases proportionally to $s^{-2}$, asymptotically for large enough $s$.

paragraphs: CountSketch compresses a high-dimensional vector using a sparse random projection while allowing its individual coordinates to be estimated. Its parameters control the size of each sketch and the number of independent estimates combined. With multiple estimates, the coordinate estimate is their median, which helps reduce the effect of unusually large errors.

Earlier analysis showed that increasing the number of estimates makes large errors exponentially less likely. That motivates many repetitions when a very small failure probability is needed. Implementations, however, often use only a small constant number. For that common choice, previous theory predicted only a constant-factor improvement.

The paper supplies a stronger variance analysis whenever t is greater than one, including a median of three estimates. The bound is O(min{||v||₁²/s², ||v||₂²/s}), where s controls sketch width. For a fixed vector and sufficiently large s, the inverse-square term improves on the familiar inverse-linear dependence. The result explains how a small number of repetitions can change variance scaling, rather than merely improving a constant.
summary.tldr: A new CountSketch analysis shows that even a median of three estimates can yield variance bounds that scale inversely with squared sketch width.

title: CountSketches, Feature Hashing and the Median of Three

abstract: Approximate bi-level optimization (ABLO) consists of (outer-level) optimization problems, involving numerical (inner-level) optimization loops. While ABLO has many applications across deep learning, it suffers from time and memory complexity proportional to the length $r$ of its inner optimization loop. To address this complexity, an earlier first-order method (FOM) was proposed as a heuristic which omits second derivative terms, yielding significant speed gains and requiring only constant memory. Despite FOM’s popularity, there is a lack of theoretical understanding of its convergence properties. We contribute by theoretically characterizing FOM’s gradient bias under mild assumptions. We further demonstrate a rich family of examples where FOM-based SGD does not converge to a stationary point of the ABLO objective. We address this concern by proposing an unbiased FOM (UFOM) enjoying constant memory complexity as a function of $r$. We characterize the introduced time-variance tradeoff, demonstrate convergence bounds, and find an optimal UFOM for a given ABLO problem. Finally, we propose an efficient adaptive UFOM scheme.
