paragraphs: Approximate bi-level optimization places a numerical optimization loop inside another optimization problem. Computing the outer update can require time and memory that grow with the length of the inner loop. A popular first-order shortcut drops second-derivative terms, gaining speed and using constant memory, but its convergence behavior has lacked a clear theoretical account.

The paper characterizes the shortcut’s gradient bias under mild assumptions. It also constructs a broad family of examples where stochastic gradient descent using that shortcut fails to converge to a stationary point of the intended objective. This establishes that the computational simplification can change the optimization outcome, beyond merely making an update less precise.

The authors introduce an unbiased first-order method, UFOM, whose memory requirement remains constant as the inner loop grows. They analyze its tradeoff between computation time and gradient variance, provide convergence bounds, and identify an optimal UFOM for a given problem. An adaptive version aims to make this correction efficient, retaining the memory benefit while addressing the bias.
summary.tldr: UFOM removes the gradient bias of a first-order bi-level optimization shortcut while retaining memory usage independent of inner-loop length.

title: Debiasing a First-order Heuristic for Approximate Bi-level Optimization

abstract: Conventional image classifiers are trained by randomly sampling mini-batches of images. To achieve state-of-the-art performance, practitioners use sophisticated data augmentation schemes to expand the amount of training data available for sampling. In contrast, meta-learning algorithms sample support data, query data, and tasks on each training step. In this complex sampling scenario, data augmentation can be used not only to expand the number of images available per class, but also to generate entirely new classes/tasks. We systematically dissect the meta-learning pipeline and investigate the distinct ways in which data augmentation can be integrated at both the image and class levels. Our proposed meta-specific data augmentation significantly improves the performance of meta-learners on few-shot classification benchmarks.

Our proposed meta-specific data augmentation significantly improves the performance of meta-learners on few-shot classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: Data augmentation expands the examples available for training an image classifier. Meta-learning introduces additional choices because each training step samples tasks as well as support and query data. This paper examines how augmentation should fit that more structured pipeline, where changing the training material can affect both individual images and the tasks built from them.

The authors systematically investigate augmentation at the image and class levels. Augmentation can increase the number of examples within a class, but it can also create new classes or tasks for meta-training. That distinction matters because a meta-learner trains across sampled tasks, so task variety is another part of its training experience.

The proposed augmentations are designed specifically for this meta-learning setup. They significantly improve meta-learner performance on few-shot classification benchmarks. The findings support treating augmentation as a choice throughout the task-sampling pipeline, with opportunities to enrich both the examples used within tasks and the collection of tasks available during training.
summary.tldr: Augmentation tailored to meta-learning improves few-shot classification by enriching training images and the classes or tasks sampled during training.

title: Data Augmentation for Meta-Learning

abstract: Anomaly detection within multivariate time series (MTS) is an essential task in both data mining and service quality management. Many recent works on anomaly detection focus on designing unsupervised probabilistic models to extract robust normal patterns of MTS. In this paper, we model sensor dependency and stochasticity within MTS by developing an embedding-guided probabilistic generative network. We combine it with adaptive variational graph convolutional recurrent network %and get variational GCRN (VGCRN) to model both spatial and temporal fine-grained correlations in MTS. To explore hierarchical latent representations, we further extend VGCRN into a deep variational network, which captures multilevel information at different layers and is robust to noisy time series. Moreover, we develop an upward-downward variational inference scheme that considers both forecasting-based and reconstruction-based losses, achieving an accurate posterior approximation of latent variables with better MTS representations. The experiments verify the superiority of the proposed method over current state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Detecting anomalies in several sensor streams requires understanding both how each stream changes over time and how sensors relate to one another. This paper develops a probabilistic model that represents these dependencies together with the randomness present in multivariate time series. The aim is to learn useful representations of normal behavior.

The model combines an embedding-guided generative network with an adaptive variational graph convolutional recurrent network. The graph component captures relationships across sensors, while the recurrent component captures temporal relationships. Extending this construction into a deeper variational network creates multiple levels of hidden representation, allowing different layers to capture different levels of information and supporting robustness to noisy series.

The authors also introduce an upward-downward inference procedure for estimating the hidden variables. It uses both forecasting losses and reconstruction losses, so representation learning considers predicting observations as well as explaining observed data. The abstract reports accurate posterior approximation, improved representations, and experimental superiority over the compared state-of-the-art methods. The central contribution is the coordinated modeling of sensor relationships, temporal structure, and uncertainty.
summary.tldr: A deep probabilistic graph-recurrent model combines sensor dependencies, temporal patterns, and hierarchical hidden representations for time-series anomaly detection.

title: Deep Variational Graph Convolutional Recurrent Network for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection

abstract: The problem of projecting a matrix onto the space of doubly stochastic matrices finds several applications in machine learning. For example, in spectral clustering, it has been shown that forming the normalized Laplacian matrix from a data affinity matrix has close connections to projecting it onto the set of doubly stochastic matrices. However, the analysis of why this projection improves clustering has been limited. In this paper we present theoretical conditions on the given affinity matrix under which its doubly stochastic projection is an ideal affinity matrix (i.e., it has no false connections between clusters, and is well-connected within each cluster). In particular, we show that a necessary and sufficient condition for a projected affinity matrix to be ideal reduces to a set of conditions on the input affinity that decompose along each cluster. Further, in the subspace clustering problem, where each cluster is defined by a linear subspace, we provide geometric conditions on the underlying subspaces which guarantee correct clustering via a continuous version of the problem. This allows us to explain theoretically the remarkable performance of a recently proposed doubly stochastic subspace clustering method.
originalAbstract: The problem of projecting a matrix onto the space of doubly stochastic matrices finds several applications in machine learning. For example, in spectral clustering, it has been shown that forming the normalized Laplacian matrix from a data affinity matrix has close connections to projecting it onto the set of doubly stochastic matrices. However, the analysis of why this projection improves clustering has been limited. In this paper we present theoretical conditions on the given affinity matrix under which its doubly stochastic projection is an ideal affinity matrix (i.e., it has no false connections between clusters, and is well-connected within each cluster). In particular, we show that a necessary and sufficient condition for a projected affinity matrix to be ideal reduces to a set of conditions on the input affinity that decompose along each cluster. Further, in the subspace clustering problem, where each cluster is defined by a linear subspace, we provide geometric conditions on the underlying subspaces which guarantee correct clustering via a continuous version of the problem. This allows us to explain theoretically the remarkable performance of a recently proposed doubly stochastic subspace clustering method.

paragraphs: Clustering methods often start from an affinity matrix describing relationships between data points. Projecting this matrix onto the set of doubly stochastic matrices is connected to normalization used in spectral clustering, but the reasons it improves clustering have been less clear. This paper provides conditions explaining when the projection produces an ideal affinity structure.

Here, ideal means that there are no incorrect connections between clusters and that points remain well connected within each cluster. The authors establish a necessary and sufficient condition for this outcome. That condition reduces to requirements on the original affinity matrix that separate along individual clusters, making the relationship between input structure and projected structure explicit.

For subspace clustering, where clusters correspond to linear subspaces, the authors also derive geometric conditions guaranteeing correct clustering through a continuous formulation. These results explain the strong performance of a recently proposed doubly stochastic subspace-clustering method. The guarantees depend on the stated affinity or geometric conditions, identifying when the projection has the desired clustering effect.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes when doubly stochastic projection produces ideal cluster connections and gives geometric guarantees for subspace clustering.

title: Understanding Doubly Stochastic Clustering

abstract: Motivated by applications to online learning in sparse estimation and Bayesian optimization, we consider the problem of online unconstrained nonsubmodular minimization with delayed costs in both full information and bandit feedback settings. In contrast to previous works on online unconstrained submodular minimization, we focus on a class of nonsubmodular functions with special structure, and prove regret guarantees for several variants of the online and approximate online bandit gradient descent algorithms in static and delayed scenarios. We derive bounds for the agent’s regret in the full information and bandit feedback setting, even if the delay between choosing a decision and receiving the incurred cost is unbounded. Key to our approach is the notion of $(\alpha, \beta)$-regret and the extension of the generic convex relaxation model from \citet{El-2020-Optimal}, the analysis of which is of independent interest. We conduct and showcase several simulation studies to demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithms.

paragraphs: Online decision-making becomes harder when the cost of an action arrives only after later decisions have already been made. This paper studies that challenge for unconstrained minimization of a specially structured class of nonsubmodular functions. Its motivation includes online learning problems arising in sparse estimation and Bayesian optimization.

The authors analyze variants of online gradient descent and approximate online bandit gradient descent. They cover both full-information feedback and bandit feedback, where the information available for learning is more limited. Their guarantees address static and delayed scenarios, including cases in which the delay between a decision and its observed cost is unbounded.

The analysis uses an adapted measure called (alpha, beta)-regret and extends a convex-relaxation framework. These choices allow guarantees suited to the structured nonsubmodular problem rather than assuming ordinary convexity or submodularity. Simulation studies demonstrate the algorithms' effectiveness. The scope is the specified function class and regret formulation; allowing unbounded delays does not itself mean that delays have no effect on performance.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes adapted regret guarantees for structured nonsubmodular online minimization with full-information or bandit feedback, including unbounded delays.

title: Online Nonsubmodular Minimization with Delayed Costs: From Full Information to Bandit Feedback

abstract: We study privacy-preserving exploration in sequential decision-making for environments that rely on sensitive data such as medical records. In particular, we focus on solving the problem of reinforcement learning (RL) subject to the constraint of (joint) differential privacy in the linear MDP setting, where both dynamics and rewards are given by linear functions. Prior work on this problem due to (Luyo et al., 2021) achieves a regret rate that has a dependence of O(K^{3/5}) on the number of episodes K. We provide a private algorithm with an improved regret rate with an optimal dependence of O($\sqrt{}$K) on the number of episodes. The key recipe for our stronger regret guarantee is the adaptivity in the policy update schedule, in which an update only occurs when sufficient changes in the data are detected. As a result, our algorithm benefits from low switching cost and only performs O(log(K)) updates, which greatly reduces the amount of privacy noise. Finally, in the most prevalent privacy regimes where the privacy parameter \epsilon is a constant, our algorithm incurs negligible privacy cost{—}in comparison with the existing non-private regret bounds, the additional regret due to privacy appears in lower-order terms.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with sensitive data must balance learning effective behavior against protecting the data used during exploration. This paper studies that problem under joint differential privacy in linear Markov decision processes, where both rewards and dynamics have linear structure. Performance is measured through regret, the accumulated cost of learning instead of acting optimally.

The proposed algorithm improves the dependence of regret on the number of episodes K from K to the three-fifths power to the optimal square-root dependence. Its key choice is an adaptive policy-update schedule: the policy changes only when the data have changed sufficiently. This produces only logarithmically many updates in K and greatly reduces the privacy noise needed.

Fewer policy changes also give the algorithm a low switching cost. When the privacy parameter epsilon is constant, the additional regret caused by privacy appears only in lower-order terms relative to existing non-private bounds. Under that regime, the result makes the privacy cost negligible in the stated comparison, while retaining an explicit privacy constraint throughout learning.
summary.tldr: Adaptive, infrequent policy updates achieve optimal square-root episode dependence for private exploration in linear MDPs while reducing privacy noise.

title: Improved Regret for Differentially Private Exploration in Linear MDP

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) agents need to be robust to variations in safety-critical environments. While system identification methods provide a way to infer the variation from online experience, they can fail in settings where fast identification is not possible. Another dominant approach is robust RL which produces a policy that can handle worst-case scenarios, but these methods are generally designed to achieve robustness to a single uncertainty set that must be specified at train time. Towards a more general solution, we formulate the multi-set robustness problem to learn a policy robust to different perturbation sets. We then design an algorithm that enjoys the benefits of both system identification and robust RL: it reduces uncertainty where possible given a few interactions, but can still act robustly with respect to the remaining uncertainty. On a diverse set of control tasks, our approach demonstrates improved worst-case performance on new environments compared to prior methods based on system identification and on robust RL alone.

paragraphs: An agent entering a changed environment may need to act before it can confidently identify the new conditions. System identification tries to infer those conditions from experience, while robust reinforcement learning prepares for worst-case possibilities. The paper addresses a gap between these approaches: identification may be too slow, and conventional robust training generally assumes one uncertainty set specified in advance.

The authors formulate a problem involving robustness across multiple perturbation sets. Their algorithm uses a few interactions to reduce uncertainty when the observations allow it, while maintaining robustness to the uncertainty that remains. This combines learning about the current environment with preparing for adverse possibilities that experience has not yet ruled out.

Across a diverse collection of control tasks, the approach improves worst-case performance in new environments compared with methods based on system identification alone or robust reinforcement learning alone. The findings support adapting the uncertainty description as experience arrives. The practical significance is the ability to benefit from limited identification without requiring uncertainty to disappear before acting robustly.
summary.tldr: The proposed policy-learning method reduces uncertainty through limited interaction while remaining robust to unresolved possibilities across multiple perturbation sets.

title: Robust Policy Learning over Multiple Uncertainty Sets

abstract: Human can leverage prior experience and learn novel tasks from a handful of demonstrations. In contrast to offline meta-reinforcement learning, which aims to achieve quick adaptation through better algorithm design, we investigate the effect of architecture inductive bias on the few-shot learning capability. We propose a Prompt-based Decision Transformer (Prompt-DT), which leverages the sequential modeling ability of the Transformer architecture and the prompt framework to achieve few-shot adaptation in offline RL. We design the trajectory prompt, which contains segments of the few-shot demonstrations, and encodes task-specific information to guide policy generation. Our experiments in five MuJoCo control benchmarks show that Prompt-DT is a strong few-shot learner without any extra finetuning on unseen target tasks. Prompt-DT outperforms its variants and strong meta offline RL baselines by a large margin with a trajectory prompt containing only a few timesteps. Prompt-DT is also robust to prompt length changes and can generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) environments. Project page: \href{https://mxu34.github.io/PromptDT/}{https://mxu34.github.io/PromptDT/}.

paragraphs: Learning a new control task from a few demonstrations requires extracting useful task information quickly. This paper investigates how architecture can support that ability in offline reinforcement learning. Its Prompt-based Decision Transformer, or Prompt-DT, combines a Transformer’s sequence-modeling capability with prompts that describe the task through examples of behavior.

The prompt consists of short segments from the available demonstration trajectories. Those segments encode task-specific information and guide the policy generated by the model. Adaptation therefore occurs by supplying a trajectory prompt, with the reported evaluations requiring no additional fine-tuning on unseen target tasks. The design makes demonstration context a direct input to policy generation.

Across five MuJoCo control benchmarks, Prompt-DT substantially outperforms its variants and strong offline meta-reinforcement-learning baselines using prompts containing only a few timesteps. The experiments also report robustness to changes in prompt length and generalization to out-of-distribution environments. These findings support trajectory prompting as an effective architectural route to few-shot policy adaptation in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Prompt-DT uses short demonstration trajectories to guide policies for unseen tasks, achieving strong few-shot control results without additional fine-tuning.

title: Prompting Decision Transformer for Few-Shot Policy Generalization

abstract: Recently, several universal methods have been proposed for online convex optimization, and attain minimax rates for multiple types of convex functions simultaneously. However, they need to design and optimize one surrogate loss for each type of functions, making it difficult to exploit the structure of the problem and utilize existing algorithms. In this paper, we propose a simple strategy for universal online convex optimization, which avoids these limitations. The key idea is to construct a set of experts to process the original online functions, and deploy a meta-algorithm over the linearized losses to aggregate predictions from experts. Specifically, the meta-algorithm is required to yield a second-order bound with excess losses, so that it can leverage strong convexity and exponential concavity to control the meta-regret. In this way, our strategy inherits the theoretical guarantee of any expert designed for strongly convex functions and exponentially concave functions, up to a double logarithmic factor. As a result, we can plug in off-the-shelf online solvers as black-box experts to deliver problem-dependent regret bounds. For general convex functions, it maintains the minimax optimality and also achieves a small-loss bound.

paragraphs: Online convex optimization requires making decisions as loss functions arrive over time. Different kinds of convexity support different performance guarantees, so a universal method aims to work well across several kinds. This paper proposes a strategy that can reuse existing online solvers without designing a separate surrogate objective for each function type.

The strategy treats those solvers as experts. Each expert processes the original functions, while a meta-algorithm combines their predictions using linearized losses. The meta-algorithm must satisfy a particular second-order bound involving excess losses. That requirement allows the analysis to exploit strong convexity and exponential concavity when controlling the extra regret from combining experts.

For strongly convex and exponentially concave functions, the combined method inherits an expert's theoretical guarantee up to a double logarithmic factor. This makes existing solvers usable as black-box components while preserving problem-dependent guarantees. For general convex functions, the strategy retains minimax optimality and also obtains a small-loss bound, extending its usefulness beyond settings with stronger curvature.
summary.tldr: An expert-aggregation strategy reuses existing online solvers while retaining strong guarantees across multiple types of convex losses.

title: A Simple yet Universal Strategy for Online Convex Optimization

abstract: Off-Policy Evaluation (OPE) serves as one of the cornerstones in Reinforcement Learning (RL). Fitted Q Evaluation (FQE) with various function approximators, especially deep neural networks, has gained practical success. While statistical analysis has proved FQE to be minimax-optimal with tabular, linear and several nonparametric function families, its practical performance with more general function approximator is less theoretically understood. We focus on FQE with general differentiable function approximators , making our theory applicable to neural function approximations. We approach this problem using the Z-estimation theory and establish the following results: The FQE estimation error is asymptotically normal with explicit variance determined jointly by the tangent space of the function class at the ground truth, the reward structure, and the distribution shift due to off-policy learning; The finite-sample FQE error bound is dominated by the same variance term, and it can also be bounded by function class-dependent divergence, which measures how the off-policy distribution shift intertwines with the function approximator. In addition, we study bootstrapping FQE estimators for error distribution inference and estimating confidence intervals, accompanied by a Cramer-Rao lower bound that matches our upper bounds. The Z-estimation analysis provides a generalizable theoretical framework for studying off-policy estimation in RL and provides sharp statistical theory for FQE with differentiable function approximators.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates a policy's performance from data generated under a different policy. Fitted Q Evaluation, or FQE, is useful in practice, including with neural networks, but its statistical behavior is less understood for general function approximators. This paper develops an analysis for differentiable approximators using Z-estimation theory.

The authors show that the estimation error is asymptotically normal. Its variance depends jointly on the function class's local structure at the ground truth, the rewards, and the distribution shift caused by off-policy data. The same variance term dominates their finite-sample error bound. They also express a bound through a divergence that captures how distribution shift interacts with the chosen function class.

The paper studies bootstrap methods for estimating error distributions and confidence intervals, and supplies a Cramer-Rao lower bound matching its upper bounds. These results connect accuracy, uncertainty estimation, and statistical limits within one framework. They also clarify why evaluating a policy depends on both the available data distribution and the representational structure of the estimator.
summary.tldr: A Z-estimation analysis characterizes FQE error and uncertainty for differentiable approximators, including neural function approximations.

title: Off-Policy Fitted Q-Evaluation with Differentiable Function Approximators: Z-Estimation and Inference Theory

abstract: Large Transformer-based models have exhibited superior performance in various natural language processing and computer vision tasks. However, these models contain enormous amounts of parameters, which restrict their deployment to real-world applications. To reduce the model size, researchers prune these models based on the weights’ importance scores. However, such scores are usually estimated on mini-batches during training, which incurs large variability/uncertainty due to mini-batch sampling and complicated training dynamics. As a result, some crucial weights could be pruned by commonly used pruning methods because of such uncertainty, which makes training unstable and hurts generalization. To resolve this issue, we propose PLATON, which captures the uncertainty of importance scores by upper confidence bound of importance estimation. In particular, for the weights with low importance scores but high uncertainty, PLATON tends to retain them and explores their capacity. We conduct extensive experiments with several Transformer-based models on natural language understanding, question answering and image classification to validate the effectiveness of PLATON. Results demonstrate that PLATON manifests notable improvement under different sparsity levels. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/QingruZhang/PLATON.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces a large model by removing weights judged to be unimportant. For Transformers, those judgments are often estimated from training mini-batches, making them noisy as sampled examples and training dynamics change. A weight that appears unimportant at one moment may still be crucial, so premature removal can destabilize training and hurt generalization.

PLATON incorporates uncertainty into the importance estimate using an upper confidence bound. In particular, it tends to retain weights whose estimated importance is low but uncertain, giving their capacity more opportunity to be explored. The pruning decision therefore considers both the current importance score and how much confidence the method has in that score.

The authors evaluate PLATON with several Transformer-based models on natural language understanding, question answering, and image classification. They report notable improvements across different sparsity levels. These findings support treating uncertainty as relevant information when deciding which parameters to remove, especially when importance estimates fluctuate during training. The method's contribution is a more cautious way to interpret low estimated importance while still pursuing a smaller model.
summary.tldr: PLATON improves Transformer pruning by accounting for uncertainty in weight importance, tending to retain weights whose low scores are unreliable.

title: PLATON: Pruning Large Transformer Models with Upper Confidence Bound of Weight Importance

abstract: Machine learning force fields (MLFF) have been proposed to accelerate molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, which finds widespread applications in chemistry and biomedical research. Even for the most data-efficient MLFFs, reaching chemical accuracy can require hundreds of frames of force and energy labels generated by expensive quantum mechanical algorithms, which may scale as $O(n^3)$ to $O(n^7)$, with $n$ proportional to the number of basis functions. To address this issue, we propose a multi-stage computational framework – ASTEROID, which lowers the data cost of MLFFs by leveraging a combination of cheap inaccurate data and expensive accurate data. The motivation behind ASTEROID is that inaccurate data, though incurring large bias, can help capture the sophisticated structures of the underlying force field. Therefore, we first train a MLFF model on a large amount of inaccurate training data, employing a bias-aware loss function to prevent the model from overfitting the potential bias of this data. We then fine-tune the obtained model using a small amount of accurate training data, which preserves the knowledge learned from the inaccurate training data while significantly improving the model’s accuracy. Moreover, we propose a variant of ASTEROID based on score matching for the setting where the inaccurate training data are unlabeled. Extensive experiments on MD datasets and downstream tasks validate the efficacy of ASTEROID. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/abukharin3/asteroid.

paragraphs: Machine learning force fields can accelerate molecular dynamics, but producing accurate energy and force labels can be expensive. Even data-efficient models may need hundreds of labeled molecular configurations generated by quantum mechanical calculations. ASTEROID addresses this data-generation cost by combining a large quantity of inexpensive, inaccurate data with a small quantity of accurate data.

The method first trains a force-field model on the cheaper data. Its motivation is that biased measurements can still reveal complicated structure in the underlying force field. A bias-aware loss discourages the model from overfitting the inexpensive data's systematic errors. Fine-tuning on accurate data then improves precision while preserving knowledge acquired during the first stage.

The authors also introduce a score-matching variant for situations where the inexpensive data lack labels. Experiments on molecular dynamics datasets and downstream tasks support the framework's effectiveness. The contribution makes training sensitive to the cost and quality of its data sources, using expensive supervision to refine a model that has already learned from cheaper information.
summary.tldr: ASTEROID lowers force-field training data costs by learning from cheap, biased data before fine-tuning on a small accurate dataset.

title: Machine Learning Force Fields with Data Cost Aware Training

abstract: Recent work has shown that forward- and reverse- mode automatic differentiation (AD) over the reals is almost always correct in a mathematically precise sense. However, actual programs work with machine-representable numbers (e.g., floating-point numbers), not reals. In this paper, we study the correctness of AD when the parameter space of a neural network consists solely of machine-representable numbers. In particular, we analyze two sets of parameters on which AD can be incorrect: the incorrect set on which the network is differentiable but AD does not compute its derivative, and the non-differentiable set on which the network is non-differentiable. For a neural network with bias parameters, we first prove that the incorrect set is always empty. We then prove a tight bound on the size of the non-differentiable set, which is linear in the number of non-differentiabilities in activation functions, and give a simple necessary and sufficient condition for a parameter to be in this set. We further prove that AD always computes a Clarke subderivative even on the non-differentiable set. We also extend these results to neural networks possibly without bias parameters.

paragraphs: Automatic differentiation is known to be almost always correct over real-valued parameter spaces in a precise mathematical sense. Actual neural network programs use machine-representable parameters, however, so this paper studies correctness on that parameter set. It separates points where a derivative exists but automatic differentiation returns the wrong result from points where the network has no ordinary derivative.

For networks with bias parameters, the authors prove that the first set is empty: at differentiable parameter points, automatic differentiation computes the derivative correctly. They also derive a tight bound on the size of the non-differentiable set, growing linearly with the number of non-differentiabilities in the activation functions, and give an exact criterion for membership in that set.

At non-differentiable points, automatic differentiation still returns a Clarke subderivative, a generalized derivative suitable for describing non-smooth functions. The paper also extends its analysis to networks that may lack biases. Together, these results give a more precise account of correctness when parameters come from machine-representable numbers.
summary.tldr: For networks with biases and machine-representable parameters, automatic differentiation returns correct derivatives where they exist and Clarke subderivatives at non-smooth points.

title: On the Correctness of Automatic Differentiation for Neural Networks with Machine-Representable Parameters

abstract: Tensor network (TN) is a powerful framework in machine learning, but selecting a good TN model, known as TN structure search (TN-SS), is a challenging and computationally intensive task. The recent approach TNLS (Li et al., 2022) showed promising results for this task. However, its computational efficiency is still unaffordable, requiring too many evaluations of the objective function. We propose TnALE, a surprisingly simple algorithm that updates each structure-related variable alternately by local enumeration, greatly reducing the number of evaluations compared to TNLS. We theoretically investigate the descent steps for TNLS and TnALE, proving that both the algorithms can achieve linear convergence up to a constant if a sufficient reduction of the objective is reached in each neighborhood. We further compare the evaluation efficiency of TNLS and TnALE, revealing that $\Omega(2^K)$ evaluations are typically required in TNLS for reaching the objective reduction, while ideally $O(KR)$ evaluations are sufficient in TnALE, where $K$ denotes the dimension of search space and $R$ reflects the “low-rankness” of the neighborhood. Experimental results verify that TnALE can find practically good TN structures with vastly fewer evaluations than the state-of-the-art algorithms.

We further compare the evaluation efficiency of TNLS and TnALE, revealing that $\Omega(2^K)$ evaluations are typically required in TNLS for reaching the objective reduction, while ideally $O(KR)$ evaluations are sufficient in TnALE, where $K$ denotes the dimension of search space and $R$ reflects the “low-rankness” of the neighborhood. paragraphs: Choosing a tensor network structure can require many expensive evaluations of candidate models. This paper introduces TnALE to reduce that search cost. Its basic procedure alternates among variables describing the structure, enumerating nearby choices for one variable at a time instead of relying on the more evaluation-intensive search used by TNLS.

The analysis compares how both algorithms decrease their objective. Both can achieve linear convergence up to a constant if each neighborhood search obtains a sufficient reduction. The evaluation comparison is also qualified: TNLS typically requires at least exponentially many evaluations in the search dimension K, while TnALE ideally needs only O(KR), where R describes the neighborhood's low-rank structure.

These statements explain where the potential efficiency gain comes from while retaining the conditions behind it. Alternating local searches can exploit favorable neighborhood structure to find improvements with fewer evaluations. Experiments support the practical value of that idea: TnALE finds good tensor network structures using vastly fewer objective evaluations than the compared state-of-the-art methods.
summary.tldr: TnALE searches tensor network structures through alternating local enumeration, finding good structures with far fewer evaluations in experiments.

title: Alternating Local Enumeration (TnALE): Solving Tensor Network Structure Search with Fewer Evaluations

abstract: Incorporating a deep generative model as the prior distribution in inverse problems has established substantial success in reconstructing images from corrupted observations. Notwithstanding, the existing optimization approaches use gradient descent largely without adapting to the non-convex nature of the problem and can be sensitive to initial values, impeding further performance improvement. In this paper, we propose an efficient amortized optimization scheme for inverse problems with a deep generative prior. Specifically, the optimization task with high degrees of difficulty is decomposed into optimizing a sequence of much easier ones. We provide a theoretical guarantee of the proposed algorithm and empirically validate it on different inverse problems. As a result, our approach outperforms baseline methods qualitatively and quantitatively by a large margin.

paragraphs: Inverse problems reconstruct an image from a corrupted observation. A deep generative model can provide a prior distribution that guides this reconstruction, and the paper builds on the success of that approach. Its focus is the optimization needed to recover an image, especially when the resulting objective is nonconvex and ordinary gradient descent is sensitive to its starting point.

The authors propose an efficient amortized optimization scheme that breaks a difficult optimization task into a sequence of easier ones. This decomposition changes how the reconstruction problem is solved, addressing the difficulty of the optimization landscape rather than simply applying gradient descent to the full task. The sequence is the central mechanism described for making the problem more manageable.

The paper provides a theoretical guarantee for the algorithm and evaluates it on several inverse problems. The reported reconstructions outperform baseline methods by a large margin in both qualitative and quantitative comparisons. These findings support the value of adapting the optimization procedure when using a deep generative prior for image recovery.
summary.tldr: An amortized optimization scheme decomposes difficult image reconstruction problems into easier stages and improves the reported reconstruction results.

title: Optimization for Amortized Inverse Problems

abstract: We study the design decision of publicly available instruction tuning methods, by reproducing and breaking down the development of Flan 2022 (Chung et al., 2022). Through careful ablation studies on the Flan Collection of tasks and methods, we tease apart the effect of design decisions which enable Flan-T5 to outperform prior work by 3-17% across evaluation settings. We find task balancing and enrichment techniques are overlooked but critical to effective instruction tuning, and in particular, training with mixed prompt settings (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought) actually yields equivalent or stronger (2%) performance in all settings. In further experiments we show Flan-T5 requires less finetuning to converge higher and faster than T5 on single downstream tasks – motivating instruction-tuned models as more computationally-efficient starting checkpoints for new tasks. Finally, to accelerate research on instruction tuning, we make the Flan 2022 collection of datasets, templates, and methods publicly available.

paragraphs: This paper examines which design choices make instruction tuning effective by reproducing and analyzing the development of Flan 2022. Through ablation studies on its task collection and methods, the authors separate the effects of individual decisions. Their analysis addresses the choices behind Flan-T5's reported 3–17% advantage over prior work across evaluation settings.

Task balancing and enrichment emerge as critical but overlooked ingredients. Mixing zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompts during training yields equivalent or stronger performance across the evaluated settings, with a reported 2% improvement. This finding supports using varied prompt formats together rather than assuming a training format must narrowly match its evaluation setting.

Further experiments compare Flan-T5 and T5 as starting points for fine-tuning on individual downstream tasks. Flan-T5 needs less fine-tuning and converges faster to higher performance, motivating instruction-tuned checkpoints as more computationally efficient starting models. The authors also release the Flan 2022 datasets, templates, and methods, making the analyzed collection available for continued research on instruction-tuning design.
summary.tldr: Flan ablations identify task balancing, enrichment, and mixed prompt formats as important ingredients for effective instruction tuning.

title: The Flan Collection: Designing Data and Methods for Effective Instruction Tuning

abstract: Quantum machine learning implemented by variational quantum circuits (VQCs) is considered a promising concept for the noisy intermediate-scale quantum computing era. Focusing on applications in quantum reinforcement learning, we propose an action decoding procedure for a quantum policy gradient approach. We introduce a quality measure that enables us to optimize the classical post-processing required for action selection, inspired by local and global quantum measurements. The resulting algorithm demonstrates a significant performance improvement in several benchmark environments. With this technique, we successfully execute a full training routine on a 5-qubit hardware device. Our method introduces only negligible classical overhead and has the potential to improve VQC-based algorithms beyond the field of quantum reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: A quantum reinforcement learning policy must turn the output of a quantum circuit into an action. This paper focuses on that decoding step for policy-gradient learning with variational quantum circuits. The authors treat classical post-processing as something to optimize explicitly within the overall learning procedure.

They introduce a quality measure for action decoding, drawing inspiration from local and global quantum measurements. This measure guides optimization of the classical processing used to select actions. The resulting procedure adds only negligible classical overhead, making the decoding change a relatively inexpensive part of the proposed approach.

The algorithm shows significant performance improvements in several benchmark environments. The authors also complete a full training routine on a five-qubit hardware device, demonstrating execution beyond the benchmark results alone. They suggest that the decoding technique could benefit other variational quantum circuit algorithms, but that broader applicability is presented as potential rather than as an established result across other application areas.
summary.tldr: Optimizing quantum action decoding improves benchmark performance with negligible classical overhead and enables a complete five-qubit hardware training run.

title: Quantum Policy Gradient Algorithm with Optimized Action Decoding

abstract: We study counterfactual identifiability in causal models with bijective generation mechanisms (BGM), a class that generalizes several widely-used causal models in the literature. We establish their counterfactual identifiability for three common causal structures with unobserved confounding, and propose a practical learning method that casts learning a BGM as structured generative modeling. Learned BGMs enable efficient counterfactual estimation and can be obtained using a variety of deep conditional generative models. We evaluate our techniques in a visual task and demonstrate its application in a real-world video streaming simulation task.

paragraphs: Counterfactual questions ask what would have happened under a different intervention for a situation already observed. The paper studies when such answers are identifiable within causal models whose generation mechanisms are bijective. This model class generalizes several commonly used causal models, making the question relevant beyond a single narrowly specified construction.

The authors establish counterfactual identifiability for three common causal structures that include unobserved confounding. The scope matters: the result concerns these structures and this class of mechanisms. It shows that hidden confounding does not automatically prevent counterfactual identification when the causal structure and generation mechanisms have the properties studied in the paper.

The work also introduces a practical learning method that treats fitting such a causal model as structured generative modeling. A variety of deep conditional generative models can be used, and the learned models support efficient counterfactual estimation. Evaluation includes a visual task and an application to a real-world video streaming simulation task. Together, the theory and method connect identifiable counterfactual questions with a practical modeling approach.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes counterfactual identifiability for bijective causal models in three confounded structures and provides a practical generative learning method.

title: Counterfactual Identifiability of Bijective Causal Models

abstract: Synthetic data generation has become an emerging tool to help improve the adversarial robustness in classification tasks, since robust learning requires a significantly larger amount of training samples compared with standard classification. Among various deep generative models, the diffusion model has been shown to produce high-quality synthetic images and has achieved good performance in improving the adversarial robustness. However, diffusion-type methods are generally slower in data generation as compared with other generative models. Although different acceleration techniques have been proposed recently, it is also of great importance to study how to improve the sample efficiency of synthetic data for the downstream task. In this paper, we first analyze the optimality condition of synthetic distribution for achieving improved robust accuracy. We show that enhancing the distinguishability among the generated data is critical for improving adversarial robustness. Thus, we propose the Contrastive-Guided Diffusion Process (Contrastive-DP), which incorporates the contrastive loss to guide the diffusion model in data generation. We validate our theoretical results using simulations and demonstrate the good performance of Contrastive-DP on image datasets.

paragraphs: Training a classifier to resist adversarial attacks requires substantially more examples than ordinary classification. Diffusion models can supply useful synthetic images, but generating them is relatively slow. This paper examines how to make synthetic data more useful for robust learning, addressing the value of the generated examples alongside the broader concern about generation cost.

The authors first analyze the conditions a synthetic-data distribution should satisfy to improve robust accuracy. Their analysis identifies distinguishability among generated examples as critical. They then propose Contrastive-DP, which incorporates a contrastive loss into the diffusion generation process to guide the model toward data with this desirable property.

Simulations support the theoretical findings, and image-dataset experiments demonstrate good performance for the proposed method. The contribution links a property of the synthetic distribution to the downstream objective of adversarial robustness. It motivates steering generation according to what robust classification needs, so that the usefulness of synthetic training data becomes an explicit part of the generation procedure.
summary.tldr: Contrastive-DP guides diffusion generation toward more distinguishable synthetic data to improve its usefulness for adversarially robust classification.

title: Improving Adversarial Robustness Through the Contrastive-Guided Diffusion Process

abstract: Compared to Euclidean convolution, existing graph convolution methods generally fail to learn diverse convolution operators under limited parameter scales and depend on additional treatments of multi-scale feature extraction. The challenges of generalizing Euclidean convolution to graphs arise from the irregular structure of graphs. To bridge the gap between Euclidean space and graph space, we propose a differentiable method for regularization on graphs that applies permutations to the input graphs. The permutations constrain all nodes in a row regardless of their input order and therefore enable the flexible generalization of Euclidean convolution. Based on the regularization of graphs, we propose Compressed Convolution Network (CoCN) for hierarchical graph representation learning. CoCN follows the local feature learning and global parameter sharing mechanisms of Convolution Neural Networks. The whole model can be trained end-to-end and is able to learn both individual node features and the corresponding structure features. We validate CoCN on several node classification and graph classification benchmarks. CoCN achieves superior performance over competitive convolutional GNNs and graph pooling models. Codes are available at https://github.com/sunjss/CoCN.

paragraphs: Convolution works naturally on regularly arranged data, but graph nodes have an irregular structure and no inherent input ordering. The paper argues that existing graph convolutions struggle to learn diverse operators with limited parameters and often need separate mechanisms for extracting features at multiple scales. Its approach begins by changing how the graph is arranged.

The authors introduce a differentiable permutation method that places graph nodes into a row regardless of their original order. This arrangement supports a more flexible transfer of ordinary convolution to graphs. Their Compressed Convolution Network builds hierarchical representations using local feature learning and parameters shared throughout the model, following core mechanisms of convolutional neural networks.

CoCN is trained end to end and learns both node features and associated structural features. Tests on node-classification and graph-classification benchmarks show better performance than competitive convolutional graph networks and graph-pooling models. The result suggests that learning a useful arrangement of an irregular graph can support effective hierarchical feature extraction within a unified architecture.
summary.tldr: CoCN learns to arrange graph nodes into a row so convolution can build effective hierarchical graph representations.

title: All in a Row: Compressed Convolution Networks for Graphs

abstract: This paper presents a novel generative model for Computer Aided Design (CAD) that 1) represents high-level design concepts of a CAD model as a three-level hierarchical tree of neural codes, from global part arrangement down to local curve geometry; and 2) controls the generation or completion of CAD models by specifying the target design using a code tree. Concretely, a novel variant of a vector quantized VAE with "masked skip connection" extracts design variations as neural codebooks at three levels. Two-stage cascaded auto-regressive transformers learn to generate code trees from incomplete CAD models and then complete CAD models following the intended design. Extensive experiments demonstrate superior performance on conventional tasks such as unconditional generation while enabling novel interaction capabilities on conditional generation tasks. The code is available at https://github.com/samxuxiang/hnc-cad.

paragraphs: Controlling a generated CAD model requires expressing design choices at different scales, from the arrangement of parts to the geometry of individual curves. This paper represents those choices through a three-level tree of neural codes. A target code tree can guide either the generation of a model or the completion of an incomplete one.

A modified vector-quantized variational autoencoder extracts codebooks at the three levels using a mechanism called a masked skip connection. Two cascaded autoregressive transformer stages then connect these representations to generation. The first produces code trees from incomplete CAD models; the second completes the models according to the design represented by those trees.

This structure gives design intent an explicit hierarchical representation within the generation process. The reported experiments show superior performance on established tasks such as unconditional generation and demonstrate new interactive capabilities for conditional generation. The contribution therefore combines generative performance with a way to specify intended designs at multiple levels, linking high-level part organization to local geometric detail.
summary.tldr: A hierarchy of neural codes lets a CAD generator follow design choices spanning overall part arrangement and local curve geometry.

title: Hierarchical Neural Coding for Controllable CAD Model Generation

abstract: With the advance of language models, privacy protection is receiving more attention. Training data extraction is therefore of great importance, as it can serve as a potential tool to assess privacy leakage. However, due to the difficulty of this task, most of the existing methods are proof-of-concept and still not effective enough. In this paper, we investigate and benchmark tricks for improving training data extraction using a publicly available dataset. Because most existing extraction methods use a pipeline of generating-then-ranking, i.e., generating text candidates as potential training data and then ranking them based on specific criteria, our research focuses on the tricks for both text generation (e.g., sampling strategy) and text ranking (e.g., token-level criteria). The experimental results show that several previously overlooked tricks can be crucial to the success of training data extraction. Based on the GPT-Neo 1.3B evaluation results, our proposed tricks outperform the baseline by a large margin in most cases, providing a much stronger baseline for future research. The code is available at https://github.com/weichen-yu/LM-Extraction.

paragraphs: Training-data extraction attempts to recover material used to train a language model and can help assess privacy leakage. The paper starts from the observation that many existing extraction methods remain demonstrations of possibility rather than especially effective evaluation tools. It investigates practical choices that can make these methods more capable.

The study follows a common two-stage process: generate text that might belong to the training data, then rank those candidates using criteria intended to identify likely matches. It benchmarks choices in both stages on a publicly available dataset. These include sampling strategies for generation and token-level criteria for ranking, keeping attention on how the overall extraction pipeline behaves.

Experiments with GPT-Neo 1.3B show that several previously overlooked choices can be crucial to extraction success. The proposed collection of tricks substantially improves over the baseline in most evaluated cases. The result supplies a stronger reference point for future extraction research and shows why assessing privacy leakage depends partly on the effectiveness of the extraction procedure.
summary.tldr: Benchmarking generation and ranking choices produces a stronger training-data extraction baseline for GPT-Neo 1.3B.

title: Bag of Tricks for Training Data Extraction from Language Models

abstract: We provide a theoretical framework for Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF). We show that when the underlying true reward is linear, under both Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model (pairwise comparison) and Plackett-Luce (PL) model ($K$-wise comparison), MLE converges under certain semi-norm for the family of linear reward. On the other hand, when training a policy based on the learned reward model, we show that MLE fails while a pessimistic MLE provides policies with good performance under certain coverage assumption. We also show that under the PL model, both the true MLE and a different MLE which splits the $K$-wise comparison into pairwise comparisons converge, while the true MLE is asymptotically more efficient. Our results validate the empirical success of the existing RLHF algorithms, and provide new insights for algorithm design. Our analysis can also be applied for the problem of online RLHF and inverse reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical account of learning from human comparisons and then using the learned reward to train a policy. It assumes that the underlying reward is linear. Under Bradley–Terry–Luce pairwise comparisons and Plackett–Luce comparisons among several alternatives, it proves convergence of maximum likelihood reward estimation in a particular semi-norm.

Accurate reward estimation in that sense does not automatically produce a good policy. The authors show that ordinary maximum likelihood estimation can fail at the policy-learning stage, while a pessimistic version gives good policy performance under a coverage assumption. This separates the statistical task of fitting preferences from the decision-making task that uses those fitted rewards.

For comparisons involving several alternatives, the paper also contrasts the full likelihood with a method that splits comparisons into pairs. Both converge under the Plackett–Luce model, but the full estimator is asymptotically more efficient. These results provide guidance for using comparison data and incorporating pessimism, with analysis that also applies to online RLHF and inverse reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: For linear rewards, comparison-based reward estimates can converge while policy learning still requires pessimism and sufficient coverage for good performance.

title: Principled Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback from Pairwise or K-wise Comparisons

abstract: Scientific computing is an essential tool for scientific discovery and engineering design, and its computational cost is always a main concern in practice. To accelerate scientific computing, it is a promising approach to use machine learning (especially meta-learning) techniques for selecting hyperparameters of traditional numerical methods. There have been numerous proposals to this direction, but many of them require automatic-differentiable numerical methods. However, in reality, many practical applications still depend on well-established but non-automatic-differentiable legacy codes, which prevents practitioners from applying the state-of-the-art research to their own problems. To resolve this problem, we propose a non-intrusive methodology with a novel gradient estimation technique to combine machine learning and legacy numerical codes without any modification. We theoretically and numerically show the advantage of the proposed method over other baselines and present applications of accelerating established non-automatic-differentiable numerical solvers implemented in PETSc, a widely used open-source numerical software library.

paragraphs: Machine learning can help accelerate numerical computation by choosing effective settings for a traditional solver. A practical obstacle is that many learning methods expect to differentiate automatically through the numerical method. Established scientific software often does not support this, making otherwise promising techniques difficult to apply to existing workflows.

This paper introduces a way to combine learning with those legacy solvers without changing their code. Its central contribution is a new gradient estimation technique that supports gradient-based meta-solving even when the underlying numerical implementation is not automatically differentiable. The learning system can therefore help select solver hyperparameters while retaining the established numerical software.

The authors support the approach with theoretical analysis and numerical comparisons showing advantages over other baselines. They also demonstrate applications using non-automatically-differentiable solvers in PETSc. The practical significance is compatibility: accelerating scientific computing need not require replacing or rewriting the solver that an application already depends on. The stated evidence concerns the proposed method and its demonstrated applications, rather than a universal acceleration guarantee.
summary.tldr: A new gradient estimator lets machine learning tune and accelerate legacy numerical solvers without modifying their code.

title: Accelerating Legacy Numerical Solvers by Non-intrusive Gradient-based Meta-solving

abstract: We develop algorithms for online linear regression which achieve optimal static and dynamic regret guarantees even in the complete absence of prior knowledge. We present a novel analysis showing that a discounted variant of the Vovk-Azoury-Warmuth forecaster achieves dynamic regret of the form $R_{T}(\vec{u})\le O\Big(d\log(T)\vee \sqrt{dP_{T}^{\gamma}(\vec{u})T}\Big)$, where $P_{T}^{\gamma}(\vec{u})$ is a measure of variability of the comparator sequence, and show that the discount factor achieving this result can be learned on-the-fly. We show that this result is optimal by providing a matching lower bound. We also extend our results to strongly-adaptive guarantees which hold over every sub-interval $[a,b]\subseteq[1,T]$ simultaneously.

paragraphs: Online linear regression must make predictions while observations arrive, including when the best predictor changes over time. This paper develops algorithms with guarantees against both a fixed predictor and a changing sequence of predictors. The central result does not require prior knowledge to obtain these static and dynamic regret guarantees.

The analysis uses a discounted version of the Vovk-Azoury-Warmuth forecaster. Its dynamic regret is bounded, up to constants, by the larger of d log(T) and the square root of d times a comparator-variability measure times T. Here d is the dimension and T is the time horizon. The discount factor needed for the guarantee can itself be learned during prediction.

A matching lower bound establishes optimality of the stated result. The authors also extend the analysis to strongly adaptive guarantees, which hold simultaneously on every time interval within the full run. This adds a local-in-time assurance to the overall performance bound. The combination matters because it addresses changing comparators, unknown tuning information, and performance within shorter periods through one discounting-based approach.
summary.tldr: An adaptively discounted linear forecaster achieves optimal static and dynamic regret without prior knowledge, with guarantees extending to every time subinterval.

title: Online Linear Regression in Dynamic Environments via Discounting

abstract: Existing few-shot semantic segmentation methods typically rely on a one-way flow of category information from support to query, ignoring the impact of intra-class diversity. To address this, drawing inspiration from cybernetics, we introduce a Query Feedback Branch (QFB) to propagate query information back to support, generating a query-related support prototype that is more aligned with the query. Subsequently, a Query Amplifier Branch (QAB) is employed to amplify target objects in the query using the acquired support prototype. To further improve the model, we propose a Query Rectification Module (QRM), which utilizes the prediction disparity in the query before and after support activation to identify challenging positive and negative samples from ambiguous regions for query self-rectification. Furthermore, we integrate the QFB, QAB, and QRM into a feedback and rectification layer and incorporate it into an iterative pipeline. This configuration enables the progressive enhancement of bidirectional reciprocative flow of category information between query and support, effectively providing query-adaptive support information and addressing the intra-class diversity problem. Extensive experiments conducted on both PASCAL-5i and COCO-20i datasets validate the effectiveness of our approach. The code is available at https://github.com/LIUYUANWEI98/IFRNet .

Furthermore, we integrate the QFB, QAB, and QRM into a feedback and rectification layer and incorporate it into an iterative pipeline. This configuration enables the progressive enhancement of bidirectional reciprocative flow of category information between query and support, effectively providing query-adaptive support information and addressing the intra-class diversity problem. Extensive experiments conducted on both PASCAL-5i and COCO-20i datasets validate the effectiveness of our approach. The code is available at https://github.com/LIUYUANWEI98/IFRNet .

paragraphs: Few-shot semantic segmentation uses a small set of labeled support images to identify an object category in a query image. A difficulty is that members of the same category can look quite different. Passing category information only from support to query can therefore provide a description that fits the examples better than the image being segmented.

The proposed method adds feedback in the opposite direction. A Query Feedback Branch uses the query to adapt the support prototype, the representation summarizing the target category. A Query Amplifier Branch then uses that adapted prototype to strengthen the target objects in the query. Support information becomes responsive to the particular query rather than remaining fixed.

A further rectification module compares query predictions before and after support activation. Their disagreements help locate difficult positive and negative samples in ambiguous regions, which guide correction of the query prediction. Repeating these components progressively refines the exchange between support and query. Experiments on PASCAL-5i and COCO-20i support the effectiveness of this approach to within-category variation.
summary.tldr: Iterative feedback adapts support representations to each query and corrects ambiguous regions in few-shot segmentation.

title: Bidirectional Reciprocative Information Communication for Few-Shot Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Few-shot open-set recognition (FSOSR) aims to detect instances from unseen classes by utilizing a small set of labeled instances from closed-set classes. Accurately rejecting instances from open-set classes in the few-shot setting is fundamentally more challenging due to the weaker supervised signals resulting from fewer labels. Transformer-based few-shot methods exploit attention mapping to achieve a consistent representation. However, the softmax-generated attention map normalizes all the instances that assign unnecessary high attentive weights to those instances not close to the closed-set classes that negatively impact the detection performance. In addition, open-set samples that are similar to a certain closed-set class also pose a significant challenge to most existing FSOSR models. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Meta Evidential Transformer (MET) based FSOSR model that uses an evidential open-set loss to learn more compact closed-set class representations by effectively leveraging similar closed-set classes. MET further integrates an evidence-to-variance ratio to detect fundamentally challenging tasks and uses an evidence-guided cross-attention mechanism to better separate the difficult open-set samples. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate consistent improvement over existing competitive methods in unseen class recognition without deteriorating closed-set performance.

paragraphs: Few-shot open-set recognition requires a model to recognize known classes from a small labeled set while rejecting examples from unseen classes. Limited supervision makes this separation difficult. Attention can also give excessive weight to examples that are distant from known classes, while unknown examples resembling a known class are particularly challenging.

The Meta Evidential Transformer addresses these problems through several connected mechanisms. An evidential open-set loss uses similar known classes to learn more compact class representations. An evidence-to-variance ratio identifies especially difficult tasks, and evidence-guided cross-attention helps separate hard unknown examples from the known classes.

Experiments on real-world datasets show consistent improvements over competitive existing methods in recognizing unseen classes, without reducing closed-set performance. This matters because better rejection is useful only alongside continued recognition of the classes the model is meant to know. The reported results support using evidence to shape both the learned representations and the attention process in this limited-label setting.
summary.tldr: Evidence-guided representations and attention improve rejection of unseen classes from few labeled examples without harming known-class performance.

title: Meta Evidential Transformer for Few-Shot Open-Set Recognition

abstract: Diffusion models lend transformative capabilities to the graph generation task, yet controlling the properties of the generated graphs remains challenging. Recent approaches augment support for controlling soft, differentiable properties but they fail to handle user-specified hard constraints that are non-differentiable. This often results in vague control, unsuitable for applications like drug discovery that demand satisfaction of precise constraints, e.g., the maximum number of bonds. To address this, we formalize the problem of controlled graph generation and introduce PRODIGY (PROjected DIffusion for controlled Graph Generation), an innovative plug-and-play approach enabling the generation of graphs with precise control, from any pre-trained diffusion model. PRODIGY employs a novel operator to project the samples at each diffusion step onto the specified constrained space. For a large class of practical constraints and a variety of graphs, our extensive experiments demonstrate that PRODIGY empowers state-of-the-art continuous and discrete diffusion models to produce graphs meeting specific, hard constraints. Our approach achieves up to 100% constraint satisfaction for non-attributed and molecular graphs, under a variety of constraints, marking a significant step forward in precise, interpretable graph generation. Code is provided on the project webpage: https://prodigy-diffusion.github.io/.

paragraphs: Generating a plausible graph does not necessarily produce one that satisfies a user's exact requirements. The paper focuses on hard constraints, such as limits on molecular bonds, that cannot always be handled through smooth, differentiable objectives. These requirements demand precise compliance rather than a general tendency toward a preferred property.

The proposed method, PRODIGY, adds control to a pretrained graph diffusion model. At each diffusion step, a projection operator moves the current sample into the space allowed by the specified constraints. Incorporating this correction throughout sampling makes the constraints part of the generation process and provides a plug-and-play approach for pretrained models.

Experiments apply the method to continuous and discrete diffusion models, covering molecular graphs and graphs without attributes. Across a large class of practical constraints, the authors report constraint satisfaction reaching 100% in some settings. That is an empirical maximum, rather than a claim that every possible constraint is always satisfied. The findings support projection as a way to make graph generation more precisely controllable.
summary.tldr: PRODIGY projects diffusion samples into a constrained space at every step, achieving up to 100% hard-constraint satisfaction in evaluated graph settings.

title: Diffuse, Sample, Project: Plug-And-Play Controllable Graph Generation

abstract: The vector field of a controlled differential equation (CDE) describes the relationship between a control path and the evolution of a solution path. Neural CDEs (NCDEs) treat time series data as observations from a control path, parameterise a CDE’s vector field using a neural network, and use the solution path as a continuously evolving hidden state. As their formulation makes them robust to irregular sampling rates, NCDEs are a powerful approach for modelling real-world data. Building on neural rough differential equations (NRDEs), we introduce Log-NCDEs, a novel, effective, and efficient method for training NCDEs. The core component of Log-NCDEs is the Log-ODE method, a tool from the study of rough paths for approximating a CDE’s solution. Log-NCDEs are shown to outperform NCDEs, NRDEs, the linear recurrent unit, S5, and MAMBA on a range of multivariate time series datasets with up to $50{,}000$ observations.

paragraphs: Neural controlled differential equations model a time series as observations of a path that drives a continuously changing hidden state. A neural network specifies how the driving path affects that state. This formulation handles irregular sampling rates, making it useful when measurements do not arrive at evenly spaced times.

The paper introduces Log-NCDEs as an effective and efficient approach to training these models, building on neural rough differential equations. Its central ingredient is the Log-ODE method from rough-path theory, which approximates the solution of a controlled differential equation. The contribution centers on how the continuous hidden-state evolution is approximated and used within the learning method.

On a range of multivariate time-series datasets with up to 50,000 observations, Log-NCDEs outperform neural controlled and rough differential equations, the linear recurrent unit, S5, and MAMBA. These results support the proposed approach across the evaluated long-sequence settings. They connect a mathematical approximation technique with improved empirical time-series modeling, while retaining the continuous-path formulation that motivates neural controlled differential equations.
summary.tldr: Log-NCDEs use a rough-path approximation method to improve neural controlled differential equation training and performance on evaluated time-series datasets.

title: Log Neural Controlled Differential Equations: The Lie Brackets Make A Difference

abstract: The transformer architecture has prevailed in various deep learning settings due to its exceptional capabilities to select and compose structural information. Motivated by these capabilities, Sanford et al. (2023) proposed the sparse token selection task, in which transformers excel while fully-connected networks (FCNs) fail in the worst case. Building upon that, we strengthen the FCN lower bound to an average-case setting and establish an algorithmic separation of transformers over FCNs. Specifically, a one-layer transformer trained with gradient descent provably learns the sparse token selection task and, surprisingly, exhibits strong out-of-distribution length generalization. We provide empirical simulations to justify our theoretical findings.
