paragraphs: The paper studies sparse token selection, a task designed to examine how neural architectures select and combine structural information. Earlier work established a worst-case separation in which transformers succeed and fully connected networks fail. This study strengthens the comparison by examining average-case difficulty and whether a transformer can actually learn the task through training.

The authors strengthen the lower bound for fully connected networks from the worst case to an average-case setting. They also prove that a one-layer transformer trained with gradient descent learns the sparse token selection task. This establishes an algorithmic separation involving both the limitations of one architecture and a successful learning procedure for the other.

The transformer also exhibits strong generalization to sequence lengths outside the training distribution, and empirical simulations support the theoretical findings. The result gives a concrete setting in which transformer structure supports learnable token selection and length generalization. Its claims concern this specified task, providing a precise architectural comparison rather than a universal ranking across learning problems.
summary.tldr: A one-layer transformer provably learns sparse token selection with gradient descent, establishing an average-case separation from fully connected networks.

title: Transformers Provably Learn Sparse Token Selection While Fully-Connected Nets Cannot

abstract: Implicit neural representations have emerged as a powerful paradigm to represent signals such as images and sounds. This approach aims to utilize neural networks to parameterize the implicit function of the signal. However, when representing implicit functions, traditional neural networks such as ReLU-based multilayer perceptrons face challenges in accurately modeling high-frequency components of signals. Recent research has begun to explore the use of Fourier Neural Networks (FNNs) to overcome this limitation. In this paper, we propose Quantum Implicit Representation Network (QIREN), a novel quantum generalization of FNNs. Furthermore, through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that QIREN possesses a quantum advantage over classical FNNs. Lastly, we conducted experiments in signal representation, image superresolution, and image generation tasks to show the superior performance of QIREN compared to state-of-the-art (SOTA) models. Our work not only incorporates quantum advantages into implicit neural representations but also uncovers a promising application direction for Quantum Neural Networks.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations describe a signal through a learned function, using a neural network to represent information such as an image or sound. A difficulty is capturing high-frequency components, which contain rapidly changing signal detail. The paper points to this challenge in conventional ReLU-based multilayer perceptrons and builds on Fourier Neural Networks as an alternative.

The proposed Quantum Implicit Representation Network, or QIREN, is a quantum generalization of Fourier Neural Networks. Its contribution therefore connects a signal-representation approach with quantum neural modeling. The authors provide theoretical analysis establishing a quantum advantage over classical Fourier Neural Networks, giving mathematical support for the proposed representation in addition to its experimental evaluation.

Experiments cover signal representation, image superresolution, and image generation. The authors report superior performance compared with state-of-the-art models on these tasks. Taken together, the theoretical comparison and empirical results identify implicit signal representation as a promising application for quantum neural networks, linking the proposed quantum construction to practical tests of representing and generating signals.
summary.tldr: QIREN generalizes Fourier Neural Networks to a quantum model, with a theoretical quantum advantage and reported gains on signal and image tasks.

title: Quantum Implicit Neural Representations

abstract: Graph Domain Adaptation (GDA) transfers knowledge from labeled source graphs to unlabeled target graphs, addressing the challenge of label scarcity. In this paper, we highlight the significance of graph homophily, a pivotal factor for graph domain alignment, which, however, has long been overlooked in existing approaches. Specifically, our analysis first reveals that homophily discrepancies exist in benchmarks. Moreover, we also show that homophily discrepancies degrade GDA performance from both empirical and theoretical aspects, which further underscores the importance of homophily alignment in GDA. Inspired by this finding, we propose a novel homophily alignment algorithm that employs mixed filters to smooth graph signals, thereby effectively capturing and mitigating homophily discrepancies between graphs. Experimental results on a variety of benchmarks verify the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Graph domain adaptation transfers knowledge from a labeled source graph to a target graph without labels. This paper examines homophily, the tendency for connected nodes to be similar, as an important part of that transfer. The authors argue that differences in homophily between source and target graphs have received insufficient attention in existing alignment approaches.

Their analysis finds homophily discrepancies in benchmark datasets and shows, through both theory and experiments, that these discrepancies degrade adaptation performance. This identifies a specific source of difficulty: knowledge learned from one graph must transfer across differences in how information is organized through connections, as well as across the domains themselves.

The proposed algorithm explicitly aligns homophily using mixed filters that smooth graph signals. These filters are designed to capture and reduce the discrepancies between graphs. Experiments on multiple benchmarks support the method’s effectiveness. The contribution is both diagnostic and practical: it establishes homophily mismatch as a relevant obstacle and introduces a corresponding alignment mechanism for transferring knowledge to unlabeled graphs.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies homophily mismatch as a barrier to graph domain adaptation and introduces mixed filters to reduce it.

title: Homophily Enhanced Graph Domain Adaptation

abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained diffusion models under limited budgets has gained great success. In particular, the recent advances that directly fine-tune the quantized weights using Low-rank Adaptation (LoRA) further reduces training costs. Despite these progress, we point out that existing adaptation recipes are not inference-efficient. Specifically, additional post-training quantization (PTQ) on tuned weights is needed during deployment, which results in noticeable performance drop when the bit-width is low. Based on this observation, we introduce IntLoRA, which adapts quantized diffusion models with integer-type low-rank parameters, to include inference efficiency during tuning. Specifically, IntLoRA enables pre-trained weights to remain quantized during training, facilitating fine-tuning on consumer-level GPUs. During inference, IntLoRA weights can be seamlessly merged into pre-trained weights to directly obtain quantized downstream weights without PTQ. Extensive experiments show our IntLoRA achieves significant speedup on both training and inference without losing performance.

Based on this observation, we introduce IntLoRA, which adapts quantized diffusion models with integer-type low-rank parameters, to include inference efficiency during tuning. paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation can reduce the cost of fine-tuning diffusion models, especially when the pretrained weights are quantized. The paper points out that inexpensive training does not automatically lead to efficient deployment. Existing adaptation recipes need another quantization step after tuning, and that step can noticeably reduce performance at low bit widths.

IntLoRA addresses this mismatch by using integer-valued low-rank adaptation parameters. The original model weights remain quantized during training, helping make fine-tuning feasible on consumer GPUs. At inference, the adaptation weights can be merged directly into the pretrained weights to produce quantized weights for the downstream task, without an additional post-training quantization stage.

This makes the deployment representation part of the tuning design from the outset. It removes the extra conversion step identified as a source of low-bit performance loss. Extensive experiments report significant speedups in both training and inference without losing performance. Those findings support the practical value of coordinating parameter-efficient adaptation with the numerical format the deployed diffusion model will actually use.
summary.tldr: IntLoRA uses integer low-rank updates to fine-tune quantized diffusion models and merge them for inference without post-training quantization.

title: IntLoRA: Integral Low-rank Adaptation of Quantized Diffusion Models

abstract: Improving time-to-first-token (TTFT) is an essentially important objective in modern large language model (LLM) inference engines. Optimizing TTFT directly results in higher maximal QPS and meets the requirements of many critical applications. However, boosting TTFT is notoriously challenging since it is compute-bounded and the performance bottleneck shifts from the self-attention that many prior works focus on to the MLP part. In this work, we present SpecPrefill, a training free framework that accelerates the inference TTFT for both long and medium context queries based on the following insight: LLMs are generalized enough to preserve the quality given only a carefully chosen subset of prompt tokens. At its core, SpecPrefill leverages a lightweight model to speculate locally important tokens based on the context. These tokens, along with the necessary positional information, are then sent to the main model for processing. We evaluate SpecPrefill with a diverse set of tasks, followed by a comprehensive benchmarking of performance improvement both in a real end-to-end setting and ablation studies. SpecPrefill manages to serve Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct-FP8 with up to 7$\times$ maximal end-to-end QPS on real downstream tasks and 7.66$\times$ TTFT improvement.

paragraphs: Time to first token measures how long a user waits before a language model starts responding. Processing the prompt can be compute-bound, with the bottleneck shifting from attention to the model's MLP components. SpecPrefill targets this initial processing cost for medium and long contexts through selective use of prompt tokens.

A lightweight model estimates which tokens are locally important given the context. It passes the selected tokens, together with necessary positional information, to the main model. The framework requires no training and rests on the insight that a carefully chosen prompt subset can preserve output quality. Reducing the amount of prompt material processed by the main model is the central acceleration mechanism.

The authors evaluate diverse tasks, end-to-end serving performance, and component choices through ablations. For Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct-FP8, they report up to sevenfold maximal end-to-end query throughput on real downstream tasks and a 7.66-fold improvement in time to first token. These are reported performance gains for the evaluated system, illustrating the potential value of lightweight token selection before expensive prompt processing.
summary.tldr: SpecPrefill uses a lightweight model to select important prompt tokens, reporting up to sevenfold throughput and 7.66-fold time-to-first-token improvements.

title: Speculative Prefill: Turbocharging TTFT with Lightweight and Training-Free Token Importance Estimation

abstract: While Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) and its variants are widely adopted for their long-context capabilities, the extension of the 1D RoPE to video, with its complex spatio-temporal structure, remains an open challenge. This work first introduces a comprehensive analysis that identifies four key characteristics essential for the effective adaptation of RoPE to video, which have not been fully considered in prior work. As part of our analysis, we introduce a challenging V-NIAH-D (Visual Needle-In-A-Haystack with Distractors) task, which adds periodic distractors into V-NIAH. The V-NIAH-D task demonstrates that previous RoPE variants, lacking appropriate temporal dimension allocation, are easily misled by distractors. Based on our analysis, we introduce VideoRoPE, with a 3D structure designed to preserve spatio-temporal relationships. VideoRoPE features low-frequency temporal allocation to mitigate periodic oscillations, a diagonal layout to maintain spatial symmetry, and adjustable temporal spacing to decouple temporal and spatial indexing. VideoRoPE consistently surpasses previous RoPE variants, across diverse downstream tasks such as long video retrieval, video understanding, and video hallucination. Our code and model weights will be publicly released.

paragraphs: Extending rotary position embeddings from one-dimensional sequences to video requires representing both space and time. This paper analyzes what makes that adaptation effective and identifies four key characteristics. It also introduces V-NIAH-D, a visual retrieval task that adds periodic distractors to a needle-in-a-haystack setting.

The distractor task shows that earlier rotary-embedding variants can be misled when temporal dimensions are allocated poorly. VideoRoPE responds with a three-dimensional structure intended to preserve spatial and temporal relationships. It assigns low frequencies to time to reduce periodic oscillations, uses a diagonal layout to preserve spatial symmetry, and makes temporal spacing adjustable so temporal and spatial indexing can be separated.

Across the reported downstream evaluations, VideoRoPE consistently outperforms previous variants on long-video retrieval, video understanding, and video hallucination tasks. The findings connect positional design choices to practical video-model behavior. In particular, the new distractor task exposes a temporal weakness, while the proposed embedding structure addresses time and space as distinct but coordinated parts of the representation.
summary.tldr: VideoRoPE redesigns rotary embeddings for spatial and temporal video structure, improving performance and resistance to periodic distractors.

title: VideoRoPE: What Makes for Good Video Rotary Position Embedding?

abstract: Actor-critic methods for decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) facilitate collaborative optimal decision making without centralized coordination, thus enabling a wide range of applications in practice. To date, however, most theoretical convergence studies for existing actor-critic decentralized MARL methods are limited to the guarantee of a stationary solution under the linear function approximation. This leaves a significant gap between the highly successful use of deep neural actor-critic for decentralized MARL in practice and the current theoretical understanding. To bridge this gap, in this paper, we make the first attempt to develop a deep neural actor-critic method for decentralized MARL, where both the actor and critic components are inherently non-linear. We show that our proposed method enjoys a global optimality guarantee with a finite-time convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$, where $T$ is the total iteration times. This marks the first global convergence result for deep neural actor-critic methods in the MARL literature. We also conduct extensive numerical experiments, which verify our theoretical results.

To date, however, most theoretical convergence studies for existing actor-critic decentralized MARL methods are limited to the guarantee of a stationary solution under the linear function approximation. This leaves a significant gap between the highly successful use of deep neural actor-critic for decentralized MARL in practice and the current theoretical understanding. To bridge this gap, in this paper, we make the first attempt to develop a deep neural actor-critic method for decentralized MARL, where both the actor and critic components are inherently non-linear. We show that our proposed method enjoys a global optimality guarantee with a finite-time convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$, where $T$ is the total iteration times. This marks the first global convergence result for deep neural actor-critic methods in the MARL literature. We also conduct extensive numerical experiments, which verify our theoretical results.

paragraphs: Decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning lets agents learn collaborative decisions without a central coordinator. Actor-critic methods divide learning between a component that chooses actions and one that evaluates them. Although deep neural versions work well in practice, the paper identifies a theoretical gap: much prior convergence analysis covers linear approximations and guarantees only stationary solutions.

The authors develop a decentralized actor-critic method in which both components are nonlinear neural models. For their proposed method, they establish a global optimality guarantee with a finite-time convergence rate of O(1/T), where T counts iterations. This is stronger than showing that updates eventually reach a stationary point, which alone does not establish global optimality.

The paper presents this as the first global convergence result for deep neural actor-critic methods in the multi-agent reinforcement learning literature. Numerical experiments are reported to verify the theoretical results. The contribution connects a more expressive model class with a quantitative convergence guarantee for the constructed method, rather than establishing the same guarantee for every deep actor-critic algorithm.
summary.tldr: A proposed decentralized deep actor-critic method receives a global optimality guarantee with an O(1/T) finite-time convergence rate.

title: Finite-Time Global Optimality Convergence in Deep Neural Actor-Critic Methods for Decentralized Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The widespread deployment of general-purpose AI (GPAI) systems introduces significant new risks. Yet the infrastructure, practices, and norms for reporting flaws in GPAI systems remain seriously underdeveloped, lagging far behind more established fields like software security. Based on a collaboration between experts from the fields of software security, machine learning, law, social science, and policy, we identify key gaps in the evaluation and reporting of flaws in GPAI systems. We call for three interventions to advance system safety. First, we propose using standardized AI flaw reports and rules of engagement for researchers in order to ease the process of submitting, reproducing, and triaging flaws in GPAI systems. Second, we propose GPAI system providers adopt broadly-scoped flaw disclosure programs, borrowing from bug bounties, with legal safe harbors to protect researchers. Third, we advocate for the development of improved infrastructure to coordinate distribution of flaw reports across the many stakeholders who may be impacted. These interventions are increasingly urgent, as evidenced by the prevalence of jailbreaks and other flaws that can transfer across different providers' GPAI systems. By promoting robust reporting and coordination in the AI ecosystem, these proposals could significantly improve the safety, security, and accountability of GPAI systems.
originalAbstract: The widespread deployment of general-purpose AI (GPAI) systems introduces significant new risks. Yet the infrastructure, practices, and norms for reporting flaws in GPAI systems remain seriously underdeveloped, lagging far behind more established fields like software security. Based on a collaboration between experts from the fields of software security, machine learning, law, social science, and policy, we identify key gaps in the evaluation and reporting of flaws in GPAI systems. We call for three interventions to advance system safety. First, we propose using standardized AI flaw reports and rules of engagement for researchers in order to ease the process of submitting, reproducing, and triaging flaws in GPAI systems. Second, we propose GPAI system providers adopt broadly-scoped flaw disclosure programs, borrowing from bug bounties, with legal safe harbors to protect researchers. Third, we advocate for the development of improved infrastructure to coordinate distribution of flaw reports across the many stakeholders who may be impacted. These interventions are increasingly urgent, as evidenced by the prevalence of jailbreaks and other flaws that can transfer across different providers' GPAI systems. By promoting robust reporting and coordination in the AI ecosystem, these proposals could significantly improve the safety, security, and accountability of GPAI systems.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that general-purpose AI needs stronger arrangements for independent evaluation and flaw reporting. Drawing on collaboration across software security, machine learning, law, social science, and policy, the authors identify gaps in current practices. They describe AI’s reporting infrastructure and norms as substantially less developed than those in software security.

The paper proposes three interventions. Standardized flaw reports and clear rules for researchers would make problems easier to submit, reproduce, and prioritize. Broad disclosure programs inspired by bug bounties would encourage external investigation, with legal protections for researchers. Better coordination infrastructure would distribute relevant reports among the different stakeholders affected by a flaw.

These proposals matter because a vulnerability may extend beyond a single provider’s system. The authors point to jailbreaks and other transferable flaws as evidence that coordinated reporting is urgent. Their contribution is a framework for making external findings actionable across the AI ecosystem. They argue that adopting it could improve safety, security, and accountability, rather than claim that the proposed arrangements have already delivered those improvements.
summary.tldr: The paper calls for standardized AI flaw reports, protected disclosure programs, and coordinated reporting across affected stakeholders.

title: Position: In-House Evaluation Is Not Enough. Towards Robust Third-Party Evaluation and Flaw Disclosure for General-Purpose AI

abstract: Applying machine learning techniques to solving long-standing mathematical conjectures can be particularly challenging due to their extreme reward sparsity. As an illustrative example, we consider Kalai’s algebraic Hirsch conjecture and recast the construction of its counterexamples as a sparse-reward reinforcement learning problem on graphs. We propose a constrained options-based HRL framework with an equivariant graph neural network policy, which allows us to learn useful temporal abstractions for this task. We evaluate our approach over a wide range of degrees and demonstrate that it consistently outperforms classical RL algorithms as well as greedy search. By exploiting the hierarchical structure of the problem, we effectively provide a first-of-its-kind application of HRL to a problem in commutative algebra.

paragraphs: Searching for mathematical counterexamples can provide very little feedback: most candidate constructions do not produce a rewarding result. This paper studies that difficulty through Kalai’s algebraic Hirsch conjecture. It formulates the construction of counterexamples as a graph-based reinforcement-learning task with sparse rewards, making the search process itself the object of learning.

The proposed method uses constrained, options-based hierarchical reinforcement learning. Options provide temporal abstractions, allowing the policy to learn useful extended behaviors within the search rather than relying solely on individual decisions. An equivariant graph neural network supplies the policy, combining graph-based representations with the hierarchical organization of actions. The approach is designed to exploit structure in the mathematical search problem.

The authors evaluate the method across a wide range of degrees and report that it consistently outperforms both classical reinforcement-learning algorithms and greedy search. They present this as a first-of-its-kind application of hierarchical reinforcement learning to commutative algebra. The stated result concerns a more effective counterexample-search method, showing how learned temporal structure can help in a setting where rewards are extremely sparse.
summary.tldr: An options-based hierarchical reinforcement-learning method improves sparse-reward graph search for counterexamples related to Kalai’s algebraic Hirsch conjecture.

title: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Sparse-Reward Search in Commutative Algebra

abstract: Traditional e-commerce search systems employ multi-stage cascading architectures that suffer from fragmented computation and optimization objective collisions across stages, ultimately limiting their performance ceiling. We propose OneSearch, the first industrial-deployed end-to-end generative framework for e-commerce search, featuring three key innovations: (1) Keyword-enhanced Hierarchical Quantization Encoding to preserve hierarchical semantics and distinctive item attributes while maintaining strong query-item relevance constraints; (2) multi-view user behavior sequence injection that constructs behavior-driven user IDs and incorporates both explicit short-term and implicit long-term sequences; and (3) a Preference-Aware Reward System with multi-stage supervised fine-tuning and adaptive reward-weighted ranking to capture fine-grained user preferences. Extensive offline evaluations demonstrate its superior performance, while online A/B tests achieve statistically significant improvements: +1.67% item CTR, +2.40% buyer, and +3.22% order volume. OneSearch reduces operational expenditure by 75.40%, improves Model FLOPs Utilization from 3.26% to 27.32%, and has been successfully deployed across multiple search scenarios in Kuaishou, serving millions of users daily. Code is in https://github.com/benchen4395/onesearch-family.

paragraphs: OneSearch unifies e-commerce search in an end-to-end generative framework. Conventional search pipelines divide computation and optimization across multiple stages, which can create conflicting objectives. The proposed system brings item representation, user behavior, and preference-aware training into a connected approach.

Its item encoding preserves hierarchical semantics and distinctive attributes while constraining query-item relevance. User representations incorporate multiple views of behavior, including explicit short-term and implicit long-term sequences. A preference-aware reward system combines multistage supervised fine-tuning with adaptive reward-weighted ranking to capture finer differences in user preferences.

Offline evaluations show superior performance, and online A/B tests report statistically significant increases of 1.67% in item click-through rate, 2.40% in the buyer metric, and 3.22% in order volume. Operational expenditure falls by 75.40%, while Model FLOPs Utilization rises from 3.26% to 27.32%. The framework has been deployed across multiple Kuaishou search scenarios serving millions of users daily. These results connect the unified architecture with both user-facing outcomes and operational efficiency.
summary.tldr: OneSearch unifies generative e-commerce search, reporting improved online engagement and orders alongside substantially lower operating expenditure.

title: OneSearch: A Preliminary Exploration of the Unified End-to-End Generative Framework for E-commerce Search

abstract: While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer broad general capabilities, deploying them on specific hardware requires real-world adaptation to bridge the embodiment gap. Since robot demonstrations are costly, this adaptation must often occur under a strict data budget. In this work, we identify a critical diversity trap: the standard heuristic of “maximizing coverage" by collecting diverse, single-shot demonstrations can be self-defeating due to non-vanishing estimation noise. We formalize this phenomenon as a Coverage–Density Trade-off. By decomposing the policy error into estimation (density) and extrapolation (coverage) terms, we characterize an interior optimal allocation of unique conditions for a fixed budget. Guided by this analysis, we propose Anchor-Centric Adaptation (ACA), a two-stage framework that first stabilizes a policy skeleton through repeated demonstrations at core anchors, then selectively expands coverage to high-risk boundaries via teacher-forced error mining and constrained residual updates. Real-robot experiments validate our trade-off framework and demonstrate that ACA significantly improves task reliability and success rates over standard diverse sampling strategies under the same budget.

paragraphs: Adapting a general robot model to particular hardware often requires collecting demonstrations under a tight budget. This paper argues that maximizing variety by recording each condition only once can be self-defeating. Spreading demonstrations too thinly leaves estimation noise, even though the data cover more situations.

The authors formalize this tension by separating policy error into a density-related estimation term and a coverage-related extrapolation term. Their analysis characterizes an interior optimum for the number of unique conditions under a fixed budget. Anchor-Centric Adaptation follows this reasoning in two stages: repeated demonstrations at core conditions first stabilize a policy skeleton, then additional data expand coverage toward high-risk boundaries.

The second stage uses teacher-forced error mining to identify where expansion is needed and constrained residual updates to adapt the policy. Real-robot experiments support the proposed coverage–density trade-off and show significantly better reliability and success rates than standard diverse sampling under the same budget. The practical implication is that strategic repetition and selective expansion can make limited demonstrations more useful than pursuing coverage alone.
summary.tldr: Anchor-Centric Adaptation combines repeated core demonstrations with targeted coverage expansion to improve robot adaptation under a fixed data budget.

title: Escaping the Diversity Trap in Robotic Manipulation via Anchor-Centric Adaptation

abstract: Despite recent breakthroughs, audio foundation models struggle in processing complex multi-source acoustic scenes. We refer to this challenging domain as audio stories, which can have multiple speakers and background/foreground sound effects. Compared to traditional audio processing tasks, audio stories introduce new layers of semantic, temporal, and physical complexity. To address this challenge, we propose AudioChat, a framework for developing audio foundation models that can generate, edit, and understand audio stories. AudioChat introduces a new paradigm in which LLM-based toolcalling agents simulate interactions between users and the system, and these simulated dialogues are used as training data. We also introduce a novel Audio Transfusion Forcing objective to train the AudioChat model, allowing it to simultaneously decompose high-level instructions via structured chain-of-thought reasoning and perform interactive multi-turn audio understanding/generation. To evaluate generation and editing performance, we develop three new metrics that directly measure task performance instead of relying upon distribution-based scoring. We highly encourage readers to visit our demo to better understand the capabilities of AudioChat: https://audiochat-icml-2026.github.io/.

The framework brings generation, editing, and understanding into a shared system.

The authors also introduce Audio Transfusion Forcing, a training objective that supports both structured decomposition of high-level instructions and interactive audio understanding or generation over multiple turns.

The paper therefore combines an interaction-oriented data pipeline, a unified training objective, and task-focused evaluation. Its stated contribution is this framework and its capabilities; the abstract does not report numerical performance improvements.
summary.tldr: AudioChat uses simulated dialogues and a unified training objective to generate, edit, and understand complex audio stories.

title: AudioChat: Unified Audio Storytelling, Editing, and Understanding with Transfusion Forcing

abstract: Existing time series foundation models (TSFMs), often based on transformer variants, lack adaptability to different sampling rates, struggle with generalization across varying context and target lengths and are computationally inefficient. We introduce FlowState, a novel TSFM architecture that achieves sampling-rate–equivariant forecasting through a unified design that pairs a state space model (SSM) encoder with a functional basis decoder (FBD). This design enables continuous-time modeling and dynamic time-scale adjustment, allowing FlowState to inherently generalize across all possible temporal resolutions, and dynamically adjust the forecasting horizons without retraining. We further propose an efficient pretraining strategy that improves robustness and accelerates training. Despite being one of the smallest TSFMs, FlowState achieves state-of-the-art results on the widely used GIFT-Eval benchmark, while demonstrating superior adaptability to unseen sampling rates. Our detailed analyses confirm the effectiveness of its components, and we demonstrate its unique ability to adapt to varying input sampling rates.

paragraphs: Time-series foundation models often struggle when measurements arrive at different sampling rates or when input and forecast lengths change. FlowState addresses these issues through an architecture designed to adjust its time scale. Its central aim is sampling-rate-equivariant forecasting: predictions should adapt coherently to changes in temporal resolution.

The architecture pairs a state space model encoder with a functional basis decoder. This combination supports continuous-time modeling and dynamic adjustment of the time scale. The authors describe it as enabling generalization across all temporal resolutions and changes to the forecast horizon without retraining. They also introduce an efficient pretraining strategy that improves robustness and accelerates training.

Despite being among the smallest time-series foundation models, FlowState achieves state-of-the-art results on GIFT-Eval and demonstrates superior adaptation to sampling rates unseen during training. Component analyses support the contributions of its design. The findings connect a structural approach to representing time with both forecasting performance and flexibility, particularly when the spacing of incoming measurements differs from the model’s previous experience.
summary.tldr: FlowState combines a state space encoder and functional decoder to adjust forecasting across sampling rates and horizons without retraining.

title: FlowState: Sampling-Rate-Equivariant Time-Series Forecasting

abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) is a prominent strategy to significantly speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), especially in byte-level LLMs, which are tokeniser-free but prohibitively slow. However, many existing MTP methods either assume independence between future tokens, sacrificing expressiveness, or generate tokens one at a time within the window, increasing latency. In this work, we investigate the trade-off between expressiveness and latency in MTP within the framework of probabilistic circuits (PCs). Our framework, MTPC, allows one to explore different ways to encode the joint distributions over future tokens by selecting circuit architectures, generalising classical models such as (hierarchical) mixture models, hidden Markov models, and tensor networks. We show the efficacy of MTPC by retrofitting existing byte-level LLMs, such as EvaByte, and byte-fied subword models, such as Llama3.2 3B. Our experiments show that, when combined with speculative decoding, MTPC substantially speeds up generation compared to MTP with independence assumptions, while guaranteeing to retain the performance of the original verifier LLM. We also rigorously study the optimal trade-off between expressiveness and latency when exploring the possible parameterisations of MTPC, such as PC architectures and partial layer sharing between the verifier and draft LLMs.

paragraphs: Byte-level language models avoid tokenizers, but generating text byte by byte can be slow. Predicting several future bytes together offers a way to accelerate generation. The difficulty is preserving relationships among those bytes: assuming independence limits what the predictor can express, while generating each byte sequentially inside the prediction window adds latency.

MTPC represents the joint distribution of future tokens using probabilistic circuits. Different circuit architectures offer different ways to capture dependencies, encompassing structures associated with mixture models, hidden Markov models, and tensor networks. This turns the balance between predictive expressiveness and computation into an explicit design choice, including how much of the draft and verifier models' layers should be shared.

The authors retrofit byte-level EvaByte models and byte-converted Llama3.2 3B models. Combined with speculative decoding, MTPC substantially accelerates generation compared with multi-token predictors that assume independence, while guaranteeing retention of the original verifier model's performance. The contribution is therefore both a flexible family of joint predictors and a study of which parameterizations best balance their additional expressiveness against latency.
summary.tldr: MTPC uses probabilistic circuits to predict dependent future bytes efficiently, accelerating speculative decoding while preserving verifier-model performance.

title: Fast and Expressive Multi-Byte Prediction with Probabilistic Circuits

abstract: Graph coarsening is a fundamental dimensionality reduction technique for scaling large graphs while preserving structural and feature information. However, most existing coarsening methods are designed for static graphs and do not extend well to dynamic settings where nodes, edges, and connectivity patterns evolve over time. Recomputing a coarsened graph from scratch after every update is often infeasible, which limits scalability and real-time applicability. To address this, we propose a unified framework for coarsening discrete-time dynamic graphs by incrementally updating the coarsening mapping matrix. The framework initializes from any static coarsening technique and then efficiently incorporates real-world graph events, including node additions, node deletions, and edge modifications. We instantiate this framework with two optimization based incremental update algorithms tailored to different dynamic regimes, one focusing on efficiently integrating growth related changes and another handling broader topology evolution with adaptive reassignment. We derive fast and scalable solvers with convergence guarantees, and provide theoretical guarantee via $\epsilon$-similarity bounds that quantify and control quality degradation in the coarsened graph. Extensive experiments under realistic dynamic scenarios show substantial improvements in runtime and memory, delivering significant speedups while maintaining or improving downstream task performance, including graph neural network accuracy.

paragraphs: Graph coarsening makes a large network smaller while retaining useful information about its connections and node features. That compression becomes difficult to maintain when the original graph changes. Rebuilding the smaller graph after every addition, deletion, or changed connection can consume too much time and memory for an evolving system.

The paper proposes updating the coarsening mapping incrementally. This mapping records how the original graph is represented in the compressed graph. The framework can start from any static coarsening method, then incorporate subsequent changes. It supplies two optimization algorithms: one emphasizes graph growth, while the other handles broader changes in connectivity by allowing adaptive reassignment.

The authors develop scalable solvers with convergence guarantees and similarity bounds that quantify degradation in the compressed representation. The contribution connects efficient updates with explicit control over representation quality.
summary.tldr: An incremental graph-coarsening framework updates compressed graphs efficiently as their nodes and connections change, with quality bounds and strong downstream results.

title: Adapting to Evolving Graphs: A Scalable Framework for Dynamic Coarsening

abstract: Offline imitation learning typically learns from expert and unlabeled demonstrations, yet often overlooks the valuable signal in explicitly undesirable behaviors. In this work, we study offline imitation learning from contrasting behaviors, where the dataset contains both expert and undesirable demonstrations along with an unlabeled set of demonstrations. We propose a novel formulation that optimizes a difference of KL divergences over the state-action visitation distributions of expert and undesirable (or bad) data. Although the resulting objective is a DC (Difference-of-Convex) program, we prove that it becomes convex when expert demonstrations outweigh undesirable demonstrations, enabling a practical and stable non-adversarial training objective. Our method avoids adversarial training and handles both positive and negative demonstrations in a unified framework. Extensive experiments on standard offline imitation learning benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

We propose a novel formulation that optimizes a difference of KL divergences over the state-action visitation distributions of expert and undesirable (or bad) data. Although the resulting objective is a DC (Difference-of-Convex) program, we prove that it becomes convex when expert demonstrations outweigh undesirable demonstrations, enabling a practical and stable non-adversarial training objective. paragraphs: Offline imitation learning uses recorded behavior to learn a policy. This paper considers datasets containing three kinds of demonstrations: expert behavior, explicitly undesirable behavior, and behavior without either label. Its starting point is that examples of what to avoid carry useful information that conventional expert-and-unlabeled formulations can overlook.

DualCOIL expresses the learning objective through a difference of KL divergences between state-action visitation distributions. These distributions describe which situations and actions occur under different behaviors. The formulation brings positive and negative demonstrations into one objective, allowing the policy-learning problem to account for both desirable and undesirable patterns without adversarial training.

A difference-of-convex objective is not generally convex, but the authors prove convexity when expert demonstrations outweigh undesirable demonstrations. That condition enables the practical, stable training objective described in the paper. Experiments on standard offline imitation-learning benchmarks show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution combines a way to use explicitly negative demonstrations with a conditional mathematical result that makes the resulting optimization more tractable.
summary.tldr: DualCOIL learns from expert and undesirable demonstrations using a non-adversarial objective that becomes convex when expert demonstrations outweigh undesirable ones.

title: DualCOIL: Offline Imitation Learning from Contrasting Demonstrations

abstract: Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning aims to design agents that can reach specified goals, notably from previously collected trajectories in the offline setting. In this context, graph-based approaches have been proposed to mitigate compounding value-estimation errors in long-horizon navigation tasks. However, existing approaches typically rely on dense keypoint coverage of the dataset support, resulting in computationally expensive planning. Moreover, they lack explicit mechanisms to adapt to topological changes (e.g., new obstacles), hindering deployment in live applications such as video game environments. To address these two shortcomings, we introduce Adaptive Quasimetric Mapping (AQM), an offline framework leveraging a “time-to-reach” quasimetric learned from the available data. Crucially, it builds a sparse cover of the dataset support, as a greedy approximation to a dominating set problem. At test-time, the resulting graph is carefully pruned by comparing the observed edge traversal time against a time-to-reach budget derived from the quasimetric, thus enabling zero-shot replanning. Empirically, we evaluate AQM on navigation tasks ranging from a classical to a video-game-like benchmark evaluating adaptation across tasks. We show that AQM achieves competitive performance while requiring up to 100$\times$ fewer keypoints than prior approaches, hence demonstrating the relevance of topological abstraction for goal-conditioned navigation.

paragraphs: Offline goal-conditioned navigation learns how to reach destinations from previously collected trajectories. Graph-based methods can help with long routes, where errors in estimated values accumulate. However, representing an environment with many keypoints makes planning expensive, and a graph built from old data may become unreliable when new obstacles appear.

Adaptive Quasimetric Mapping addresses both problems using a learned estimate of the time needed to travel between states. This estimate is a quasimetric, allowing travel difficulty to depend on direction. The method selects a sparse collection of representative points through a greedy approximation to a dominating set problem, producing a smaller navigation graph.

During deployment, AQM compares actual traversal times with budgets derived from its learned travel-time estimates. It prunes the graph when these checks indicate problems, enabling zero-shot replanning. Across navigation benchmarks, including a video-game-like setting, it achieves competitive performance with up to 100 times fewer keypoints than prior approaches. The findings support sparse graph representations that can respond to changes encountered during navigation.
summary.tldr: AQM builds sparse navigation graphs from offline data and prunes unreliable routes during deployment, achieving competitive results with up to 100 times fewer keypoints.

title: Adaptive Quasimetric Mapping : Principled Topological Abstraction for Robust Offline Goal-Conditioned Navigation

abstract: Differentiable logic gate networks map directly to gate-level circuits, enabling ultra-low-latency inference, yet their logic footprint often exceeds FPGA capacity budgets. Tightly fitting a trained model to a target FPGA requires a post-training mechanism to trade off network complexity and accuracy—analogous to pruning in standard neural networks. To this end, we introduce unit tying: a simplification that forces selected gates to constants (0 or 1), enabling constant propagation and downstream logic elimination. However, we observe that naively extending pruning criteria to logic networks is unreliable under such near-discrete modifications. We therefore propose a two-stage algorithm for unit tying: (i) a fast Gauss–Newton screening step under a teacher-referenced logit-distortion objective that constructs a high-recall overshoot set and (ii) a refinement step that corrects approximation and interaction-driven errors using a small number of finite-difference evaluations. On CIFAR-10 and MNIST, our method consistently improves the accuracy–area trade-off over common saliency baselines, yielding substantial post-synthesis LUT reductions of up to 48% on CIFAR-10 and 43% on MNIST, with modest accuracy degradation.

However, we observe that naively extending pruning criteria to logic networks is unreliable under such near-discrete modifications. On CIFAR-10 and MNIST, our method consistently improves the accuracy–area trade-off over common saliency baselines, yielding substantial post-synthesis LUT reductions of up to 48% on CIFAR-10 and 43% on MNIST, with modest accuracy degradation.

paragraphs: Differentiable logic gate networks can translate directly into circuits for very low-latency inference, but their logic requirements may exceed an FPGA’s capacity. This paper introduces unit tying as a post-training way to reduce that footprint. Selected gates are fixed to zero or one, allowing constant propagation to eliminate additional downstream logic.

Because these changes are nearly discrete, criteria borrowed directly from neural-network pruning can be unreliable. The proposed algorithm first uses a fast Gauss–Newton approximation to screen candidates against a teacher-referenced logit-distortion objective. It deliberately creates an oversized candidate set with high recall. A second stage uses a small number of finite-difference evaluations to correct approximation errors and errors caused by interactions between changes.

On CIFAR-10 and MNIST, the method consistently improves the accuracy–area tradeoff over common saliency baselines. Reported post-synthesis lookup-table reductions reach up to 48% and 43%, respectively, with modest accuracy degradation. These are maximum reported reductions, and the result supports staged screening and refinement as a practical way to fit logic networks into smaller hardware budgets.
summary.tldr: Two-stage unit tying reduces logic-network hardware usage by fixing selected gates to constants and refining choices to preserve accuracy.

title: Two-Stage Unit Tying for Simplifying Differentiable Logic Gate Networks

abstract: Test-time training (TTT) with KV binding as sequence modeling layer is commonly interpreted as a form of online meta-learning that memorizes a key–value mapping at test time. However, our analysis reveals multiple phenomena that contradict this memorization-based interpretation. Motivated by these findings, we revisit the formulation of TTT and show that a broad class of TTT architectures can be expressed as a form of learned linear attention operator. Beyond explaining previously puzzling model behaviors, this perspective yields multiple practical benefits: it enables principled architectural simplifications, admits fully parallel formulations that preserve performance while improving efficiency, and provides a systematic reduction of diverse TTT variants to a standard linear attention form. Overall, our results reframe TTT not as test-time memorization, but as learned linear attention with enhanced representational capacity. Project page: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/sil/projects/tttla/.

paragraphs: Test-time training with key–value binding is often described as a sequence layer that learns to memorize mappings while processing an input. This paper identifies model behaviors that conflict with that explanation. It revisits the mathematical formulation and shows that a broad class of these architectures can instead be expressed as learned linear attention operators.

The reformulation supplies a common description for multiple test-time training variants. It explains previously puzzling behaviors while showing how their computation relates to a standard linear attention form with enhanced representational capacity. The scope is a broad class of architectures using this formulation, rather than a statement about every method that adapts during inference.

This interpretation also has practical consequences. It enables principled simplifications of model architecture and fully parallel formulations that preserve performance while improving efficiency. Reducing diverse variants to a common operator makes their computational structure easier to analyze and reorganize. The contribution therefore combines a revised account of what these layers compute with concrete opportunities to make that computation simpler and more efficient.
summary.tldr: A broad class of key–value test-time training layers can be reformulated as learned linear attention, enabling simpler and more parallel computation.

title: Test-Time Training with KV Binding Is Secretly Linear Attention

abstract: Autoregressive (AR) generation is the standard decoding paradigm for Large Language Models (LLMs), but its token-by-token nature limits parallelism at inference time. Diffusion Language Models (DLLMs) offer parallel decoding by recovering multiple masked tokens per step; however, in practice they often fail to translate this parallelism into speed gains over optimized AR engines (e.g., vLLM). A key reason is that many DLLMs rely on bidirectional attention, which breaks standard prefix KV caching. We propose WeDLM, a diffusion decoding framework built entirely on standard causal attention to make parallel generation prefix-cache friendly. The core idea is to let each masked position condition on all observed tokens while keeping a causal mask, achieved by Topological Reordering that moves observed tokens to the physical prefix while preserving their logical positions. Building on this, we introduce a streaming decoding procedure that continuously commits confident tokens into a growing left-to-right prefix, avoiding the stop-and-wait behavior common in block diffusion methods. Experiments show that WeDLM preserves the quality of strong AR backbones while delivering substantial speedups, approaching 3$\times$ on challenging reasoning benchmarks and up to 10$\times$ in low-entropy generation regimes; critically, our comparisons are against AR baselines served by vLLM under matched deployment settings.

Recovering multiple masked tokens per step can offer parallelism, but bidirectional attention often prevents standard prefix key–value caching. That incompatibility helps explain why some diffusion approaches fail to outperform optimized autoregressive inference engines.

Observed tokens move to the physical prefix while keeping their logical positions, allowing masked positions to condition on all observed tokens. title: WeDLM: Reconciling Diffusion Language Models with Standard Causal Attention for Fast Inference

abstract: Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs) sometimes fail to reproduce the physical smoothness of the quantum potential energy surface (PES), leading to erroneous behavior in downstream simulations that standard energy and force regression evaluations can miss. Existing evaluations, such as microcanonical molecular dynamics (MD), are computationally expensive and primarily probe near-equilibrium states. To improve evaluation metrics for MLIPs, we introduce the Bond Smoothness Characterization Test (BSCT). This efficient benchmark probes the PES via controlled bond deformations and detects non-smoothness, including discontinuities, artificial minima, and spurious forces, both near and far from equilibrium. We show that BSCT correlates strongly with MD stability while requiring a fraction of the cost of MD. To demonstrate how BSCT can guide iterative model design, we utilize an unconstrained Transformer backbone as a testbed, illustrating how refinements such as a new differentiable $k$-nearest neighbors algorithm and temperature-controlled attention reduce artifacts identified by our metric. By optimizing model design systematically based on BSCT, the resulting MLIP simultaneously achieves a low conventional E/F regression error, stable MD simulations, and robust atomistic property predictions. Our results establish BSCT as both a validation metric for practitioners to assess MLIP utility and as an "in-the-loop" model design proxy that alerts MLIP developers to physical challenges that cannot be efficiently evaluated by current MLIP benchmarks.

paragraphs: Machine-learning interatomic potentials predict energies and forces for atomistic simulations. Good prediction errors alone can miss an important physical property: the energy surface should change smoothly as atomic configurations change. Artificial jumps, minima, or forces can therefore cause simulation problems even when conventional regression scores look favorable.

The paper introduces the Bond Smoothness Characterization Test, which probes predicted energy surfaces through controlled bond deformations. It checks configurations both close to equilibrium and farther away. The test detects several kinds of non-smooth behavior and correlates strongly with molecular-dynamics stability, while costing a fraction of the molecular-dynamics evaluation. This makes smoothness a practical signal for repeated model assessment.

The authors also use the test to guide architecture changes in an unconstrained Transformer. A differentiable nearest-neighbor algorithm and temperature-controlled attention reduce artifacts identified by the test. The resulting model combines low energy and force errors with stable molecular dynamics and robust atomistic property predictions. The contribution thus extends beyond scoring finished models: it provides feedback that can guide their design.
summary.tldr: A low-cost bond-deformation test detects energy-surface artifacts and guides interatomic model changes that improve simulation behavior.

title: From Evaluation to Design: Using Potential Energy Surface Smoothness Metrics to Guide ML Interatomic Potential Architectures

abstract: Recent advances in $\textit{de novo}$ protein binder design have enabled increasing experimental validation, yet reported $\textit{in silico}$ metrics remain difficult to interpret or compare across studies due to non-standardized evaluation protocols. We introduce $\textbf{ProtDBench}$, a standardized and throughput-aware evaluation framework for protein binder design. ProtDBench defines unified benchmark tasks, evaluation protocols, and success criteria, enabling systematic analysis of how evaluation design influences observed performance. Using a large wet-lab annotated dataset, we analyze commonly used structure prediction models as evaluation verifiers, revealing substantial verifier-dependent bias and limited agreement under identical filtering protocols. We then benchmark representative open-source generative binder design methods across ten diverse protein targets under a fixed evaluation protocol. Beyond per-sequence success rates, ProtDBench incorporates throughput-aware metrics based on a fixed 24-hour budget, as well as cluster-level success criteria to account for structural diversity. Together, these results expose systematic differences induced by filtering rules, success definitions, and throughput-aware evaluation between computational efficiency, success rate, and structural diversity. Overall, ProtDBench provides a fair and reproducible evaluation pipeline that supports systematic and controlled comparison of protein binder design methods under realistic evaluation settings.

paragraphs: ProtDBench addresses a comparison problem in protein binder design: computational success metrics can mean different things under different evaluation protocols. The framework standardizes tasks, filtering procedures, and success criteria so that observed differences between design methods can be assessed under controlled conditions.

Using a large dataset annotated with wet-lab outcomes, the authors examine structure-prediction models used to verify candidate binders. They find substantial verifier-dependent bias and limited agreement even under identical filtering rules. This shows that the choice of evaluation model can materially influence which designs appear successful. The paper then evaluates representative open-source generative methods across ten diverse protein targets using a fixed protocol.

The framework also looks beyond success per generated sequence. It measures output within a fixed 24-hour budget and uses cluster-level success criteria to account for structural diversity. These views expose differences associated with filtering, success definitions, and computational throughput. ProtDBench makes the relationship between efficiency, success rate, and diversity more visible, supporting comparisons that reflect both candidate quality and the practical amount of useful output.
summary.tldr: ProtDBench standardizes protein binder evaluation and reveals how verifier choice, throughput, and diversity criteria alter apparent performance.

title: ProtDBench: A Unified Benchmark of Protein Binder Design and Evaluation

abstract: Causal discovery is essential for advancing data-driven fields such as scientific AI and data analysis, yet existing approaches face significant time- and space-efficiency bottlenecks when scaling to large graphs. To address this challenge, we present CauScale, a neural architecture designed for efficient causal discovery that scales inference to graphs with up to 1000 nodes. CauScale improves time efficiency via a reduction unit that compresses data embeddings and improves space efficiency by adopting tied attention weights to avoid maintaining axis-specific attention maps. To keep high causal discovery accuracy, CauScale adopts a two-stream design: a data stream extracts relational evidence from high-dimensional observations, while a graph stream integrates statistical graph priors and preserves key structural signals. CauScale successfully scales to 500-node graphs during training, where prior work fails due to space limitations. Across testing data with varying graph scales and causal mechanisms, CauScale achieves 99.6% mAP on in-distribution data and 84.4% on out-of-distribution data, while delivering 4$\times$–13,000$\times$ inference speedups over prior methods.

paragraphs: Causal discovery methods seek causal graph structure from data, but computation and memory become major obstacles as graphs grow. CauScale addresses both bottlenecks with a neural architecture that supports inference on graphs containing up to 1,000 nodes. Its design aims to retain useful structural evidence while reducing the resources needed to process it.

A reduction unit compresses data embeddings to improve time efficiency. Tied attention weights reduce memory requirements by avoiding separate attention maps for different axes. Two interacting streams preserve complementary information: one extracts relationships from observations, while the other incorporates statistical graph priors and maintains structural signals.

The method trains on 500-node graphs, a scale where the compared prior work encounters memory limits. Across tests varying graph size and causal mechanisms, the authors report 99.6% mean average precision in distribution and 84.4% out of distribution, with inference speedups ranging from fourfold to 13,000-fold over prior methods. These results show substantial scaling gains alongside strong reported discovery accuracy.
summary.tldr: CauScale combines compressed data representations and shared attention with two-stream reasoning to scale causal discovery to 1,000-node inference.

title: CauScale: Neural Causal Discovery at Scale

abstract: High-throughput gene perturbation experiments can test several genetic interventions in parallel, yet experimental budgets remain limited. A central goal is hit discovery: identifying as many perturbations as possible whose phenotypic effect exceeds a predefined threshold. Pure exploration strategies are statistically inefficient, wasting budget on low-value regions. Bayesian optimization methods offer a principled alternative but target a single global optimum, over-exploiting dominant modes while neglecting other high-value regions. We formalize hit discovery as a sequential experimental design problem and propose Probability-of-Hit, an acquisition function that directly targets threshold exceedance by ranking candidates according to their posterior probability of being a hit. We prove asymptotic optimality of this approach and demonstrate strong empirical performance on both synthetic benchmarks and real biological immunology datasets, including upto 6.4% improvement over baselines on the Schmidt IL-2 dataset.

paragraphs: Gene perturbation experiments can evaluate multiple interventions together, but their budgets remain limited. This paper focuses on finding as many interventions as possible whose effects exceed a chosen threshold. That objective gives value to every newly discovered hit, making the allocation of experiments across promising regions an important part of the problem.

The authors formulate hit discovery as sequential experimental design and propose Probability-of-Hit as the rule for choosing candidates. It ranks each candidate by its posterior probability of exceeding the threshold. This directly aligns experimental selection with the desired outcome. The motivation is that broad exploration can spend resources on low-value regions, while optimization for one global best result can overlook other regions containing useful hits.

The paper proves asymptotic optimality of the proposed approach and evaluates it on synthetic benchmarks and real immunology datasets. Reported gains include up to 6.4% over baselines on the Schmidt IL-2 dataset. The theoretical statement concerns asymptotic behavior, while the experiments provide evidence of useful hit discovery under the evaluated conditions.
summary.tldr: Probability-of-Hit selects experiments by their chance of exceeding a target threshold, aiming to discover many useful perturbations.

title: Many Needles in a Haystack: Active Hit Discovery for Perturbation Experiments

abstract: Inference-time LLM alignment methods, particularly activation steering, offer an alternative to fine-tuning by directly modifying activations during generation. Existing methods, however, often rely on non-anticipative interventions that ignore how perturbations propagate through transformer layers and lack online error feedback, resulting in suboptimal, open-loop control. To address this, we show empirically that layer-wise dynamics across multiple LLM architectures and scales are well-approximated by locally-linear models, despite the nonlinear structure of transformer blocks. Exploiting this property, we model LLM inference as a linear time-varying dynamical system and adapt the classical linear quadratic regulator to compute feedback controllers using layer-wise Jacobians, steering activations toward desired semantic setpoints in closed-loop with minimal computational overhead and no offline training. We also derive theoretical bounds on setpoint tracking error, enabling formal guarantees on steering performance. Using a novel adaptive semantic feature setpoint signal, our method yields robust, fine-grained behavior control across models, scales, and tasks, including state-of-the-art modulation of toxicity, truthfulness, refusal, and arbitrary concepts, surpassing baseline steering methods.

This paper approaches steering as a feedback-control problem, using a model of how activations evolve.

The key connection is between the observed local linearity and a controller that can anticipate propagation and respond to error, giving steering both an explicit dynamical model and feedback.
summary.tldr: Empirical local linearity enables feedback controllers that steer language-model activations toward semantic targets without offline training.

title: Local Linearity of LLMs Enables Activation Steering via Model-Based Linear Optimal Control

abstract: We present Move-Then-Operate, a Vision–language–action framework that explicitly decouples robotic manipulation into two distinct behavioral phases: coarse relocation (move) and contact-critical interaction (operate). Unlike monolithic policies that conflate these heterogeneous regimes, our architecture employs a dual-expert policy routed by a learnable phase selector, introducing a structural inductive bias that isolates phase-specific dynamics. Phase labels are automatically generated via an MLLM-based pipeline conditioned on lightweight contextual cues such as end-effector velocity and subtask decomposition to ensure alignment with human motor patterns. Evaluated on the RoboTwin2 benchmark, our method achieves an average success rate of $68.9%$, outperforming the monolithic $\pi_0$ baseline by +$24%$. It matches or exceeds models trained on $10\times$ more data and reaches peak performance in $40%$ fewer training steps, demonstrating that architectural disentanglement of move and operate phases is a highly effective and efficient strategy for mastering high-precision manipulation.

paragraphs: Robotic manipulation combines broad movements with precise interactions where contact matters. Move-Then-Operate builds this distinction into a vision–language–action model. It separates coarse relocation from contact-critical operation so that the policy can learn the different dynamics associated with each phase of a manipulation task.

The architecture uses two experts and a learned selector that routes behavior between them. Training phase labels are generated automatically through a multimodal language-model pipeline using lightweight context, including end-effector velocity and subtask decomposition. This provides supervision intended to align the split with human motor patterns without treating the entire task as one undifferentiated behavior.

On RoboTwin2, the method achieves 68.9% average success and reports a +24% improvement over the monolithic π₀ baseline. It also matches or exceeds models trained on ten times more data and reaches peak performance in 40% fewer training steps. These results support phase-specific specialization as an effective architectural choice for efficient, high-precision manipulation in the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: Move-Then-Operate separates relocation and precise interaction into two learned experts, improving robotic manipulation success and training efficiency.

title: Move-Then-Operate: Behavioral Phasing for Human-Like Robotic Manipulation

abstract: Foundation models have driven rapid progress in computer vision, yet the two dominant paradigms, vision-language foundation models (VLMs) and vision-only foundation models (VFMs), remain only partially compatible. VLMs offer language-grounded semantic alignment but are often visually coarse, while VFMs learn discriminative perceptual geometry but lack semantic grounding. We propose GPUA, a Geometry-Preserving Unsupervised Alignment framework that integrates the complementary strengths of VFMs and VLMs. Inspired by cross-lingual alignment, GPUA treats VFM features as a visual language and learns an orthogonal mapping that translates the VFM space into the VLM semantic space, preserving geometry and narrowing the modality gap without labels or model parameter updates. GPUA is task-agnostic and requires only feature-level access to pretrained models. Experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate improved cross-model compatibility and strong gains in downstream zero-shot recognition and segmentation with negligible overhead. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Yuteam14/GPUA.

paragraphs: Vision-language and vision-only foundation models offer complementary representations. The former connect images to language-based meaning but can represent visual detail coarsely. The latter capture discriminative visual relationships but lack that semantic connection. GPUA addresses the partial incompatibility between their feature spaces so these strengths can work together.

The framework treats vision-only features as a visual language and learns an orthogonal mapping into the vision-language model's semantic space. Orthogonality preserves the geometry of the original features during alignment, retaining their visual relationships while narrowing the modality gap. The mapping is learned without labels or updates to the pretrained models themselves, and the method needs only access to their features.

Experiments across diverse benchmarks show better compatibility between models and strong improvements in zero-shot recognition and segmentation with negligible overhead. The framework is also task-agnostic, so its alignment is not defined around a single downstream application. The findings support feature-space translation as a practical route for combining perceptual structure with language-grounded semantics.
summary.tldr: GPUA aligns vision-only features with language-grounded features through a geometry-preserving mapping, improving zero-shot recognition and segmentation without updating pretrained models.

title: Geometry-Preserving Unsupervised Alignment for Heterogeneous Foundation Models

abstract: Precise camera pose control is critical for video diffusion, yet maintaining geometric consistency remains a challenge. Existing methods that directly inject numerical camera parameters into the diffusion backbone often fail to bridge the gap between abstract coordinates and visual content, leading to structural distortions. To address this issue, we propose CameraNoise, a flow-to-noise warping method that encodes camera motion into a temporally coherent stochastic representation. Unlike conventional conditioning, CameraNoise embeds camera poses directly into the noise space. This decouples motion from scene appearance while faithfully preserving trajectory dynamics. Specifically, we introduce a novel Geometry-guided Reprojection Flow and a noise warping algorithm, which jointly preserve the Gaussian prior of diffusion and ensure consistent noise propagation under camera transformations. By integrating CameraNoise into the diffusion process, our framework delivers stable, high-fidelity videos. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms prior methods in both visual quality and trajectory faithfulness.

paragraphs: Controlling a generated video's camera requires translating a requested trajectory into consistent changes in visible geometry. The paper identifies a weakness in methods that feed numerical camera parameters directly into a diffusion model: those coordinates can be poorly connected to image content, producing structural distortions. CameraNoise changes where camera information enters the generation process.

The method encodes camera poses in the noise used by diffusion. A geometry-guided reprojection flow describes how content should move under camera transformations, and a noise-warping algorithm carries that movement into a temporally coherent random representation. The two components preserve the Gaussian prior expected by diffusion while maintaining consistent noise propagation across camera changes.

This design separates motion control from scene appearance while preserving the dynamics of the requested trajectory. The authors report stable, high-fidelity videos and significant experimental improvements over prior methods in visual quality and trajectory faithfulness. The contribution is a geometrically structured noise representation that connects camera movement more directly to the visual generation process.
summary.tldr: CameraNoise encodes camera motion through geometry-guided noise warping to improve generated videos' visual quality and trajectory faithfulness.

title: CameraNoise: Enabling Faithful Camera Control in Video Diffusion through Geometry-Flow-Guided Noise Warping

abstract: Counterfactual explanations (CFs) help understand machine learning models by identifying minimal input changes that would lead to alternative model outcomes. Recent work demonstrates their utility for reconstructing black-box models, enabling third-party auditing of opaque decision systems for fairness and accountability. Still, CF-based reconstruction may suffer from decision boundary shifts, overfitting, and restrictive assumptions requiring online query access to target platforms. We propose REconstruction via Counterfactual-Aware waSserstein opTimization (RECAST) under limited data and restricted access, a behavioral surrogate model based on Wasserstein barycenteric prototypes. Our approach addresses decision boundary shifts by incorporating CFs as informative, though less representative, samples for both classes, maintaining high surrogate fidelity in low-sample regimes without requiring online access during reconstruction. To enhance fairness auditing, our method enables systematic group fairness diagnostics. Experiments on real-world datasets and various setups show that RECAST effectively achieves high fidelity and query efficiency, as well as stable results even when the access is limited and noisy.

We propose REconstruction via Counterfactual-Aware waSserstein opTimization (RECAST) under limited data and restricted access, a behavioral surrogate model based on Wasserstein barycenteric prototypes. paragraphs: Counterfactual explanations identify small input changes that would alter a model's decision. They can also help build a surrogate that reproduces an opaque model's behavior for auditing. However, reconstruction from these examples can suffer from shifted decision boundaries and overfitting, and some methods require ongoing access to the target system.

RECAST builds a behavioral surrogate from limited data using Wasserstein barycentric prototypes. It incorporates counterfactuals as informative but less representative samples for both classes. This treatment addresses decision-boundary shifts without treating counterfactual examples as fully representative observations. Reconstruction does not require online access to the target platform during that stage.

The method also supports systematic group fairness diagnostics, connecting behavioral reconstruction to auditing needs. Experiments on real-world datasets and different setups report high fidelity, query efficiency, and stable results under limited and noisy access. The findings support using available counterfactual information carefully when direct access is restricted, while preserving enough of the target model's behavior to support structured examination.
summary.tldr: RECAST uses counterfactual-aware Wasserstein prototypes to reconstruct black-box behavior from limited data without online access during reconstruction.

title: RECAST: Model Reconstruction via Counterfactual-Aware Wasserstein Geometry under Limited Data

abstract: Although semi-supervised learning has been an active area of research, its use in deployed applications is still relatively rare because the methods are often difficult to implement, fragile in tuning, or lacking in scalability. This paper presents expectation regularization, a semi-supervised learning method for exponential family parametric models that augments the traditional conditional label-likelihood objective function with an additional term that encourages model predictions on unlabeled data to match certain expectations—such as label priors. The method is extremely easy to implement, scales as well as logistic regression, and can handle non-independent features. We present experiments on five different data sets, showing accuracy improvements over other semi-supervised methods.
