This paper presents expectation regularization, a semi-supervised learning method for exponential family parametric models that augments the traditional conditional label-likelihood objective function with an additional term that encourages model predictions on unlabeled data to match certain expectations—such as label priors. The method is extremely easy to implement, scales as well as logistic regression, and can handle non-independent features. We present experiments on five different data sets, showing accuracy improvements over other semi-supervised methods.

paragraphs: Expectation regularization is a semi-supervised method designed to make unlabeled data useful within exponential-family parametric models. The paper is motivated by practical obstacles to deploying semi-supervised learning, including difficult implementation, fragile tuning, and limited scalability. It introduces an additional training signal that can be combined with the usual labeled-data objective.

Specifically, the method augments conditional label likelihood with a term encouraging predictions on unlabeled examples to match specified expectations. Label priors are one example of such expectations. This lets information about expected predictions influence learning even when individual examples do not have labels, alongside the direct supervision available from labeled data.

The authors describe the method as very easy to implement, report scalability comparable to logistic regression, and state that it can handle non-independent features. Experiments on five datasets show accuracy improvements over other semi-supervised methods. These results support a practical way to incorporate expectations into training, connecting a simple objective modification with gains in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Expectation regularization uses expected predictions on unlabeled data to improve semi-supervised learning while retaining logistic-regression-like scalability.

title: Simple, robust, scalable semi-supervised learning via expectation regularization

abstract: We present a generalized version of spectral clustering using the graph p-Laplacian, a nonlinear generalization of the standard graph Laplacian. We show that the second eigenvector of the graph p-Laplacian interpolates between a relaxation of the normalized and the Cheeger cut. Moreover, we prove that in the limit as p tends towards one the cut found by thresholding the second eigenvector of the graph p-Laplacian converges to the optimal Cheeger cut. Furthermore, we provide an efficient numerical scheme to compute the second eigenvector of the graph p- Laplacian. The experiments show that the clustering found by p-spectral clustering is at least as good as normal spectral clustering, but often leads to signi cantly better results.

We show that the second eigenvector of the graph p-Laplacian interpolates between a relaxation of the normalized and the Cheeger cut. Moreover, we prove that in the limit as p tends towards one the cut found by thresholding the second eigenvector of the graph p-Laplacian converges to the optimal Cheeger cut. Furthermore, we provide an efficient numerical scheme to compute the second eigenvector of the graph p- Laplacian. The experiments show that the clustering found by p-spectral clustering is at least as good as normal spectral clustering, but often leads to signi cantly better results.

paragraphs: This paper generalizes spectral clustering through the graph p-Laplacian, a nonlinear extension of the standard graph Laplacian. The parameter p changes the mathematical object used to derive a clustering. The authors investigate how this extension connects spectral methods to graph-cut objectives, giving the parameter a theoretical interpretation.

They show that the second eigenvector interpolates between a relaxation of the normalized cut and the Cheeger cut. More strongly, as p approaches one, thresholding that eigenvector produces a cut that converges to the optimal Cheeger cut. This is a limiting result tied to p approaching one, rather than a statement that every parameter choice immediately yields the optimal cut.

The paper also supplies an efficient numerical scheme for computing the second eigenvector. In the reported experiments, p-spectral clustering performs at least as well as ordinary spectral clustering and often significantly better. The work combines a theoretical connection to cut optimality with a computational method and empirical evidence that the generalized formulation can improve clustering.
summary.tldr: Graph p-Laplacian clustering connects spectral methods to optimal Cheeger cuts in a limit and often improves experimental clustering results.

title: Spectral clustering based on the graph p-Laplacian

abstract: We consider Markov decision processes under parameter uncertainty. Previous studies all restrict to the case that uncertainties among different states are uncoupled, which leads to conservative solutions. In contrast, we introduce an intuitive concept, termed 'Lightning Does not Strike Twice,' to model coupled uncertain parameters. Specifically, we require that the system can deviate from its nominal parameters only a bounded number of times. We give probabilistic guarantees indicating that this model represents real life situations and devise tractable algorithms for computing optimal control policies using this concept.
originalAbstract: We consider Markov decision processes under parameter uncertainty. Previous studies all restrict to the case that uncertainties among different states are uncoupled, which leads to conservative solutions. In contrast, we introduce an intuitive concept, termed 'Lightning Does not Strike Twice,' to model coupled uncertain parameters. Specifically, we require that the system can deviate from its nominal parameters only a bounded number of times. We give probabilistic guarantees indicating that this model represents real life situations and devise tractable algorithms for computing optimal control policies using this concept.

paragraphs: A Markov decision process can be difficult to control when its parameters are uncertain. The paper argues that treating uncertainty at different states as uncoupled leads to conservative solutions. Such a treatment does not connect the uncertain behavior encountered at one state with what can happen elsewhere in the decision process.

The proposed alternative couples uncertainty by limiting how many times the system may deviate from its nominal parameters. This is the precise modeling idea behind the title's lightning metaphor. The restriction places a shared bound on deviations, allowing the control problem to represent uncertainty that is constrained across the process rather than handled independently at each state.

The authors provide probabilistic guarantees supporting the model's relevance to real-life situations and develop tractable algorithms for computing optimal control policies within it. The resulting policies are optimal for this bounded-deviation formulation. The contribution combines a different representation of parameter uncertainty with algorithms that make the representation computationally usable.
summary.tldr: Bounding the number of parameter deviations couples uncertainty across an MDP and enables tractable optimal-policy computation.

title: Lightning Does Not Strike Twice: Robust MDPs with Coupled Uncertainty

abstract: AdaBoost has proved to be an effective method to improve the performance of base classifiers both theoretically and empirically. However, previous studies have shown that AdaBoost might suffer from the overfitting problem, especially for noisy data. In addition, most current work on boosting assumes that the combination weights are fixed constants and therefore does not take particular input patterns into consideration. In this paper, we present a new boosting algorithm, “WeightBoost”, which tries to solve these two problems by introducing an input-dependent regularization factor to the combination weight. Similarly to AdaBoost, we derive a learning procedure for WeightBoost, which is guaranteed to minimize training errors. Empirical studies on eight different UCI data sets and one text categorization data set show that WeightBoost almost always achieves a considerably better classification accuracy than AdaBoost. Furthermore, experiments on data with artificially controlled noise indicate that the WeightBoost is more robust to noise than AdaBoost.
originalAbstract: AdaBoost has proved to be an effective method to improve the performance of base classifiers both theoretically and empirically. However, previous studies have shown that AdaBoost might suffer from the overfitting problem, especially for noisy data. In addition, most current work on boosting assumes that the combination weights are fixed constants and therefore does not take particular input patterns into consideration. In this paper, we present a new boosting algorithm, “WeightBoost”, which tries to solve these two problems by introducing an input-dependent regularization factor to the combination weight. Similarly to AdaBoost, we derive a learning procedure for WeightBoost, which is guaranteed to minimize training errors. Empirical studies on eight different UCI data sets and one text categorization data set show that WeightBoost almost always achieves a considerably better classification accuracy than AdaBoost. Furthermore, experiments on data with artificially controlled noise indicate that the WeightBoost is more robust to noise than AdaBoost.

paragraphs: Boosting improves classification by combining base classifiers. This paper addresses two concerns about AdaBoost and existing boosting approaches: AdaBoost can overfit, particularly when data contain noise, and fixed combination weights do not account for the particular input being classified. The authors ask whether changing how classifier contributions are weighted can help address both concerns.

Their algorithm, WeightBoost, introduces a regularization factor that depends on the input into the combination weight. This makes the weighting responsive to the input pattern while adding regularization intended to address overfitting. The authors also derive a learning procedure, analogous to AdaBoost’s, with a guarantee of minimizing training errors. That guarantee concerns performance on training data; the paper separately evaluates classification accuracy and noise robustness through experiments.

Across eight UCI datasets and one text categorization dataset, WeightBoost achieves considerably higher classification accuracy than AdaBoost in almost all of the reported comparisons. Experiments that artificially control the amount of noise also indicate greater robustness than AdaBoost. Together, these findings support input-dependent regularization as a promising way to improve boosting’s accuracy and handling of noise, with the reported advantage being empirical and nearly, rather than entirely, consistent across the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: WeightBoost adds input-dependent regularization to classifier combination weights, achieving better accuracy than AdaBoost in almost all reported dataset comparisons and showing greater noise robustness experimentally.

title: A New Boosting Algorithm Using Input-Dependent Regularizer
